Sections from madaidan's guide that are IRRELEVANT/NON-APPLICABLE:
Sections from madaidan's guide requiring manual user intervention:
Options omitted due to already being used by default on NixOS:

documents.title: Option: appstream.enable
documents.content: Whether to install files to support the AppStream metadata specification.

documents.title: Option: boot.bcache.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable bcache mount support.

documents.title: Option: boot.bcachefs.package
documents.content: The bcachefs-tools package to use. This package should also provide a passthru 'kernelModule' attribute to build the out-of-tree kernel module.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.addEmulatedSystemsToNixSandbox
documents.content: Whether to add the {option}boot.binfmt.emulatedSystems to {option}nix.settings.extra-platforms. Disable this to use remote builders for those platforms, while allowing testing binaries locally.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.emulatedSystems
documents.content: List of systems to emulate. Will also configure Nix to support your new systems. Warning: the builder can execute all emulated systems within the same build, which introduces impurities in the case of cross compilation.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.preferStaticEmulators
documents.content:
Whether to use static emulators when available.
This enables the kernel to preload the emulator binaries when the binfmt registrations are added, obviating the need to make the emulator binaries available inside chroots and chroot-like sandboxes.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations
documents.content: Extra binary formats to register with the kernel. See https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/binfmt-misc.html for more details.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.fixBinary
documents.content:
Whether to open the interpreter file as soon as the registration is loaded, rather than waiting for a relevant file to be invoked.
See the description of the 'F' flag in the kernel docs for more details.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.interpreter
documents.content:
The interpreter to invoke to run the program.
Note that the actual registration will point to /run/binfmt/${name}, so the kernel interpreter length limit doesn't apply.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.magicOrExtension
documents.content: The magic number or extension to match on.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.mask
documents.content: A mask to be ANDed with the byte sequence of the file before matching

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.matchCredentials
documents.content:
Whether to launch with the credentials and security token of the binary, not the interpreter (e.g. setuid bit).
See the description of the 'C' flag in the kernel docs for more details.
Implies/requires openBinary = true.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.offset
documents.content: The byte offset of the magic number used for recognition.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.openBinary
documents.content: Whether to pass the binary to the interpreter as an open file descriptor, instead of a path.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.preserveArgvZero
documents.content:
Whether to pass the original argv[0] to the interpreter.
See the description of the 'P' flag in the kernel docs for more details;

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.recognitionType
documents.content: Whether to recognize executables by magic number or extension.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.wrapInterpreterInShell
documents.content:
Whether to wrap the interpreter in a shell script.
This allows a shell command to be set as the interpreter.

documents.title: Option: boot.blacklistedKernelModules
documents.content: Set of names of kernel modules that should not be loaded automatically by the hardware probing code. This can either be a list of modules or an attrset. In an attrset, names that are set to true represent modules that will be blacklisted.

documents.title: Option: boot.bootspec.enableValidation
documents.content: Whether to enable the validation of bootspec documents for each build. This will introduce Go in the build-time closure as we are relying on Cuelang for schema validation. Enable this option if you want to ascertain that your documents are correct .

documents.title: Option: boot.bootspec.extensions
documents.content:
User-defined data that extends the bootspec document.
To reduce incompatibility and prevent names from clashing between applications, it is highly recommended to use a unique namespace for your extensions.

documents.title: Option: boot.bootspec.package
documents.content: The bootspec package to use.

documents.title: Option: boot.consoleLogLevel
documents.content: The kernel console loglevel. All Kernel Messages with a log level smaller than this setting will be printed to the console.

documents.title: Option: boot.crashDump.enable
documents.content: If enabled, NixOS will set up a kernel that will boot on crash, and leave the user in systemd rescue to be able to save the crashed kernel dump at /proc/vmcore. It also activates the NMI watchdog.

documents.title: Option: boot.crashDump.kernelParams
documents.content: Parameters that will be passed to the kernel kexec-ed on crash.

documents.title: Option: boot.crashDump.reservedMemory
documents.content: The amount of memory reserved for the crashdump kernel. If you choose a too high value, dmesg will mention "crashkernel reservation failed".

documents.title: Option: boot.devShmSize
documents.content: Size limit for the /dev/shm tmpfs. Look at {manpage}mount(8), tmpfs size option, for the accepted syntax.

documents.title: Option: boot.devSize
documents.content: Size limit for the /dev tmpfs. Look at {manpage}mount(8), tmpfs size option, for the accepted syntax.

documents.title: Option: boot.enableContainers
documents.content: Whether to enable support for NixOS containers.

documents.title: Option: boot.extraModprobeConfig
documents.content: Any additional configuration to be appended to the generated {file}modprobe.conf. This is typically used to specify module options. See {manpage}modprobe.d(5) for details.

documents.title: Option: boot.extraModulePackages
documents.content: A list of additional packages supplying kernel modules.

documents.title: Option: boot.extraSystemdUnitPaths
documents.content: Additional paths that get appended to the SYSTEMD_UNIT_PATH environment variable that can contain mutable unit files.

documents.title: Option: boot.growPartition
documents.content: Whether to enable growing the root partition on boot.

documents.title: Option: boot.hardwareScan
documents.content: Whether to try to load kernel modules for all detected hardware. Usually this does a good job of providing you with the modules you need, but sometimes it can crash the system or cause other nasty effects.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.allowMissingModules
documents.content:
Whether the initrd can be built even though modules listed in {option}boot.initrd.kernelModules or {option}boot.initrd.availableKernelModules are missing from the kernel. This is useful when combining configurations that include a lot of modules, such as {option}hardware.enableAllHardware, with kernels that don't provide as many modules as typical NixOS kernels.
Note that enabling this is discouraged. Instead, try disabling individual modules by setting e.g. boot.initrd.availableKernelModules.foo = lib.mkForce false;

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.availableKernelModules
documents.content:
The set of kernel modules in the initial ramdisk used during the boot process. This set must include all modules necessary for mounting the root device. That is, it should include modules for the physical device (e.g., SCSI drivers) and for the file system (e.g., ext3). The set specified here is automatically closed under the module dependency relation, i.e., all dependencies of the modules list here are included automatically. The modules listed here are available in the initrd, but are only loaded on demand (e.g., the ext3 module is loaded automatically when an ext3 filesystem is mounted, and modules for PCI devices are loaded when they match the PCI ID of a device in your system). To force a module to be loaded, include it in {option}boot.initrd.kernelModules.
This can either be a list of modules, or an attrset. In an attrset, names that are set to true represent modules that will be included. Note that setting these names to false does not prevent the module from being loaded. For that, use {option}boot.blacklistedKernelModules.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.checkJournalingFS
documents.content: Whether to run {command}fsck on journaling filesystems such as ext3.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.clevis.devices
documents.content: Encrypted devices that need to be unlocked at boot using Clevis

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.clevis.devices.<name>.secretFile
documents.content: Clevis JWE file used to decrypt the device at boot, in concert with the chosen pin (one of TPM2, Tang server, or SSS).

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.clevis.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Clevis in initrd.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.clevis.package
documents.content: The clevis package to use.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.clevis.useTang
documents.content: Whether the Clevis JWE file used to decrypt the devices uses a Tang server as a pin.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.clevisLuksAskpass.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable clevis-luks-askpass in initrd.
Watches for systemd password requests during boot and answers them using clevis tokens bound to LUKS headers. Runs in parallel with the interactive password prompt. If clevis cannot unlock a device (tang unreachable, no binding, etc.) the user can still type the passphrase.
Prerequisites:
Bind clevis to each LUKS device: clevis luks bind -d /dev/xxx tang '{"url":"..."}'
Configure networking in the initrd so tang servers are reachable .

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.clevisLuksAskpass.package
documents.content: The clevis package to use.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.clevisLuksAskpass.useTang
documents.content: Whether the Clevis headers used to decrypt the devices uses a Tang server as a pin.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.compressor
documents.content:
The compressor to use on the initrd image. May be any of:
The name of one of the predefined compressors, see {file}pkgs/build-support/kernel/initrd-compressor-meta.nix for the definitions.
A function which, given the nixpkgs package set, returns the path to a compressor tool, e.g. pkgs: "${pkgs.pigz}/bin/pigz"
(not recommended, because it does not work when cross-compiling) the full path to a compressor tool, e.g. "${pkgs.pigz}/bin/pigz"

The given program should read data from stdin and write it to stdout compressed.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.compressorArgs
documents.content: Arguments to pass to the compressor for the initrd image, or null to use the compressor's defaults.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the NixOS initial RAM disk (initrd). This may be needed to perform some initialisation tasks (like mounting network/encrypted file systems) before continuing the boot process.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.extraFiles
documents.content: Extra files to link and copy in to the initrd.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.extraFiles.<name>.source
documents.content: The object to make available inside the initrd.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.extraFirmwarePaths
documents.content: Other firmware files (relative to "${config.hardware.firmware}/lib/firmware") to include in the final initrd we are building.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.includeDefaultModules
documents.content: This option, if set, adds a collection of default kernel modules to {option}boot.initrd.availableKernelModules and {option}boot.initrd.kernelModules.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.kernelModules
documents.content:
Set of modules that are always loaded by the initrd.
This can either be a list of modules, or an attrset. In an attrset, names that are set to true represent modules that will be included. Note that setting these names to false does not prevent the module from being loaded. For that, use {option}boot.blacklistedKernelModules.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.cryptoModules
documents.content: A list of cryptographic kernel modules needed to decrypt the root device(s). The default includes all common modules.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices
documents.content: The encrypted disk that should be opened before the root filesystem is mounted. Both LVM-over-LUKS and LUKS-over-LVM setups are supported. The unencrypted devices can be accessed as {file}/dev/mapper/«name».

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.allowDiscards
documents.content: Whether to allow TRIM requests to the underlying device. This option has security implications; please read the LUKS documentation before activating it. This option is incompatible with authenticated encryption (dm-crypt stacked over dm-integrity).

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.bypassWorkqueues
documents.content: Whether to bypass dm-crypt's internal read and write workqueues. Enabling this should improve performance on SSDs; see here for more information. Needs Linux 5.9 or later.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.crypttabExtraOpts
documents.content:
Only used with systemd stage 1.
Extra options to append to the last column of the generated crypttab file.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.device
documents.content: Path of the underlying encrypted block device.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.fallbackToPassword
documents.content: Whether to fallback to interactive passphrase prompt if the keyfile cannot be found. This will prevent unattended boot should the keyfile go missing.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.fido2.credential
documents.content: The FIDO2 credential ID.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.fido2.credentials
documents.content:
List of FIDO2 credential IDs.
Use this if you have multiple FIDO2 keys you want to use for the same luks device.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.fido2.gracePeriod
documents.content: Time in seconds to wait for the FIDO2 key.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.fido2.passwordLess
documents.content:
Defines whatever to use an empty string as a default salt.
Enable only when your device is PIN protected, such as Trezor.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.gpgCard
documents.content: The option to use this LUKS device with a GPG encrypted luks password by the GPG Smartcard. If null (the default), GPG-Smartcard will be disabled for this device.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.gpgCard.encryptedPass
documents.content: Path to the GPG encrypted passphrase.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.gpgCard.gracePeriod
documents.content: Time in seconds to wait for the GPG Smartcard.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.gpgCard.publicKey
documents.content: Path to the Public Key.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.header
documents.content: The name of the file or block device that should be used as header for the encrypted device.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.keyFile
documents.content: The name of the file (can be a raw device or a partition) that should be used as the decryption key for the encrypted device. If not specified, you will be prompted for a passphrase instead.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.keyFileOffset
documents.content: The offset of the key file. Use this in combination with keyFileSize to use part of a file as key file (often the case if a raw device or partition is used as a key file). If not specified, the key begins at the first byte of keyFile.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.keyFileSize
documents.content: The size of the key file. Use this if only the beginning of the key file should be used as a key (often the case if a raw device or partition is used as key file). If not specified, the whole keyFile will be used decryption, instead of just the first keyFileSize bytes.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.keyFileTimeout
documents.content: The amount of time in seconds for a keyFile to appear before timing out and trying passwords.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.postOpenCommands
documents.content: Commands that should be run right after we have mounted our LUKS device.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.preLVM
documents.content: Whether the luksOpen will be attempted before LVM scan or after it.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.preOpenCommands
documents.content: Commands that should be run right before we try to mount our LUKS device. This can be useful, if the keys needed to open the drive is on another partition.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.tryEmptyPassphrase
documents.content: If keyFile fails then try an empty passphrase first before prompting for password.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.yubikey
documents.content: The options to use for this LUKS device in YubiKey-PBA. If null (the default), YubiKey-PBA will be disabled for this device.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.yubikey.gracePeriod
documents.content: Time in seconds to wait for the YubiKey.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.yubikey.iterationStep
documents.content: How much the iteration count for PBKDF2 is increased at each successful authentication.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.yubikey.keyLength
documents.content: Length of the LUKS slot key derived with PBKDF2 in byte.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.yubikey.saltLength
documents.content: Length of the new salt in byte (64 is the effective maximum).

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.yubikey.slot
documents.content: Which slot on the YubiKey to challenge.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.yubikey.storage.device
documents.content: An unencrypted device that will temporarily be mounted in stage-1. Must contain the current salt to create the challenge for this LUKS device.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.yubikey.storage.fsType
documents.content: The filesystem of the unencrypted device.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.yubikey.storage.path
documents.content: Absolute path of the salt on the unencrypted device with that device's root directory as "/".

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.devices.<name>.yubikey.twoFactor
documents.content: Whether to use a passphrase and a YubiKey (true), or only a YubiKey (false).

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.fido2Support
documents.content: Enables support for authenticating with FIDO2 devices.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.gpgSupport
documents.content: Enables support for authenticating with a GPG encrypted password.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.mitigateDMAAttacks
documents.content:
Unless enabled, encryption keys can be easily recovered by an attacker with physical access to any machine with PCMCIA, ExpressCard, ThunderBolt or FireWire port. More information is available at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DMA_attack.
This option blacklists FireWire drivers, but doesn't remove them. You can manually load the drivers if you need to use a FireWire device, but don't forget to unload them!

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.reusePassphrases
documents.content:
When opening a new LUKS device try reusing last successful passphrase.
Useful for mounting a number of devices that use the same passphrase without retyping it several times.
Such setup can be useful if you use {command}cryptsetup luksSuspend. Different LUKS devices will still have different master keys even when using the same passphrase.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.luks.yubikeySupport
documents.content: Enables support for authenticating with a YubiKey on LUKS devices. See the NixOS wiki for information on how to properly setup a LUKS device and a YubiKey to work with this feature.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.enable
documents.content:
Add network connectivity support to initrd. The network may be configured using the ip kernel parameter, as described in the kernel documentation. Otherwise, if {option}networking.useDHCP is enabled, an IP address is acquired using DHCP.
You should add the module(s) required for your network card to boot.initrd.availableKernelModules. lspci -v | grep -iA8 'network\|ethernet' will tell you which.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.flushBeforeStage2
documents.content:
Whether to clear the configuration of the interfaces that were set up in the initrd right before stage 2 takes over. Stage 2 will do the regular network configuration based on the NixOS networking options.
The default is false when systemd is enabled in initrd, because the systemd-networkd documentation suggests it.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ifstate.allowIfstateToDrasticlyIncreaseInitrdSize
documents.content: IfState in initrd drastically increases the size of initrd, your boot partition may be too small and/or you may have significantly fewer generations. By setting this option, you acknowledge this fact and keep it in mind when reporting issues.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ifstate.cleanupSettings
documents.content: Content of IfState's initrd cleanup configuration file. See https://ifstate.net/2.0/schema/ for details. This configuration gets applied before systemd switches to stage two. The goal is to deconfigurate the whole network in order to prevent access to services, before the firewall is configured. The stage two IfState configuration will start after the firewall is configured.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ifstate.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable initrd networking using IfState.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ifstate.package
documents.content: The initrd IfState package to use.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ifstate.settings
documents.content: Content of IfState's initrd configuration file. See https://ifstate.net/2.2/schema/ for details.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.openvpn.configuration
documents.content:
The configuration file for OpenVPN.
::: {.warning} Unless your bootloader supports initrd secrets, this configuration is stored insecurely in the global Nix store. :::

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.openvpn.enable
documents.content: Starts an OpenVPN client during initrd boot. It can be used to e.g. remotely accessing the SSH service controlled by {option}boot.initrd.network.ssh or other network services included. Service is killed when stage-1 boot is finished.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.postCommands
documents.content: Shell commands to be executed after stage 1 of the boot has initialised the network.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ssh.authorizedKeyFiles
documents.content: Authorized keys taken from files for the root user on initrd. You can combine the authorizedKeyFiles and authorizedKeys options.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ssh.authorizedKeys
documents.content: Authorized keys for the root user on initrd. You can combine the authorizedKeys and authorizedKeyFiles options.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ssh.enable
documents.content:
Start SSH service during initrd boot. It can be used to debug failing boot on a remote server, enter pasphrase for an encrypted partition etc. Service is killed when stage-1 boot is finished.
The sshd configuration is largely inherited from {option}services.openssh.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ssh.extraConfig
documents.content: Verbatim contents of {file}sshd_config.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ssh.hostKeys
documents.content:
Specify SSH host keys to import into the initrd.
To generate keys, use {manpage}ssh-keygen(1) as root:
::: {.warning} Unless your bootloader supports initrd secrets, these keys are stored insecurely in the global Nix store. Do NOT use your regular SSH host private keys for this purpose or you'll expose them to regular users!
Additionally, even if your initrd supports secrets, if you're using initrd SSH to unlock an encrypted disk then using your regular host keys exposes the private keys on your unencrypted boot partition. :::

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ssh.ignoreEmptyHostKeys
documents.content: Allow leaving {option}config.boot.initrd.network.ssh.hostKeys empty, to deploy ssh host keys out of band.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ssh.port
documents.content: Port on which SSH initrd service should listen.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.ssh.shell
documents.content: Login shell of the remote user. Can be used to limit actions user can do.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.udhcpc.enable
documents.content: Enables the udhcpc service during stage 1 of the boot process. This defaults to {option}networking.useDHCP. Therefore, this useful if useDHCP is off but the initramfs should do dhcp.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.network.udhcpc.extraArgs
documents.content: Additional command-line arguments passed verbatim to udhcpc if {option}boot.initrd.network.enable and {option}boot.initrd.network.udhcpc.enable are enabled.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.nix-store-veritysetup.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable nix-store-veritysetup.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.postDeviceCommands
documents.content: Shell commands to be executed immediately after stage 1 of the boot has loaded kernel modules and created device nodes in {file}/dev.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.postMountCommands
documents.content: Shell commands to be executed immediately after the stage 1 filesystems have been mounted.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.postResumeCommands
documents.content: Shell commands to be executed immediately after attempting to resume.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.preDeviceCommands
documents.content: Shell commands to be executed before udev is started to create device nodes.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.preFailCommands
documents.content: Shell commands to be executed before the failure prompt is shown.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.preLVMCommands
documents.content: Shell commands to be executed immediately before LVM discovery.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.prepend
documents.content: Other initrd files to prepend to the final initrd we are building.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.secrets
documents.content:
Secrets to append to the initrd. The attribute name is the path the secret should have inside the initrd, the value is the path it should be copied from (or null for the same path inside and out).
Note that nixos-rebuild switch will generate the initrd also for past generations, so if secrets are moved or deleted you will also have to garbage collect the generations that use those secrets.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.services.bcache.enable
documents.content:
This will only be used when systemd is used in stage 1.
Whether to enable bcache support in the initrd.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.services.lvm.enable
documents.content:
This will only be used when systemd is used in stage 1.
Whether to enable booting from LVM2 in the initrd.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.services.resolved.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable resolved for stage 1 networking. Uses the toplevel 'services.resolved' options for 'resolved.conf'

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.services.udev.binPackages
documents.content:
This will only be used when systemd is used in stage 1.
Packages to search for binaries that are referenced by the udev rules in stage 1. This list always contains /bin of the initrd.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.services.udev.packages
documents.content:
This will only be used when systemd is used in stage 1.
List of packages containing {command}udev rules that will be copied to stage 1. All files found in {file}«pkg»/etc/udev/rules.d and {file}«pkg»/lib/udev/rules.d will be included.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.services.udev.rules
documents.content: {command}udev rules to include in the initrd only. They'll be written into file {file}99-local.rules. Thus they are read and applied after the essential initrd rules.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.stage1Greeting
documents.content: The greeting message displayed during NixOS stage 1 boot.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.supportedFilesystems
documents.content: Names of supported filesystem types, or an attribute set of file system types and their state. The set form may be used together with lib.mkForce to explicitly disable support for specific filesystems, e.g. to disable ZFS with an unsupported kernel.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.additionalUpstreamUnits
documents.content: Additional units shipped with systemd that shall be enabled.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.automounts
documents.content: Definition of systemd automount units. This is a list instead of an attrSet, because systemd mandates the names to be derived from the 'where' attribute.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.contents
documents.content: Set of files that have to be linked into the initrd

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.contents.<name>.dlopen.features
documents.content: Features to enable via dlopen ELF notes. These will be in addition to anything included via 'usePriority', regardless of their priority.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.contents.<name>.dlopen.usePriority
documents.content:
Priority of dlopen ELF notes to include. "required" is minimal, "recommended" includes "required", and "suggested" includes "recommended".
See: https://systemd.io/ELF_DLOPEN_METADATA/

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.contents.<name>.enable

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.dbus.enable

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.dmVerity.enable
documents.content:
Mount verity-protected block devices in the initrd.
Enabling this option allows to use systemd-veritysetup and systemd-veritysetup-generator in the initrd.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.emergencyAccess
documents.content:
Set to true for unauthenticated emergency access, and false or null for no emergency access.
Can also be set to a hashed super user password to allow authenticated access to the emergency mode.
For emergency access after initrd, use systemd.enableEmergencyMode instead.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable systemd in initrd. The unit options such as {option}boot.initrd.systemd.services are the same as their stage 2 counterparts such as {option}systemd.services, except that restartTriggers and reloadTriggers are not supported.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.extraBin
documents.content: Tools to add to /bin

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.fido2.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable systemd FIDO2 support.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.groups
documents.content: Groups to include in initrd.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.groups.<name>.gid
documents.content: ID of the group in initrd.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.initrdBin
documents.content: Packages to include in /bin for the stage 1 emergency shell.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.managerEnvironment
documents.content: Environment variables of PID 1. These variables are not passed to started units.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.mounts
documents.content: Definition of systemd mount units. This is a list instead of an attrSet, because systemd mandates the names to be derived from the 'where' attribute.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.network.config
documents.content: Definition of global systemd network config.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.network.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable networkd or not.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.network.netdevs
documents.content: Definition of systemd network devices.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.network.networks
documents.content: Definition of systemd networks.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.network.wait-online.anyInterface
documents.content:
Whether to consider the network online when any interface is online, as opposed to all of them. This is useful on portable machines with a wired and a wireless interface, for example.
This is on by default if {option}networking.useDHCP is enabled.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.network.wait-online.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable the systemd-networkd-wait-online service.
systemd-networkd-wait-online can timeout and fail if there are no network interfaces available for it to manage. When systemd-networkd is enabled but a different service is responsible for managing the system's internet connection (for example, NetworkManager or connman are used to manage WiFi connections), this service is unnecessary and can be disabled.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.network.wait-online.extraArgs
documents.content:
Extra command-line arguments to pass to systemd-networkd-wait-online. These also affect per-interface systemd-network-wait-online@ services.
See {manpage}systemd-networkd-wait-online.service(8) for all available options.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.network.wait-online.ignoredInterfaces
documents.content: Network interfaces to be ignored when deciding if the system is online.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.network.wait-online.timeout
documents.content: Time to wait for the network to come online, in seconds. Set to 0 to disable.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.package
documents.content: The systemd package to use.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.packages
documents.content: Packages providing systemd units and hooks.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.paths
documents.content: Definition of systemd path units.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.repart.device
documents.content:
The device to operate on.
If device == null, systemd-repart will operate on the device backing the root partition. So in order to dynamically create the root partition in the initrd you need to set a device.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.repart.discard
documents.content:
Controls whether to issue the BLKDISCARD I/O control command on the space taken up by any added partitions or on the space in between them. Usually, it's a good idea to issue this request since it tells the underlying hardware that the covered blocks shall be considered empty, improving performance.
See {manpage}systemd-repart(8) for details.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.repart.empty
documents.content: Controls how to operate on empty devices that contain no partition table yet. See {manpage}systemd-repart(8) for details.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.repart.enable
documents.content:
Grow and add partitions to a partition table at boot time in the initrd. systemd-repart only works with GPT partition tables.
To run systemd-repart after the initrd, see options.systemd.repart.enable.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.repart.extraArgs
documents.content:
Extra command-line arguments to pass to systemd-repart.
See {manpage}systemd-repart(8) for all available options.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.systemd.root
documents.content: Controls how systemd will interpret the root FS in initrd. See {manpage}kernel-command-line(7). NixOS currently does not allow specifying the root file system itself this way. Instead, the fstab value is used in order to interpret the root file system specified with the fileSystems option. If root shall be omitted, set this option to null.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernel.randstructSeed
documents.content: Provides a custom seed for the {var}RANDSTRUCT security option of the Linux kernel. Note that {var}RANDSTRUCT is only enabled in NixOS hardened kernels. Using a custom seed requires building the kernel and dependent packages locally, since this customization happens at build time.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernel.sysctl
documents.content: Runtime parameters of the Linux kernel, as set by {manpage}sysctl(8). Note that sysctl parameters names must be enclosed in quotes (e.g. "vm.swappiness" instead of vm.swappiness). The value of each parameter may be a string, integer, boolean, or null (signifying the option will not appear at all).

documents.title: Option: boot.kernel.sysctl."net.core.rmem_max"
documents.content: The maximum receive socket buffer size in bytes. In case of conflicting values, the highest will be used.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernel.sysctl."net.core.wmem_max"
documents.content: The maximum send socket buffer size in bytes. In case of conflicting values, the highest will be used.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernel.sysfs
documents.content:
sysfs attributes to be set as soon as they become available.
Attribute names represent path components in the sysfs filesystem and cannot be . or .. nor contain any slash character (/).
Names may contain shell‐style glob patterns (*, ? and […]) matching a single path component, these should however be used with caution, as they may produce unexpected results if attribute paths overlap.
Values will be converted to strings, with list elements concatenated with commata and booleans converted to numeric values (0 or 1).
null values are ignored, allowing removal of values defined in other modules, as are empty attribute sets.
List values defined in different modules will not be concatenated.
This option may only be used for attributes which can be set idempotently, as the configured values might be written more than once.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernelModules
documents.content:
The set of kernel modules to be loaded in the second stage of the boot process. Note that modules that are needed to mount the root file system should be added to {option}boot.initrd.availableKernelModules or {option}boot.initrd.kernelModules.
This can either be a list of modules, or an attrset. In an attrset, names that are set to true represent modules that will be included. Note that setting these names to false does not prevent the module from being loaded. For that, use {option}boot.blacklistedKernelModules.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernelPackages
documents.content:
This option allows you to override the Linux kernel used by NixOS. Since things like external kernel module packages are tied to the kernel you're using, it also overrides those. This option is a function that takes Nixpkgs as an argument (as a convenience), and returns an attribute set containing at the very least an attribute {var}kernel. Additional attributes may be needed depending on your configuration. For instance, if you use the NVIDIA X driver, then it also needs to contain an attribute {var}nvidia_x11.
Please note that we strictly support kernel versions that are maintained by the Linux developers only. More information on the availability of kernel versions is documented in the Linux section of the manual.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernelParams
documents.content: Parameters added to the kernel command line.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernelPatches
documents.content:
A list of additional patches to apply to the kernel.
Every item should be an attribute set with the following attributes:
There's a small set of existing kernel patches in Nixpkgs, available as pkgs.kernelPatches, that follow this format and can be used directly.

documents.title: Option: boot.kexec.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable kexec.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.efi.canTouchEfiVariables
documents.content: Whether the installation process is allowed to modify EFI boot variables.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.efi.efiSysMountPoint
documents.content: Where the EFI System Partition is mounted.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.external.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable using an external tool to install your bootloader.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.external.installHook
documents.content:
The full path to a program of your choosing which performs the bootloader installation process.
The program will be called with an argument pointing to the output of the system's toplevel.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.generationsDir.copyKernels
documents.content: Whether to copy the necessary boot files into /boot, so /nix/store is not needed by the boot loader.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.generationsDir.enable
documents.content:
Whether to create symlinks to the system generations under /boot. When enabled, /boot/default/kernel, /boot/default/initrd, etc., are updated to point to the current generation's kernel image, initial RAM disk, and other bootstrap files.
This optional is not necessary with boot loaders such as GNU GRUB for which the menu is updated to point to the latest bootstrap files. However, it is needed for U-Boot on platforms where the boot command line is stored in flash memory rather than in a menu file.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.generic-extlinux-compatible.configurationLimit
documents.content: Maximum number of configurations in the boot menu.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.generic-extlinux-compatible.enable
documents.content:
Whether to generate an extlinux-compatible configuration file under /boot/extlinux.conf. For instance, U-Boot's generic distro boot support uses this file format.
See U-boot's documentation for more information.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.generic-extlinux-compatible.mirroredBoots
documents.content: Mirror the boot configuration to multiple paths.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.generic-extlinux-compatible.mirroredBoots.*.path
documents.content: The path to the boot directory where the extlinux-compatible configuration files will be written.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.generic-extlinux-compatible.populateCmd
documents.content: Contains the builder command used to populate an image, honoring all options except the -c <path-to-default-configuration> argument. Useful to have for sdImage.populateRootCommands

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.generic-extlinux-compatible.useGenerationDeviceTree
documents.content:
Whether to generate Device Tree-related directives in the extlinux configuration.
When enabled, the bootloader will attempt to load the device tree binaries from the generation's kernel.
Note that this affects all generations, regardless of the setting value used in their configurations.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.backgroundColor
documents.content: Background color to be used for GRUB to fill the areas the image isn't filling.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.configurationLimit
documents.content: Maximum of configurations in boot menu. GRUB has problems when there are too many entries.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.configurationName
documents.content: GRUB entry name instead of default.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.copyKernels
documents.content: Whether the GRUB menu builder should copy kernels and initial ramdisks to /boot. This is done automatically if /boot is on a different partition than /.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.default
documents.content: Index of the default menu item to be booted. Can also be set to "saved", which will make GRUB select the menu item that was used at the last boot.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.device
documents.content: The device on which the GRUB boot loader will be installed. The special value nodev means that a GRUB boot menu will be generated, but GRUB itself will not actually be installed. To install GRUB on multiple devices, use boot.loader.grub.devices.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.devices
documents.content: The devices on which the boot loader, GRUB, will be installed. Can be used instead of device to install GRUB onto multiple devices.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.efiInstallAsRemovable
documents.content:
Whether to invoke grub-install with --removable.
Unless you turn this on, GRUB will install itself somewhere in boot.loader.efi.efiSysMountPoint (exactly where depends on other config variables). If you've set boot.loader.efi.canTouchEfiVariables AND you are currently booted in UEFI mode, then GRUB will use efibootmgr to modify the boot order in the EFI variables of your firmware to include this location. If you are not booted in UEFI mode at the time GRUB is being installed, the NVRAM will not be modified, and your system will not find GRUB at boot time. However, GRUB will still return success so you may miss the warning that gets printed ("efibootmgr: EFI variables are not supported on this system.").
If you turn this feature on, GRUB will install itself in a special location within efiSysMountPoint (namely EFI/boot/boot$arch.efi) which the firmwares are hardcoded to try first, regardless of NVRAM EFI variables.
To summarize, turn this on if:
You are installing NixOS and want it to boot in UEFI mode, but you are currently booted in legacy mode
You want to make a drive that will boot regardless of the NVRAM state of the computer (like a USB "removable" drive)
You simply dislike the idea of depending on NVRAM state to make your drive bootable

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.efiSupport
documents.content: Whether GRUB should be built with EFI support.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the GNU GRUB boot loader.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.enableCryptodisk
documents.content: Enable support for encrypted partitions. GRUB should automatically unlock the correct encrypted partition and look for filesystems.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.entryOptions
documents.content: Options applied to the primary NixOS menu entry.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.extraConfig
documents.content: Additional GRUB commands inserted in the configuration file just before the menu entries.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.extraEntries
documents.content: Any additional entries you want added to the GRUB boot menu.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.extraEntriesBeforeNixOS
documents.content: Whether extraEntries are included before the default option.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.extraFiles
documents.content: A set of files to be copied to {file}/boot. Each attribute name denotes the destination file name in {file}/boot, while the corresponding attribute value specifies the source file.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.extraGrubInstallArgs
documents.content:
Additional arguments passed to grub-install.
A use case for this is to build specific GRUB2 modules directly into the GRUB2 kernel image, so that they are available and activated even in the grub rescue shell.
They are also necessary when the BIOS/UEFI is bugged and cannot correctly read large disks (e.g. above 2 TB), so GRUB2's own nativedisk and related modules can be used to use its own disk drivers. The example shows one such case. This is also useful for booting from USB. See the GRUB source code for which disk modules are available.
The list elements are passed directly as argv arguments to the grub-install program, in order.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.extraInstallCommands
documents.content: Additional shell commands inserted in the bootloader installer script after generating menu entries.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.extraPerEntryConfig
documents.content: Additional GRUB commands inserted in the configuration file at the start of each NixOS menu entry.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.extraPrepareConfig
documents.content: Additional bash commands to be run at the script that prepares the GRUB menu entries.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.font
documents.content: Path to a TrueType, OpenType, or pf2 font to be used by Grub.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.fontSize
documents.content: Font size for the grub menu. Ignored unless font is set to a ttf or otf font.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.forceInstall
documents.content: Whether to try and forcibly install GRUB even if problems are detected. It is not recommended to enable this unless you know what you are doing.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.forcei686
documents.content: Whether to force the use of a ia32 boot loader on x64 systems. Required to install and run NixOS on 64bit x86 systems with 32bit (U)EFI.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.fsIdentifier
documents.content: Determines how GRUB will identify devices when generating the configuration file. A value of uuid / label signifies that grub will always resolve the uuid or label of the device before using it in the configuration. A value of provided means that GRUB will use the device name as show in {command}df or {command}mount. Note, zfs zpools / datasets are ignored and will always be mounted using their labels.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.gfxmodeBios
documents.content: The gfxmode to pass to GRUB when loading a graphical boot interface under BIOS.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.gfxmodeEfi
documents.content: The gfxmode to pass to GRUB when loading a graphical boot interface under EFI.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.gfxpayloadBios
documents.content: The gfxpayload to pass to GRUB when loading a graphical boot interface under BIOS.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.gfxpayloadEfi
documents.content: The gfxpayload to pass to GRUB when loading a graphical boot interface under EFI.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.ipxe
documents.content: Set of iPXE scripts available for booting from the GRUB boot menu.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.memtest86.enable
documents.content: Make Memtest86+, a memory testing program, available from the GRUB boot menu.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.memtest86.params
documents.content:
Parameters added to the Memtest86+ command line. As of memtest86+ 5.01 the following list of (apparently undocumented) parameters are accepted:
console=..., set up a serial console. Examples: console=ttyS0, console=ttyS0,9600 or console=ttyS0,115200n8.
btrace, enable boot trace.
maxcpus=N, limit number of CPUs.
onepass, run one pass and exit if there are no errors.
tstlist=..., list of tests to run. Example: 0,1,2.
cpumask=..., set a CPU mask, to select CPUs to use for testing.

This list of command line options was obtained by reading the Memtest86+ source code.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.mirroredBoots
documents.content: Mirror the boot configuration to multiple partitions and install grub to the respective devices corresponding to those partitions.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.mirroredBoots.*.devices
documents.content: The path to the devices which will have the GRUB MBR written. Note these are typically device paths and not paths to partitions.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.mirroredBoots.*.efiBootloaderId
documents.content: The id of the bootloader to store in efi nvram. The default is to name it NixOS and append the path or efiSysMountPoint. This is only used if boot.loader.efi.canTouchEfiVariables is true.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.mirroredBoots.*.efiSysMountPoint
documents.content: The path to the efi system mount point. Usually this is the same partition as the above path and can be left as null.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.mirroredBoots.*.path
documents.content: The path to the boot directory where GRUB will be written. Generally this boot path should double as an EFI path.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.splashImage
documents.content:
Background image used for GRUB. Set to null to run GRUB in text mode.
::: {.note} File must be one of .png, .tga, .jpg, or .jpeg. JPEG images must not be progressive. The image will be scaled if necessary to fit the screen. :::

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.splashMode
documents.content: Whether to stretch the image or show the image in the top-left corner unstretched.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.storePath
documents.content: Path to the Nix store when looking for kernels at boot. Only makes sense when copyKernels is false.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.subEntryOptions
documents.content: Options applied to the secondary NixOS submenu entry.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.theme
documents.content: Path to the grub theme to be used.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.timeoutStyle
documents.content:
menu shows the menu.
countdown uses a text-mode countdown.
hidden hides GRUB entirely.

When using a theme, the default value (menu) is appropriate for the graphical countdown.
When attempting to do flicker-free boot, hidden should be used.
See the GRUB documentation section about timeout_style.
::: {.note} If this option is set to ‘countdown’ or ‘hidden’ [...] and ESC or F4 are pressed, or SHIFT is held down during that time, it will display the menu and wait for input. :::
From: Simple configuration handling page, under GRUB_TIMEOUT_STYLE.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.useOSProber
documents.content: If set to true, append entries for other OSs detected by os-prober.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.users
documents.content: User accounts for GRUB. When specified, the GRUB command line and all boot options except the default are password-protected. All passwords and hashes provided will be stored in /boot/grub/grub.cfg, and will be visible to any local user who can read this file. Additionally, any passwords and hashes provided directly in a Nix configuration (as opposed to external files) will be copied into the Nix store, and will be visible to all local users.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.users.<name>.hashedPassword
documents.content: Specifies the password hash for the account, generated with grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2. This hash will be copied to the Nix store, and will be visible to all local users.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.users.<name>.hashedPasswordFile
documents.content: Specifies the path to a file containing the password hash for the account, generated with grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2. This hash will be stored in /boot/grub/grub.cfg, and will be visible to any local user who can read this file.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.users.<name>.password
documents.content: Specifies the clear text password for the account. This password will be copied to the Nix store, and will be visible to all local users.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.users.<name>.passwordFile
documents.content: Specifies the path to a file containing the clear text password for the account. This password will be stored in /boot/grub/grub.cfg, and will be visible to any local user who can read this file.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.grub.zfsSupport
documents.content: Whether GRUB should be built against libzfs.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.initScript.enable
documents.content:
Some systems require a /sbin/init script which is started. Or having it makes starting NixOS easier. This applies to some kind of hosting services and user mode linux.
Additionally this script will create /boot/init-other-configurations-contents.txt containing contents of remaining configurations. You can copy paste them into /sbin/init manually running a rescue system or such.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.additionalFiles
documents.content: A set of files to be copied to {file}/boot. Each attribute name denotes the destination file name in {file}/boot, while the corresponding attribute value specifies the source file.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.biosDevice
documents.content: Device to install the BIOS version of limine on.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.biosSupport
documents.content: Whether or not to install limine for BIOS.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.efiInstallAsRemovable
documents.content:
Whether or not to install the limine EFI files as removable.
See {option}boot.loader.grub.efiInstallAsRemovable

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.efiSupport
documents.content: Whether or not to install the limine EFI files.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the Limine Bootloader.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.enableEditor
documents.content: Whether to allow editing the boot entries before booting them. It is recommended to set this to false, as it allows gaining root access by passing init=/bin/sh as a kernel parameter.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.enrollConfig
documents.content: Whether or not to enroll the config. Only works on EFI!

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.extraConfig
documents.content: A string which is prepended to limine.conf. The config format can be found here.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.extraEntries
documents.content: A string which is appended to the end of limine.conf. The config format can be found here.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.force
documents.content: Force installation even if the safety checks fail, use absolutely only if necessary!

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.maxGenerations
documents.content: Maximum number of latest generations in the boot menu. Useful to prevent boot partition of running out of disk space. null means no limit i.e. all generations that were not garbage collected yet.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.package
documents.content: The limine package to use.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.panicOnChecksumMismatch
documents.content: Whether or not checksum validation failure should be a fatal error at boot time.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.partitionIndex
documents.content: The 1-based index of the dedicated partition for limine's second stage.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.resolution
documents.content:
The framebuffer resolution to set when booting Linux entries. This controls the GOP mode that Limine sets before handing off to the kernel, which affects early boot graphics (e.g., simpledrm, efifb).
Format: <width>x<height> or <width>x<height>x<bpp>. If bpp is omitted, defaults to 32.
Note: Refresh rate is not supported because the UEFI GOP protocol only defines framebuffer dimensions and pixel format, not display timing. Refresh rate is determined later by the GPU driver based on EDID.
This is distinct from {option}boot.loader.limine.style.interface.resolution which only affects the Limine bootloader's own menu interface.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.secureBoot.autoEnrollKeys.enable
documents.content: Enroll automatically generated keys

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.secureBoot.autoEnrollKeys.extraArgs
documents.content: Extra arguments passed to sbctl

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.secureBoot.autoGenerateKeys
documents.content: Generate keys automatically when none exists during bootloader installation

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.secureBoot.enable
documents.content:
Whether to use sign the limine binary with sbctl.
::: {.note} This requires you to already have generated the keys and enrolled them with {command}sbctl.
To create keys use {command}sbctl create-keys.
To enroll them first reset secure boot to "Setup Mode". This is device specific. Then enroll them using {command}sbctl enroll-keys -m -f.
You can now rebuild your system with this option enabled.
Afterwards turn setup mode off and enable secure boot. :::

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.limine.secureBoot.sbctl

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.refind.additionalFiles

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.configurationLimit
documents.content:
Maximum number of latest generations in the boot menu. Useful to prevent boot partition running out of disk space.
null means no limit i.e. all generations that have not been garbage collected yet.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.consoleMode
documents.content:
The resolution of the console. The following values are valid:
"0": Standard UEFI 80x25 mode
"1": 80x50 mode, not supported by all devices
"2": The first non-standard mode provided by the device firmware, if any
"5": Applicable for SteamDeck where this mode represent horizontal mode
"auto": Pick a suitable mode automatically using heuristics
"max": Pick the highest-numbered available mode
"keep": Keep the mode selected by firmware (the default)

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.editor
documents.content: Whether to allow editing the kernel command-line before boot. It is recommended to set this to false, as it allows gaining root access by passing init=/bin/sh as a kernel parameter. However, it is enabled by default for backwards compatibility.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.edk2-uefi-shell.enable
documents.content: Make the EDK2 UEFI Shell available from the systemd-boot menu. It can be used to manually boot other operating systems or for debugging.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.edk2-uefi-shell.sortKey
documents.content:
systemd-boot orders the menu entries by their sort keys, so if you want something to appear after all the NixOS entries, it should start with {file}o or onwards.
See also {option}boot.loader.systemd-boot.sortKey..

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the systemd-boot (formerly gummiboot) EFI boot manager. For more information about systemd-boot: https://www.freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/systemd/systemd-boot/

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.extraEntries
documents.content:
Any additional entries you want added to the systemd-boot menu. These entries will be copied to {file}$BOOT/loader/entries. Each attribute name denotes the destination file name, and the corresponding attribute value is the contents of the entry.
To control the ordering of the entry in the boot menu, use the sort-key field, see https://uapi-group.org/specifications/specs/boot_loader_specification/#sorting and {option}boot.loader.systemd-boot.sortKey.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.extraFiles
documents.content: A set of files to be copied to {file}$BOOT. Each attribute name denotes the destination file name in {file}$BOOT, while the corresponding attribute value specifies the source file.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.extraInstallCommands
documents.content: Additional shell commands inserted in the bootloader installer script after generating menu entries. It can be used to expand on extra boot entries that cannot incorporate certain pieces of information (such as the resulting init= kernel parameter).

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.graceful
documents.content:
Invoke bootctl install with the --graceful option, which ignores errors when EFI variables cannot be written or when the EFI System Partition cannot be found. Currently only applies to random seed operations.
Only enable this option if systemd-boot otherwise fails to install, as the scope or implication of the --graceful option may change in the future.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.installDeviceTree
documents.content: Install the devicetree blob specified by config.hardware.deviceTree.name to the ESP and instruct systemd-boot to pass this DTB to linux.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.memtest86.enable
documents.content: Make Memtest86+ available from the systemd-boot menu. Memtest86+ is a program for testing memory.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.memtest86.sortKey
documents.content:
systemd-boot orders the menu entries by their sort keys, so if you want something to appear after all the NixOS entries, it should start with {file}o or onwards.
See also {option}boot.loader.systemd-boot.sortKey.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.netbootxyz.enable
documents.content: Make netboot.xyz available from the systemd-boot menu. netboot.xyz is a menu system that allows you to boot OS installers and utilities over the network.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.netbootxyz.sortKey
documents.content:
systemd-boot orders the menu entries by their sort keys, so if you want something to appear after all the NixOS entries, it should start with {file}o or onwards.
See also {option}boot.loader.systemd-boot.sortKey.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.rebootForBitlocker
documents.content:
Enable EXPERIMENTAL BitLocker support.
Try to detect BitLocker encrypted drives along with an active TPM. If both are found and Windows Boot Manager is selected in the boot menu, set the "BootNext" EFI variable and restart the system. The firmware will then start Windows Boot Manager directly, leaving the TPM PCRs in expected states so that Windows can unseal the encryption key.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.sortKey
documents.content:
The sort key used for the NixOS bootloader entries. This key determines sorting relative to non-NixOS entries. See also https://uapi-group.org/specifications/specs/boot_loader_specification/#sorting
This option can also be used to control the sorting of NixOS specialisations.
By default, specialisations inherit the sort key of their parent generation and will have the same value for both the sort-key and the version (i.e. the generation number), systemd-boot will therefore sort them based on their file name, meaning that in your boot menu you will have each main generation directly followed by its specialisations sorted alphabetically by their names.
If you want a different ordering for a specialisation, you can override its sort-key which will cause the specialisation to be uncoupled from its parent generation. It will then be sorted by its new sort-key just like any other boot entry.
The sort-key is stored in the generation's bootspec, which means that generations keep their sort-keys even if the original definition of the generation was removed from the NixOS configuration. It also means that updating the sort-key will only affect new generations, while old ones will keep the sort-key that they were originally built with.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.windows
documents.content:
Make Windows bootable from systemd-boot. This option is not necessary when Windows and NixOS use the same EFI System Partition (ESP). In that case, Windows will automatically be detected by systemd-boot.
However, if Windows is installed on a separate drive or ESP, you can use this option to add a menu entry for each installation manually.
The attribute name is used for the title of the menu entry and internal file names.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.windows.<name>.efiDeviceHandle
documents.content:
The device handle of the EFI System Partition (ESP) where the Windows bootloader is located. This is the device handle that the EDK2 UEFI Shell uses to load the bootloader.
To find this handle, follow these steps:
Set {option}boot.loader.systemd-boot.edk2-uefi-shell.enable to true
Run nixos-rebuild boot
Reboot and select "EDK2 UEFI Shell" from the systemd-boot menu
Run map -c to list all consistent device handles
For each device handle (for example, HD0c1), run ls HD0c1:\EFI
If the output contains the directory Microsoft, you might have found the correct device handle
Run HD0c1:\EFI\Microsoft\Boot\Bootmgfw.efi to check if Windows boots correctly
If it does, this device handle is the one you need (in this example, HD0c1)

This option is required, there is no useful default.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.windows.<name>.sortKey
documents.content:
systemd-boot orders the menu entries by their sort keys, so if you want something to appear after all the NixOS entries, it should start with {file}o or onwards.
See also {option}boot.loader.systemd-boot.sortKey..

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.windows.<name>.title
documents.content: The title of the boot menu entry.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.systemd-boot.xbootldrMountPoint
documents.content:
Where the XBOOTLDR partition is mounted.
If set, this partition will be used as $BOOT to store boot loader entries and extra files instead of the EFI partition. As per the bootloader specification, it is recommended that the EFI and XBOOTLDR partitions be mounted at /efi and /boot, respectively.

documents.title: Option: boot.loader.timeout
documents.content: Timeout (in seconds) until loader boots the default menu item. Use null if the loader menu should be displayed indefinitely.

documents.title: Option: boot.modprobeConfig.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable modprobe config. This is useful for systems like containers which do not require a kernel.

documents.title: Option: boot.modprobeConfig.useUbuntuModuleBlacklist
documents.content: Whether to enable Ubuntu distro's module blacklist.

documents.title: Option: boot.nixStoreMountOpts
documents.content:
Defines the mount options used on a bind mount for the {file}/nix/store. This affects the whole system except the nix store daemon, which will undo the bind mount.
ro enforces immutability of the Nix store. The store daemon should already not put device mappers or suid binaries in the store, meaning nosuid and nodev enforce what should already be the case.

documents.title: Option: boot.plymouth.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Plymouth boot splash screen.

documents.title: Option: boot.plymouth.extraConfig
documents.content: Literal string to append to configFile and the config file generated by the plymouth module.

documents.title: Option: boot.plymouth.font
documents.content: Font file made available for displaying text on the splash screen.

documents.title: Option: boot.plymouth.logo
documents.content: Logo which is displayed on the splash screen. Currently supports PNG file format only.

documents.title: Option: boot.plymouth.package
documents.content: The plymouth package to use.

documents.title: Option: boot.plymouth.theme
documents.content: Splash screen theme.

documents.title: Option: boot.plymouth.themePackages
documents.content: Extra theme packages for plymouth.

documents.title: Option: boot.plymouth.tpm2-totp.enable
documents.content: Whether to display a TOTP during boot using tpm2-totp and Plymouth.

documents.title: Option: boot.plymouth.tpm2-totp.package
documents.content: The tpm2-totp package to use.

documents.title: Option: boot.postBootCommands
documents.content: Shell commands to be executed just before systemd is started.

documents.title: Option: boot.resumeDevice
documents.content: Device for manual resume attempt during boot. This should be used primarily if you want to resume from file. If left empty, the swap partitions are used. Specify here the device where the file resides. You should also use {var}boot.kernelParams to specify «resume_offset».

documents.title: Option: boot.runSize
documents.content: Size limit for the /run tmpfs. Look at {manpage}mount(8), tmpfs size option, for the accepted syntax.

documents.title: Option: boot.specialFileSystems.<name>.depends
documents.content:
List of paths that should be mounted before this one. This filesystem's {option}device and {option}mountPoint are always checked and do not need to be included explicitly. If a path is added to this list, any other filesystem whose mount point is a parent of the path will be mounted before this filesystem. The paths do not need to actually be the {option}mountPoint of some other filesystem.
This is useful for mounts which require keys and/or configuration files residing on another filesystem.

documents.title: Option: boot.specialFileSystems.<name>.device
documents.content:
The device as passed to mount.
This can be any of:
a filename of a block special device such as /dev/sdc3
a tag such as UUID=fdd68895-c307-4549-8c9c-90e44c71f5b7
(for bind mounts only) the source path
something else depending on the {option}fsType. For example, nfs device may look like knuth.cwi.nl:/dir

This is called device in {manpage}mount(8) and fs_spec in {manpage}fstab(5).

documents.title: Option: boot.specialFileSystems.<name>.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the filesystem mount.

documents.title: Option: boot.specialFileSystems.<name>.fsType
documents.content:
Type of the file system.
This is the fstype passed to -t in the {manpage}mount(8) command, and is called fs_vfstype in {manpage}fstab(5).

documents.title: Option: boot.specialFileSystems.<name>.mountPoint
documents.content:
Location where the file system will be mounted.
This is called mountpoint in {manpage}mount(8) and fs_file in {manpage}fstab(5)

documents.title: Option: boot.specialFileSystems.<name>.options
documents.content:
Options used to mount the file system.
This is called options in {manpage}mount(8) and fs_mntops in {manpage}fstab(5)
Some options that can be used for all mounts are documented in {manpage}mount(8) under FILESYSTEM-INDEPENDENT MOUNT OPTIONS.
Options that systemd understands are documented in {manpage}systemd.mount(5) under FSTAB.
Each filesystem supports additional options, see the docs for that filesystem.

documents.title: Option: boot.specialFileSystems.<name>.stratis.poolUuid
documents.content:
UUID of the stratis pool that the fs is located in
This is only relevant if you are using stratis.

documents.title: Option: boot.stage2Greeting
documents.content: The greeting message displayed during NixOS stage 2 boot.

documents.title: Option: boot.supportedFilesystems
documents.content: Names of supported filesystem types, or an attribute set of file system types and their state. The set form may be used together with lib.mkForce to explicitly disable support for specific filesystems, e.g. to disable ZFS with an unsupported kernel.

documents.title: Option: boot.swraid.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable support for Linux MD RAID arrays.
When this is enabled, mdadm will be added to the system path, and MD RAID arrays will be detected and activated automatically, both in stage-1 (initramfs) and in stage-2 (the final NixOS system).
This should be enabled if you want to be able to access and/or boot from MD RAID arrays. {command}nixos-generate-config should detect it correctly in the standard installation procedure.

documents.title: Option: boot.swraid.mdadmConf
documents.content: Contents of {file}/etc/mdadm.conf.

documents.title: Option: boot.systemdExecutable
documents.content: The program to execute to start systemd.

documents.title: Option: boot.tmp.cleanOnBoot
documents.content: Whether to delete all files in {file}/tmp during boot.

documents.title: Option: boot.tmp.tmpfsHugeMemoryPages
documents.content:
never - Do not allocate huge memory pages. This is the default.
always - Attempt to allocate huge memory page every time a new page is needed.
within_size - Only allocate huge memory pages if it will be fully within i_size. Also respect madvise(2) hints. Recommended.
advise - Only allocate huge memory pages if requested with madvise(2).

documents.title: Option: boot.tmp.tmpfsSize
documents.content: Size of tmpfs in percentage. Percentage is defined by systemd.

documents.title: Option: boot.tmp.useTmpfs
documents.content:
Whether to mount a tmpfs on {file}/tmp during boot.
::: {.note} Large Nix builds can fail if the mounted tmpfs is not large enough. In such a case either increase the tmpfsSize or disable this option. :::

documents.title: Option: boot.tmp.useZram
documents.content:
Whether to mount a zram device on {file}/tmp during boot.
::: {.note} Large Nix builds can fail if the mounted zram device is not large enough. In such a case either increase the zramSettings.zram-size or disable this option. :::

documents.title: Option: boot.tmp.zramSettings.compression-algorithm
documents.content:
The compression algorithm to use for the zram device.
See: https://github.com/systemd/zram-generator/blob/main/zram-generator.conf.example

documents.title: Option: boot.tmp.zramSettings.fs-type
documents.content:
The file system to put on the device.
See: https://github.com/systemd/zram-generator/blob/main/zram-generator.conf.example

documents.title: Option: boot.tmp.zramSettings.options
documents.content:
By default, file systems and swap areas are trimmed on-the-go by setting "discard". Setting this to the empty string clears the option.
See: https://github.com/systemd/zram-generator/blob/main/zram-generator.conf.example

documents.title: Option: boot.tmp.zramSettings.zram-size
documents.content:
The size of the zram device, as a function of MemTotal, both in MB. For example, if the machine has 1 GiB, and zram-size=ram/4, then the zram device will have 256 MiB. Fractions in the range 0.1–0.5 are recommended
See: https://github.com/systemd/zram-generator/blob/main/zram-generator.conf.example

documents.title: Option: boot.uki.configFile
documents.content:
The configuration file passed to {manpage}ukify(1) to create the UKI.
By default this configuration file is created from {option}boot.uki.settings.

documents.title: Option: boot.uki.name
documents.content: Name of the UKI

documents.title: Option: boot.uki.settings
documents.content: The configuration settings for ukify. These control what the UKI contains and how it is built.

documents.title: Option: boot.uki.tries
documents.content:
Number of boot attempts before this UKI is considered bad.
If no tries are specified (the default) automatic boot assessment remains inactive.
See documentation on Automatic Boot Assessment and boot counting for more information.

documents.title: Option: boot.uki.version
documents.content: Version of the image or generation the UKI belongs to

documents.title: Option: boot.uvesafb.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable uvesafb.

documents.title: Option: boot.uvesafb.gfx-mode
documents.content: Screen resolution in modedb format. See uvesafb and modedb documentation for more details. The default value is a sensible default but may be not ideal for all setups.

documents.title: Option: boot.uvesafb.v86d.package
documents.content: Which v86d package to use with uvesafb

documents.title: Option: boot.vesa
documents.content: (Deprecated) This option, if set, activates the VESA 800x600 video mode on boot and disables kernel modesetting. It is equivalent to specifying [ "vga=0x317" "nomodeset" ] in the {option}boot.kernelParams option. This option is deprecated as of 2020: Xorg now works better with modesetting, and you might want a different VESA vga setting, anyway.

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.devNodes
documents.content:
Name of directory from which to import ZFS device, this is passed to zpool import as the value of the -d option.
For guidance on choosing this value, see the ZFS documentation.

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.enabled
