documents.content: True if ZFS filesystem support is enabled

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.extraPools
documents.content:
Name or GUID of extra ZFS pools that you wish to import during boot.
Usually this is not necessary. Instead, you should set the mountpoint property of ZFS filesystems to legacy and add the ZFS filesystems to NixOS's {option}fileSystems option, which makes NixOS automatically import the associated pool.
However, in some cases (e.g. if you have many filesystems) it may be preferable to exclusively use ZFS commands to manage filesystems. If so, since NixOS/systemd will not be managing those filesystems, you will need to specify the ZFS pool here so that NixOS automatically imports it on every boot.

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.forceImportAll
documents.content:
Forcibly import all ZFS pool(s).
It is highly recommended to keep this option disabled as it bypasses ZFS safeguard that protect your pools.
See {option}boot.zfs.forceImportRoot for details.

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.forceImportRoot
documents.content:
Forcibly import the ZFS root pool(s) during early boot.
It is highly recommended to keep this option disabled as it bypasses ZFS safeguard that protect your pools.
If NixOS fails to boot because it cannot import the root pool, you should boot with the zfs_force=1 option as a kernel parameter (e.g. by manually editing the kernel params via your bootloader). You should only need to do this after unclean shutdowns.

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.package
documents.content: Configured ZFS userland tools package.

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.passwordTimeout
documents.content:
Timeout in seconds to wait for password entry for decrypt at boot.
Defaults to 0, which waits forever.

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.pools
documents.content: Configuration for individual pools to override global defaults.

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.pools.<name>.devNodes
documents.content:
Name of directory from which to import ZFS device, this is passed to zpool import as the value of the -d option.
For guidance on choosing this value, see the ZFS documentation.

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.removeLinuxDRM
documents.content:
Patch the kernel to change symbols needed by ZFS from EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL to EXPORT_SYMBOL.
Currently has no effect, but may again in future if a kernel update breaks ZFS due to symbols being newly changed to GPL.

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.requestEncryptionCredentials
documents.content: If true on import encryption keys or passwords for all encrypted datasets are requested. To only decrypt selected datasets supply a list of dataset names instead. For root pools the encryption key can be supplied via both an interactive prompt (keylocation=prompt) and from a file (keylocation=file://).

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.unsafeAllowHibernation
documents.content: Allow hibernation (suspend to disk) support. This is generally considered UNSAFE, is not well supported by openzfs, and could lead to corruption and data loss.

documents.title: Option: boot.zfs.useKeyringForCredentials
documents.content: Whether to enable Uses the kernel keyring for encryption credentials with keyname=zfs-.

documents.title: Option: boot.zswap.acceptThresholdPercent
documents.content:
Threshold percentage at which zswap starts accepting pages again after the pool becomes full (1-100).
This parameter provides hysteresis to prevent pool oscillation. When the pool usage drops below this threshold, zswap starts accepting new pages. Default is 90% as recommended by kernel documentation.

documents.title: Option: boot.zswap.compressor
documents.content:
Compression algorithm to use for zswap.
Available options:
'zstd': Best compression ratio, excellent for Nix builds (default)
'lz4': Fastest compression, lowest latency
'lz4hc': High-compression variant of lz4, slower but better ratio
'lzo': Good balance of speed and compression (kernel default)
'deflate': Higher compression, slower processing
'842': Hardware-accelerated compression on supported systems

Note: The chosen algorithm must be supported by your kernel configuration.

documents.title: Option: boot.zswap.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Zswap (Compressed Cache for Swap Pages).

documents.title: Option: boot.zswap.maxPoolPercent
documents.content:
The maximum percentage of system memory that Zswap can occupy (1-100).
Higher values provide more compression cache but increase memory pressure. Default is 25% (higher than kernel default of 20%) for better Nix build performance.
Recommended ranges:
Desktop systems: 15-25%
Low-memory systems: 30-50%
Server systems: 10-20%

documents.title: Option: boot.zswap.shrinkerEnabled
documents.content:
Enable the zswap shrinker to reclaim memory when under pressure.
When enabled, the shrinker will automatically reclaim compressed pages from the zswap pool when the system is under memory pressure, helping to prevent out-of-memory situations.
It is recommended to keep this enabled for most workloads, especially on systems with limited memory.

documents.title: Option: boot.zswap.zpool
documents.content:
Kernel zpool allocator. 'zsmalloc' is strongly recommended for kernels >= 6.3 as it offers the best density. For older kernels, 'zbud' is the fallback.
Note: 'z3fold' was removed from Linux kernel 6.8 and later.

documents.title: Option: console.colors
documents.content: The 16 colors palette used by the virtual consoles. Leave empty to use the default colors. Colors must be in hexadecimal format and listed in order from color 0 to color 15.

documents.title: Option: console.earlySetup
documents.content: Enable setting virtual console options as early as possible (in initrd).

documents.title: Option: console.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable virtual console.

documents.title: Option: console.font
documents.content:
The font used for the virtual consoles. Can be null, a font name, or a path to a PSF font file.
Use null to let the kernel choose a built-in font. The default is 8x16, and, as of Linux 5.3, Terminus 32 bold for display resolutions of 2560x1080 and higher. These fonts cover the IBM437 character set.

documents.title: Option: console.keyMap
documents.content: The keyboard mapping table for the virtual consoles.

documents.title: Option: console.packages
documents.content: List of additional packages that provide console fonts, keymaps and other resources for virtual consoles use.

documents.title: Option: console.useXkbConfig
documents.content: If set, configure the virtual console keymap from the xserver keyboard settings.

documents.title: Option: containers
documents.content: A set of NixOS system configurations to be run as lightweight containers. Each container appears as a service container-«name» on the host system, allowing it to be started and stopped via {command}systemctl.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.additionalCapabilities
documents.content: Grant additional capabilities to the container. See the {manpage}capabilities(7) and {manpage}systemd-nspawn(1) man pages for more information.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.allowedDevices
documents.content: A list of device nodes to which the containers has access to.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.allowedDevices.*.modifier
documents.content: Device node access modifier. Takes a combination r (read), w (write), and m (mknod). See the {manpage}systemd.resource-control(5) man page for more information.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.allowedDevices.*.node
documents.content: Path to device node

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.autoStart
documents.content: Whether the container is automatically started at boot-time.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.bindMounts
documents.content: An extra list of directories that is bound to the container.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.bindMounts.<name>.hostPath
documents.content: Location of the host path to be mounted.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.bindMounts.<name>.isReadOnly
documents.content: Determine whether the mounted path will be accessed in read-only mode.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.bindMounts.<name>.mountPoint
documents.content: Mount point on the container file system.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.config
documents.content: A specification of the desired configuration of this container, as a NixOS module.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.enableTun
documents.content: Allows the container to create and setup tunnel interfaces by granting the NET_ADMIN capability and enabling access to /dev/net/tun.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.ephemeral
documents.content:
Runs container in ephemeral mode with the empty root filesystem at boot. This way container will be bootstrapped from scratch on each boot and will be cleaned up on shutdown leaving no traces behind. Useful for completely stateless, reproducible containers.
Note that this option might require to do some adjustments to the container configuration, e.g. you might want to set {var}systemd.network.networks.$interface.dhcpV4Config.ClientIdentifier to "mac" if you use {var}macvlans option. This way dhcp client identifier will be stable between the container restarts.
Note that the container journal will not be linked to the host if this option is enabled.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraFlags
documents.content: Extra flags passed to the systemd-nspawn command. See {manpage}systemd-nspawn(1) for details.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraVeths
documents.content: Extra veth-pairs to be created for the container.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraVeths.<name>.forwardPorts
documents.content: List of forwarded ports from host to container. Each forwarded port is specified by protocol, hostPort and containerPort. By default, protocol is tcp and hostPort and containerPort are assumed to be the same if containerPort is not explicitly given.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraVeths.<name>.forwardPorts.*.containerPort
documents.content: Target port of container

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraVeths.<name>.forwardPorts.*.hostPort
documents.content: Source port of the external interface on host

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraVeths.<name>.forwardPorts.*.protocol
documents.content: The protocol specifier for port forwarding between host and container

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraVeths.<name>.hostAddress
documents.content: The IPv4 address assigned to the host interface. (Not used when hostBridge is set.)

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraVeths.<name>.hostAddress6
documents.content: The IPv6 address assigned to the host interface. (Not used when hostBridge is set.)

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraVeths.<name>.hostBridge
documents.content: Put the host-side of the veth-pair into the named bridge. Only one of hostAddress* or hostBridge can be given.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraVeths.<name>.localAddress
documents.content: The IPv4 address assigned to the interface in the container. If a hostBridge is used, this should be given with netmask to access the whole network. Otherwise the default netmask is /32 and routing is set up from localAddress to hostAddress and back.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraVeths.<name>.localAddress6
documents.content: The IPv6 address assigned to the interface in the container. If a hostBridge is used, this should be given with netmask to access the whole network. Otherwise the default netmask is /128 and routing is set up from localAddress6 to hostAddress6 and back.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.extraVeths.<name>.localMacAddress
documents.content: The MAC address assigned to the interface in the container. This address is assigned early during container boot, and can thus be reliably used for setups like IPv6 SLAAC with router advertisements. If this option is not specified, the veth devices gets assigned a random, locally-administered unicast MAC address.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.flake
documents.content: The Flake URI of the NixOS configuration to use for the container. Replaces the option {option}containers.<name>.path.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.forwardPorts
documents.content: List of forwarded ports from host to container. Each forwarded port is specified by protocol, hostPort and containerPort. By default, protocol is tcp and hostPort and containerPort are assumed to be the same if containerPort is not explicitly given.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.forwardPorts.*.containerPort
documents.content: Target port of container

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.forwardPorts.*.hostPort
documents.content: Source port of the external interface on host

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.forwardPorts.*.protocol
documents.content: The protocol specifier for port forwarding between host and container

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.hostAddress
documents.content: The IPv4 address assigned to the host interface. (Not used when hostBridge is set.)

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.hostAddress6
documents.content: The IPv6 address assigned to the host interface. (Not used when hostBridge is set.)

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.hostBridge
documents.content: Put the host-side of the veth-pair into the named bridge. Only one of hostAddress* or hostBridge can be given.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.interfaces
documents.content: The list of interfaces to be moved into the container.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.localAddress
documents.content: The IPv4 address assigned to the interface in the container. If a hostBridge is used, this should be given with netmask to access the whole network. Otherwise the default netmask is /32 and routing is set up from localAddress to hostAddress and back.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.localAddress6
documents.content: The IPv6 address assigned to the interface in the container. If a hostBridge is used, this should be given with netmask to access the whole network. Otherwise the default netmask is /128 and routing is set up from localAddress6 to hostAddress6 and back.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.localMacAddress
documents.content: The MAC address assigned to the interface in the container. This address is assigned early during container boot, and can thus be reliably used for setups like IPv6 SLAAC with router advertisements. If this option is not specified, the veth devices gets assigned a random, locally-administered unicast MAC address.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.macvlans
documents.content: The list of host interfaces from which macvlans will be created. For each interface specified, a macvlan interface will be created and moved to the container.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.networkNamespace
documents.content: Takes the path to a file representing a kernel network namespace that the container shall run in. The specified path should refer to a (possibly bind-mounted) network namespace file, as exposed by the kernel below /proc//ns/net. This makes the container enter the given network namespace. One of the typical use cases is to give a network namespace under /run/netns created by {manpage}ip-netns(8). Note that this option cannot be used together with other network-related options, such as --private-network or --network-interface=.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.nixpkgs
documents.content:
A path to the nixpkgs that provide the modules, pkgs and lib for evaluating the container.
To only change the pkgs argument used inside the container modules, set the nixpkgs.* options in the container {option}config. Setting config.nixpkgs.pkgs = pkgs speeds up the container evaluation by reusing the system pkgs, but the nixpkgs.config option in the container config is ignored in this case.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.path
documents.content: As an alternative to specifying {option}config, you can specify the path to the evaluated NixOS system configuration, typically a symlink to a system profile.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.privateNetwork
documents.content: Whether to give the container its own private virtual Ethernet interface. The interface is called eth0, and is hooked up to the interface ve-«container-name» on the host. If this option is not set, then the container shares the network interfaces of the host, and can bind to any port on any interface.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.privateUsers
documents.content:
Whether to give the container its own private UIDs/GIDs space (user namespacing). Disabled by default (no).
If set to a number (usually above host's UID/GID range: 65536), user namespacing is enabled and the container UID/GIDs will start at that number.
If set to identity, mostly equivalent to 0, this will only provide process capability isolation (no UID/GID isolation, as they are the same as host).
If set to pick, user namespacing is enabled and the UID/GID range is automatically chosen, so that no overlapping UID/GID ranges are assigned to multiple containers. This is the recommanded option as it enhances container security massively and operates fully automatically in most cases.
See https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd-nspawn.html#--private-users= for details.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.restartIfChanged
documents.content: Whether the container should be restarted during a NixOS configuration switch if its definition has changed.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.specialArgs
documents.content: A set of special arguments to be passed to NixOS modules. This will be merged into the specialArgs used to evaluate the NixOS configurations.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.timeoutStartSec
documents.content: Time for the container to start. In case of a timeout, the container processes get killed. See {manpage}systemd.time(7) for more information about the format.

documents.title: Option: containers.<name>.tmpfs
documents.content: Mounts a set of tmpfs file systems into the container. Multiple paths can be specified. Valid items must conform to the --tmpfs argument of systemd-nspawn. See {manpage}systemd-nspawn(1) for details.

documents.title: Option: documentation.dev.enable
documents.content:
Whether to install documentation targeted at developers.
This includes man pages targeted at developers if {option}documentation.man.enable is set (this also includes "devman" outputs).
This includes info pages targeted at developers if {option}documentation.info.enable is set (this also includes "devinfo" outputs).
This includes other pages targeted at developers if {option}documentation.doc.enable is set (this also includes "devdoc" outputs).

documents.title: Option: documentation.doc.enable
documents.content: Whether to install documentation distributed in packages' /share/doc. Usually plain text and/or HTML. This also includes "doc" outputs.

documents.title: Option: documentation.enable
documents.content:
Whether to install documentation of packages from {option}environment.systemPackages into the generated system path.
See "Multiple-output packages" chapter in the nixpkgs manual for more info.

documents.title: Option: documentation.info.enable
documents.content: Whether to install info pages and the {command}info command. This also includes "info" outputs.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.cache.enable
documents.content: Whether to generate the manual page index caches. This allows searching for a page or keyword using utilities like {manpage}apropos(1) and the -k option of {manpage}man(1).

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.cache.generateAtRuntime
documents.content:
Whether to generate the manual page index caches at runtime using a systemd service.
::: {.note} This is currently only supported by the man-db module. :::

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.enable
documents.content: Whether to install manual pages. This also includes man outputs.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.man-db.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable man-db as the default man page viewer.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.man-db.manualPages
documents.content: The manual pages to generate caches for if {option}documentation.man.cache.enable is enabled. Must be a path to a directory with man pages under /share/man; see the source for an example. Advanced users can make this a content-addressed derivation to save a few rebuilds.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.man-db.package
documents.content: The man-db derivation to use. Useful to override configuration options used for the package.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.cachePath
documents.content: Change the paths where mandoc {manpage}makewhatis(8)generates the manual page index caches. {option}documentation.man.cache.enable should be enabled to allow cache generation. This list should only include the paths to manpages installed in the system configuration, i. e. /run/current-system/sw/share/man. {manpage}makewhatis(8) creates a database in each directory using the files mansection/[arch/]title.section and catsection/[arch/]title.0 in it. If a directory contains no manual pages, no database is created in that directory. This option only needs to be set manually if extra paths should be indexed or {option}documentation.man.manPath contains paths that can't be indexed.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable mandoc as the default man page viewer.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.extraConfig
documents.content: Extra configuration to write to {manpage}man.conf(5).

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.manPath
documents.content: Change the paths included in the MANPATH environment variable, i. e. the directories where {manpage}man(1) looks for section-specific directories of man pages. You only need to change this setting if you want extra man pages (e. g. in non-english languages). All values must be strings that are a valid path from the target prefix (without including it). The first value given takes priority. Note that this will not add manpath directives to {manpage}man.conf(5).

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.package
documents.content: The mandoc derivation to use. Useful to override configuration options used for the package.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.settings
documents.content: Configuration for {manpage}man.conf(5)

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.settings.manpath
documents.content: Override the default search path for {manpage}man(1), {manpage}apropos(1), and {manpage}makewhatis(8). It can be used multiple times to specify multiple paths, with the order determining the manual page search order. This is not recommended in favor of {option}documentation.man.mandoc.manPath, but if it's needed to specify the manpath in this way, set {option}documentation.man.mandoc.manPath to an empty list ([]).

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.settings.output.fragment
documents.content: Whether to omit the <!DOCTYPE> declaration and the , , and elements and only emit the subtree below the element in HTML output of {manpage}mandoc(1). The style argument will be ignored. This is useful when embedding manual content within existing documents.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.settings.output.includes
documents.content: A string of relative path used as a template for the output path of linked header files (usually via the In macro) in HTML output. Instances of %I are replaced with the include filename. The default is not to present a hyperlink.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.settings.output.indent
documents.content: Number of blank characters at the left margin for normal text, default of 5 for {manpage}mdoc(7) and 7 for {manpage}man(7). Increasing this is not recommended; it may result in degraded formatting, for example overfull lines or ugly line breaks. When output is to a pager on a terminal that is less than 66 columns wide, the default is reduced to three columns.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.settings.output.man
documents.content: A template for linked manuals (usually via the Xr macro) in HTML output. Instances of ‘%N’ and ‘%S’ are replaced with the linked manual's name and section, respectively. If no section is included, section 1 is assumed. The default is not to present a hyperlink. If two formats are given and a file %N.%S exists in the current directory, the first format is used; otherwise, the second format is used.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.settings.output.paper
documents.content: This option is for generating PostScript and PDF output. The paper size name may be one of a3, a4, a5, legal, or letter. You may also manually specify dimensions as NNxNN, width by height in millimetres. If an unknown value is encountered, letter is used. Output pages default to letter sized and are rendered in the Times font family, 11-point. Margins are calculated as 1/9 the page length and width. Line-height is 1.4m.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.settings.output.style
documents.content: Path to the file used for an external style-sheet. This must be a valid absolute or relative URI.

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.settings.output.toc
documents.content: Whether to enable printing a table of contents near the beginning of the HTML output of {manpage}mandoc(1) if an input file contains at least two non-standard sections .

documents.title: Option: documentation.man.mandoc.settings.output.width
documents.content: The ASCII and UTF-8 output width, default is 78. When output is a pager on a terminal that is less than 79 columns wide, the default is reduced to one less than the terminal width. In any case, lines that are output in literal mode are never wrapped and may exceed the output width.

documents.title: Option: documentation.nixos.checkRedirects
documents.content: Check redirects for manualHTML.

documents.title: Option: documentation.nixos.enable
documents.content:
Whether to install NixOS's own documentation.
This includes man pages like {manpage}configuration.nix(5) if {option}documentation.man.enable is set.
This includes the HTML manual and the {command}nixos-help command if {option}documentation.doc.enable is set.

documents.title: Option: documentation.nixos.extraModuleSources
documents.content: Which extra NixOS module paths the generated NixOS's documentation should strip from options.

documents.title: Option: documentation.nixos.extraModules
documents.content: Modules for which to show options even when not imported.

documents.title: Option: documentation.nixos.includeAllModules
documents.content: Whether the generated NixOS's documentation should include documentation for all the options from all the NixOS modules included in the current configuration.nix. Disabling this will make the manual generator to ignore options defined outside of baseModules.

documents.title: Option: documentation.nixos.options.splitBuild
documents.content: Whether to split the option docs build into a cacheable and an uncacheable part. Splitting the build can substantially decrease the amount of time needed to build the manual, but some user modules may be incompatible with this splitting.

documents.title: Option: documentation.nixos.options.warningsAreErrors
documents.content: Treat warning emitted during the option documentation build (eg for missing option descriptions) as errors.

documents.title: Option: ec2.zfs.datasets
documents.content:
Datasets to create under the tank and boot zpools.
NOTE: This option is used only at image creation time, and does not attempt to declaratively create or manage datasets on an existing system.

documents.title: Option: ec2.zfs.datasets.<name>.mount
documents.content: Where to mount this dataset.

documents.title: Option: ec2.zfs.datasets.<name>.properties
documents.content: Properties to set on this dataset.

documents.title: Option: environment.budgie.excludePackages
documents.content: Which packages Budgie should exclude from the default environment.

documents.title: Option: environment.checkConfigurationOptions
documents.content: Alias of {option}_module.check.

documents.title: Option: environment.cinnamon.excludePackages
documents.content: Which packages cinnamon should exclude from the default environment

documents.title: Option: environment.corePackages
documents.content:
Set of core packages for a normal interactive system.
Only change this if you know what you're doing!
Like with systemPackages, packages are installed to {file}/run/current-system/sw. They are automatically available to all users, and are automatically updated every time you rebuild the system configuration.

documents.title: Option: environment.cosmic.excludePackages
documents.content: List of packages to exclude from the COSMIC environment.

documents.title: Option: environment.debuginfodServers
documents.content:
List of urls of debuginfod servers for tools like {command}gdb and {command}valgrind to use.
Unrelated to {option}environment.enableDebugInfo.

documents.title: Option: environment.defaultPackages
documents.content:
Set of default packages that aren't strictly necessary for a running system, entries can be removed for a more minimal NixOS installation.
Like with systemPackages, packages are installed to {file}/run/current-system/sw. They are automatically available to all users, and are automatically updated every time you rebuild the system configuration.

documents.title: Option: environment.enableAllTerminfo
documents.content: Whether to install all terminfo outputs

documents.title: Option: environment.enableDebugInfo
documents.content: Some NixOS packages provide debug symbols. However, these are not included in the system closure by default to save disk space. Enabling this option causes the debug symbols to appear in {file}/run/current-system/sw/lib/debug/.build-id, where tools such as {command}gdb can find them. If you need debug symbols for a package that doesn't provide them by default, you can enable them as follows:

documents.title: Option: environment.enlightenment.excludePackages
documents.content: Which packages Enlightenment should exclude from the default environment

documents.title: Option: environment.etc
documents.content: Set of files that have to be linked in {file}/etc.

documents.title: Option: environment.etc.<name>.enable
documents.content: Whether this /etc file should be generated. This option allows specific /etc files to be disabled.

documents.title: Option: environment.etc.<name>.gid
documents.content: GID of created file. Only takes effect when the file is copied (that is, the mode is not 'symlink').

documents.title: Option: environment.etc.<name>.group
documents.content:
Group name of file owner.
Only takes effect when the file is copied (that is, the mode is not symlink).
When services.userborn.enable, this option has no effect. You have to assign a gid instead. Otherwise this option takes precedence over gid.

documents.title: Option: environment.etc.<name>.mode
documents.content: If set to something else than symlink, the file is copied instead of symlinked, with the given file mode.

documents.title: Option: environment.etc.<name>.source
documents.content: Path of the source file.

documents.title: Option: environment.etc.<name>.target
documents.content: Name of symlink (relative to {file}/etc). Defaults to the attribute name.

documents.title: Option: environment.etc.<name>.text
documents.content: Text of the file.

documents.title: Option: environment.etc.<name>.uid
documents.content: UID of created file. Only takes effect when the file is copied (that is, the mode is not 'symlink').

documents.title: Option: environment.etc.<name>.user
documents.content:
User name of file owner.
Only takes effect when the file is copied (that is, the mode is not symlink).
When services.userborn.enable, this option has no effect. You have to assign a uid instead. Otherwise this option takes precedence over uid.

documents.title: Option: environment.extraInit
documents.content: Shell script code called during global environment initialisation after all variables and profileVariables have been set. This code is assumed to be shell-independent, which means you should stick to pure sh without sh word split.

documents.title: Option: environment.extraOutputsToInstall
documents.content:
Entries listed here will be appended to the meta.outputsToInstall attribute for each package in environment.systemPackages, and the files from the corresponding derivation outputs symlinked into {file}/run/current-system/sw.
For example, this can be used to install the dev and info outputs for all packages in the system environment, if they are available.
To use specific outputs instead of configuring them globally, select the corresponding attribute on the package derivation, e.g. libxml2.dev or coreutils.info.

documents.title: Option: environment.extraSetup
documents.content: Shell fragments to be run after the system environment has been created. This should only be used for things that need to modify the internals of the environment, e.g. generating MIME caches. The environment being built can be accessed at $out.

documents.title: Option: environment.freetds
documents.content: Configure freetds database entries. Each attribute denotes a section within freetds.conf, and the value (a string) is the config content for that section. When at least one entry is configured the global environment variables FREETDSCONF, FREETDS and SYBASE will be configured to allow the programs that use freetds to find the library and config.

documents.title: Option: environment.gnome.excludePackages
documents.content: Which packages gnome should exclude from the default environment

documents.title: Option: environment.homeBinInPath
documents.content: Include ~/bin/ in $PATH.

documents.title: Option: environment.interactiveShellInit
documents.content: Shell script code called during interactive shell initialisation. This code is assumed to be shell-independent, which means you should stick to pure sh without sh word split.

documents.title: Option: environment.ldso
documents.content: The executable to link into the normal FHS location of the ELF loader.

documents.title: Option: environment.ldso32
documents.content:
The executable to link into the normal FHS location of the 32-bit ELF loader.
This currently only works on x86_64 architectures.

documents.title: Option: environment.localBinInPath
documents.content: Add ~/.local/bin/ to $PATH

documents.title: Option: environment.loginShellInit
documents.content: Shell script code called during login shell initialisation. This code is assumed to be shell-independent, which means you should stick to pure sh without sh word split.

documents.title: Option: environment.lxqt.excludePackages
documents.content: Which LXQt packages to exclude from the default environment

documents.title: Option: environment.mate.excludePackages
documents.content: Which MATE packages to exclude from the default environment

documents.title: Option: environment.memoryAllocator.provider
documents.content:
The system-wide memory allocator.
Briefly, the system-wide memory allocator providers are:
libc: the standard allocator provided by libc
graphene-hardened: Hardened memory allocator coming from GrapheneOS project. The default configuration template has all normal optional security features enabled and is quite aggressive in terms of sacrificing performance and memory usage for security.
graphene-hardened-light: Hardened memory allocator coming from GrapheneOS project. The light configuration template disables the slab quarantines, write after free check, slot randomization and raises the guard slab interval from 1 to 8 but leaves zero-on-free and slab canaries enabled. The light configuration has solid performance and memory usage while still being far more secure than mainstream allocators with much better security properties.
jemalloc: A general purpose allocator that emphasizes fragmentation avoidance and scalable concurrency support.
mimalloc: A compact and fast general purpose allocator, which may optionally be built with mitigations against various heap vulnerabilities.
scudo: A user-mode allocator based on LLVM Sanitizer’s CombinedAllocator, which aims at providing additional mitigations against heap based vulnerabilities, while maintaining good performance.

::: {.warning} Selecting an alternative allocator (i.e., anything other than libc) may result in instability, data loss, and/or service failure. :::

documents.title: Option: environment.pantheon.excludePackages
documents.content: Which packages pantheon should exclude from the default environment

documents.title: Option: environment.pathsToLink
documents.content: List of directories to be symlinked in {file}/run/current-system/sw.

documents.title: Option: environment.plasma6.excludePackages
documents.content: List of default packages to exclude from the configuration

documents.title: Option: environment.profileRelativeEnvVars
documents.content: Attribute set of environment variable. Each attribute maps to a list of relative paths. Each relative path is appended to the each profile of {option}environment.profiles to form the content of the corresponding environment variable.

documents.title: Option: environment.profileRelativeSessionVariables
documents.content:
Attribute set of environment variable used in the global environment. These variables will be set by PAM early in the login process.
Variable substitution is available as described in {manpage}pam_env.conf(5).
Each attribute maps to a list of relative paths. Each relative path is appended to the each profile of {option}environment.profiles to form the content of the corresponding environment variable.
Also, these variables are merged into and it is therefore not possible to use PAM style variables such as @{HOME}.

documents.title: Option: environment.profiles
documents.content: A list of profiles used to setup the global environment.

documents.title: Option: environment.sessionVariables
documents.content:
A set of environment variables used in the global environment. These variables will be set by PAM early in the login process.
The value of each session variable can be either a string or a list of strings. The latter is concatenated, interspersed with colon characters.
Setting a variable to null does nothing. You can override a variable set by another module to null to unset it.
Note, due to limitations in the PAM format values may not contain the " character.
Also, these variables are merged into and it is therefore not possible to use PAM style variables such as @{HOME}.

documents.title: Option: environment.shellAliases
documents.content: An attribute set that maps aliases (the top level attribute names in this option) to command strings or directly to build outputs. The aliases are added to all users' shells. Aliases mapped to null are ignored.

documents.title: Option: environment.shellInit
documents.content: Shell script code called during shell initialisation. This code is assumed to be shell-independent, which means you should stick to pure sh without sh word split.

documents.title: Option: environment.shells
documents.content: A list of permissible login shells for user accounts. No need to mention /bin/sh here, it is placed into this list implicitly.

documents.title: Option: environment.stub-ld.enable
documents.content: Install a stub ELF loader to print an informative error message in the event that a user attempts to run an ELF binary not compiled for NixOS.

documents.title: Option: environment.systemPackages
documents.content: The set of packages that appear in /run/current-system/sw. These packages are automatically available to all users, and are automatically updated every time you rebuild the system configuration. (The latter is the main difference with installing them in the default profile, {file}/nix/var/nix/profiles/default.

documents.title: Option: environment.unixODBCDrivers
documents.content: Specifies Unix ODBC drivers to be registered in {file}/etc/odbcinst.ini. You may also want to add pkgs.unixodbc to the system path to get a command line client to connect to ODBC databases.

documents.title: Option: environment.variables
documents.content:
A set of environment variables used in the global environment. These variables will be set on shell initialisation (e.g. in /etc/profile).
The value of each variable can be either a string or a list of strings. The latter is concatenated, interspersed with colon characters.
Setting a variable to null does nothing. You can override a variable set by another module to null to unset it.

documents.title: Option: environment.wordlist.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable environment variables for lists of words.

documents.title: Option: environment.wordlist.lists
documents.content:
A set with the key names being the environment variable you'd like to set and the values being a list of paths to text documents containing lists of words. The various files will be merged, sorted, duplicates removed, and extraneous spacing removed.
If you have a handful of words that you want to add to an already existing wordlist, you may find builtins.toFile useful for this task.

documents.title: Option: environment.wvdial.dialerDefaults
documents.content: Contents of the "Dialer Defaults" section of /etc/wvdial.conf.

documents.title: Option: environment.wvdial.pppDefaults
documents.content: Default ppp settings for wvdial.

documents.title: Option: environment.xfce.excludePackages
documents.content: Which packages XFCE should exclude from the default environment

documents.title: Option: fileSystems
documents.content:
The file systems to be mounted. It must include an entry for the root directory (mountPoint = "/"). Each entry in the list is an attribute set with the following fields: mountPoint, device, fsType (a file system type recognised by {command}mount), and options (the mount options passed to {command}mount using the {option}-o flag; defaults to [ "defaults" ]).
Instead of specifying device, you can also specify a volume label (label) for file systems that support it, such as ext2/ext3 (see {command}mke2fs -L).

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.autoFormat
documents.content: If the device does not currently contain a filesystem (as determined by {command}blkid), then automatically format it with the filesystem type specified in {option}fsType. Use with caution.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.autoResize
documents.content: If set, the filesystem is grown to its maximum size before being mounted. (This is typically the size of the containing partition.) This is currently only supported for ext2/3/4 filesystems that are mounted during early boot.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.depends
documents.content:
List of paths that should be mounted before this one. This filesystem's {option}device and {option}mountPoint are always checked and do not need to be included explicitly. If a path is added to this list, any other filesystem whose mount point is a parent of the path will be mounted before this filesystem. The paths do not need to actually be the {option}mountPoint of some other filesystem.
This is useful for mounts which require keys and/or configuration files residing on another filesystem.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.device
documents.content:
The device as passed to mount.
This can be any of:
a filename of a block special device such as /dev/sdc3
a tag such as UUID=fdd68895-c307-4549-8c9c-90e44c71f5b7
(for bind mounts only) the source path
something else depending on the {option}fsType. For example, nfs device may look like knuth.cwi.nl:/dir

This is called device in {manpage}mount(8) and fs_spec in {manpage}fstab(5).

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the filesystem mount.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.encrypted.blkDev
documents.content: Location of the backing encrypted device.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.encrypted.enable
documents.content: The block device is backed by an encrypted one, adds this device as a initrd luks entry.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.encrypted.keyFile
documents.content: Path to a keyfile used to unlock the backing encrypted device. When systemd stage 1 is not enabled, at the time this keyfile is accessed, the neededForBoot filesystems (see utils.fsNeededForBoot) will have been mounted under /mnt-root, so the keyfile path should usually start with "/mnt-root/". When systemd stage 1 is enabled, fsNeededForBoot file systems will be mounted as needed under /sysroot, and the keyfile will not be accessed until its requisite mounts are done.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.encrypted.label
documents.content: Label of the unlocked encrypted device. Set fileSystems.<name?>.device to /dev/mapper/<label> to mount the unlocked device.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.fsType
documents.content:
Type of the file system.
This is the fstype passed to -t in the {manpage}mount(8) command, and is called fs_vfstype in {manpage}fstab(5).

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.label
documents.content: Label of the device. This simply sets {option}device to /dev/disk/by-label/${label}. Note that devices will not have a label unless they contain a filesystem which supports labels, such as ext4 or fat32.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.mountPoint
documents.content:
Location where the file system will be mounted.
This is called mountpoint in {manpage}mount(8) and fs_file in {manpage}fstab(5)

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.neededForBoot
documents.content: If set, this file system will be mounted in the initial ramdisk. Note that the file system will always be mounted in the initial ramdisk if its mount point is one of the following: {file}/, {file}/nix, {file}/nix/store, {file}/var, {file}/var/log, {file}/var/lib, {file}/var/lib/nixos, {file}/etc, {file}/usr.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.noCheck
documents.content: Disable running fsck on this filesystem.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.options
documents.content:
Options used to mount the file system.
This is called options in {manpage}mount(8) and fs_mntops in {manpage}fstab(5)
Some options that can be used for all mounts are documented in {manpage}mount(8) under FILESYSTEM-INDEPENDENT MOUNT OPTIONS.
Options that systemd understands are documented in {manpage}systemd.mount(5) under FSTAB.
Each filesystem supports additional options, see the docs for that filesystem.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.overlay.lowerdir
documents.content:
The list of path(s) to the lowerdir(s).
To create a writable overlay, you MUST provide an upperdir and a workdir.
You can create a read-only overlay when you provide multiple (at least 2!) lowerdirs and neither an upperdir nor a workdir.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.overlay.upperdir
documents.content:
The path to the upperdir.
If this is null, a read-only overlay is created using the lowerdir.
If the filesystem is neededForBoot, this will be prefixed with /sysroot, unless useStage1BaseDirectories is set to true.
If you set this to some value you MUST also set workdir.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.overlay.useStage1BaseDirectories
documents.content:
If enabled, lowerdir, upperdir and workdir will be prefixed with /sysroot.
Disabling this can be useful to create an overlay over directories which aren't on the real root.
Disabling this does not work with the scripted (i.e. non-systemd) initrd.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.overlay.workdir
documents.content:
The path to the workdir.
If the filesystem is neededForBoot, this will be prefixed with /sysroot, unless useStage1BaseDirectories is set to true.
This MUST be set if you set upperdir.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.stratis.poolUuid
documents.content:
UUID of the stratis pool that the fs is located in
This is only relevant if you are using stratis.

documents.title: Option: fonts.enableDefaultPackages
documents.content: Enable a basic set of fonts providing several styles and families and reasonable coverage of Unicode.

documents.title: Option: fonts.enableGhostscriptFonts
documents.content: Whether to add the fonts provided by Ghostscript (such as various URW fonts and the “Base-14” Postscript fonts) to the list of system fonts, making them available to X11 applications.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontDir.decompressFonts
documents.content: Whether to decompress fonts in {file}/run/current-system/sw/share/X11/fonts.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontDir.enable
documents.content: Whether to create a directory with links to all fonts in {file}/run/current-system/sw/share/X11/fonts.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.allowBitmaps
documents.content: Allow bitmap fonts. Set to false to ban all bitmap fonts.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.allowType1
documents.content: Allow Type-1 fonts. Default is false because of poor rendering.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.antialias
documents.content: Enable font antialiasing. At high resolution (> 200 DPI), antialiasing has no visible effect; users of such displays may want to disable this option.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.cache32Bit
documents.content: Generate system fonts cache for 32-bit applications.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.defaultFonts.emoji
documents.content:
System-wide default emoji font(s). Multiple fonts may be listed in case a font does not support all emoji.
Note that fontconfig matches color emoji fonts preferentially, so if you want to use a black and white font while having a color font installed (eg. Noto Color Emoji installed alongside Noto Emoji), fontconfig will still choose the color font even when it is later in the list.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.defaultFonts.monospace
documents.content: System-wide default monospace font(s). Multiple fonts may be listed in case multiple languages must be supported.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.defaultFonts.sansSerif
documents.content: System-wide default sans serif font(s). Multiple fonts may be listed in case multiple languages must be supported.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.defaultFonts.serif
documents.content: System-wide default serif font(s). Multiple fonts may be listed in case multiple languages must be supported.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.enable
documents.content: If enabled, a Fontconfig configuration file will be built pointing to a set of default fonts. If you don't care about running X11 applications or any other program that uses Fontconfig, you can turn this option off and prevent a dependency on all those fonts.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.hinting.autohint
documents.content: Enable the autohinter in place of the default interpreter. The results are usually lower quality than correctly-hinted fonts, but better than unhinted fonts.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.hinting.enable
documents.content: Enable font hinting. Hinting aligns glyphs to pixel boundaries to improve rendering sharpness at low resolution. At high resolution (> 200 dpi) hinting will do nothing (at best); users of such displays may want to disable this option.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.hinting.style
documents.content:
Hintstyle is the amount of font reshaping done to line up to the grid.
slight will make the font more fuzzy to line up to the grid but will be better in retaining font shape, while full will be a crisp font that aligns well to the pixel grid but will lose a greater amount of font shape.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.includeUserConf
documents.content: Include the user configuration from {file}~/.config/fontconfig/fonts.conf or {file}~/.config/fontconfig/conf.d.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.localConf
documents.content: System-wide customization file contents, has higher priority than defaultFonts settings.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.subpixel.lcdfilter
documents.content: FreeType LCD filter. At high resolution (> 200 DPI), LCD filtering has no visible effect; users of such displays may want to select none.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.subpixel.rgba
documents.content: Subpixel order. The overwhelming majority of displays are rgb in their normal orientation. Select vrgb for mounting such a display 90 degrees clockwise from its normal orientation or vbgr for mounting 90 degrees counter-clockwise. Select bgr in the unlikely event of mounting 180 degrees from the normal orientation. Reverse these directions in the improbable event that the display's native subpixel order is bgr.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.useEmbeddedBitmaps
documents.content: Use embedded bitmaps in fonts like Calibri.

documents.title: Option: fonts.packages
documents.content: List of primary font packages.

documents.title: Option: gtk.iconCache.enable
documents.content: Whether to build icon theme caches for GTK applications.

documents.title: Option: hardware.acpilight.enable
documents.content: Enable acpilight. This will allow brightness control via xbacklight from users in the video group

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.cardAliases
documents.content:
Assign custom names and reorder the sound cards.
::: {.note} You can find the card ids by looking at /proc/asound/cards. :::

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.cardAliases.<name>.driver
documents.content: Name of the kernel module that provides the card.

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.cardAliases.<name>.id
documents.content: The ID of the sound card

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.config
documents.content:
The content of the system-wide ALSA configuration (/etc/asound.conf).
Documentation of the configuration language and examples can be found in the unofficial ALSA wiki: https://alsa.opensrc.org/Asoundrc

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.controls
documents.content: Virtual volume controls (softvols) to add to a sound card. These can be used to control the volume of specific applications or a digital output device (HDMI video card).

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.controls.<name>.card
documents.content: Name of the PCM card to control (slave).

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.controls.<name>.device
documents.content: Name of the PCM device to control (slave).

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.controls.<name>.maxVolume
documents.content: The maximum volume in dB.

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.controls.<name>.name
documents.content: Name of the control, as it appears in alsamixer. If null it will be the same as the softvol device name.

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.defaultDevice.capture
documents.content:
The default capture device (i.e. microphone). Leave empty to let ALSA pick the default automatically.
::: {.note} The device can be changed at runtime by setting the ALSA_AUDIO_IN environment variables (but only before starting a program). :::

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.defaultDevice.playback
documents.content:
The default playback device. Leave empty to let ALSA pick the default automatically.
::: {.note} The device can be changed at runtime by setting the ALSA_AUDIO_OUT environment variables (but only before starting a program). :::

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.deviceAliases
documents.content: Assign custom names to sound cards.

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.enable
documents.content:
Whether to set up the user space part of the Advanced Linux Sound Architecture (ALSA)
::: {.warning} Enable this option only if you want to use ALSA as your main sound system, not if you're using a sound server (e.g. PulseAudio or Pipewire). :::

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.enableBluetooth
documents.content: Whether to enable Bluetooth audio support via BlueALSA.

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.enableOSSEmulation
documents.content: Whether to enable the OSS emulation.

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.enablePersistence
documents.content: Whether to enable ALSA sound card state saving on shutdown. This is generally not necessary if you're using an external sound server.

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.enableRecorder
documents.content:
Whether to set up a loopback device that continuously records and allows to play back audio from the computer.
The loopback device is named pcm.recorder, audio can be saved by capturing from this device as with any microphone.
::: {.note} By default the output is duplicated to the recorder assuming stereo audio, for a more complex layout you have to override the pcm.splitter device using hardware.alsa.config. See the generated /etc/asound.conf for its definition. :::

documents.title: Option: hardware.alsa.plugins
documents.content: List of ALSA plugins to be added to the search path.

documents.title: Option: hardware.amdgpu.initrd.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable loading amdgpu kernelModule in stage 1. Can fix lower resolution in boot screen during initramfs phase .

documents.title: Option: hardware.amdgpu.legacySupport.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable using amdgpu kernel driver instead of radeon for Southern Islands (Radeon HD 7000) series and Sea Islands (Radeon HD 8000) series cards. Note: this removes support for analog video outputs, which is only available in the radeon driver .

documents.title: Option: hardware.amdgpu.opencl.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable OpenCL support using ROCM runtime library.

documents.title: Option: hardware.amdgpu.overdrive.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable amdgpu overdrive mode for overclocking.

documents.title: Option: hardware.amdgpu.overdrive.ppfeaturemask
documents.content: Sets the amdgpu.ppfeaturemask kernel option. It can be used to enable the overdrive bit. Default is 0xfffd7fff as it is less likely to cause flicker issues. Setting it to 0xffffffff enables all features, but also can be unstable. See the kernel documentation for more information.

documents.title: Option: hardware.amdgpu.zluda.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable CUDA support using ZLUDA runtime library.

documents.title: Option: hardware.amdgpu.zluda.package
documents.content: The zluda package to use.

documents.title: Option: hardware.apple.touchBar.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable support for the Touch Bar on some Apple laptops using tiny-dfr.

documents.title: Option: hardware.apple.touchBar.package
documents.content: The tiny-dfr package to use.

documents.title: Option: hardware.apple.touchBar.settings
documents.content: Configuration for tiny-dfr. See example configuration for available options.

documents.title: Option: hardware.bladeRF.enable
documents.content: Enables udev rules for BladeRF devices. By default grants access to users in the "bladerf" group. You may want to install the libbladeRF package.

documents.title: Option: hardware.block.defaultScheduler
documents.content:
Default block I/O scheduler.
Unless null, the value is assigned through a udev rule matching all block devices.

documents.title: Option: hardware.block.defaultSchedulerExclude
documents.content:
Device name pattern to exclude from default scheduler assignment through {option}config.hardware.block.defaultScheduler and {option}config.hardware.block.defaultSchedulerRotational.
By default this excludes loop devices which generally do not benefit from extra I/O scheduling in addition to the scheduling already performed for their backing devices.
This setting does not affect {option}config.hardware.block.scheduler.

documents.title: Option: hardware.block.defaultSchedulerRotational
documents.content:
Default block I/O scheduler for rotational drives (e.g. hard disks).
Unless null, the value is assigned through a udev rule matching all rotational block devices.
This option takes precedence over {option}config.hardware.block.defaultScheduler.

documents.title: Option: hardware.block.scheduler
documents.content:
Assign block I/O scheduler by device name pattern.
Names are matched using the {manpage}udev(7) pattern syntax:
* : Matches zero or more characters.
? : Matches any single character.
[] : Matches any single character specified in the brackets. Ranges are supported via the - character.
| : Separates alternative patterns.
Please note that overlapping patterns may produce unexpected results. More complex configurations requiring these should instead be specified directly through custom udev rules, for example via {option}config.services.udev.extraRules, to ensure correct ordering.
Available schedulers depend on the kernel configuration but modern Linux systems typically support:
none : No‐operation scheduler with no re‐ordering of requests. Suitable for devices with fast random I/O such as NVMe SSDs.
mq-deadline : Simple latency‐oriented general‐purpose scheduler.
kyber : Simple latency‐oriented scheduler for fast multi‐queue devices like NVMe SSDs.
bfq : Complex fairness‐oriented scheduler. Higher processing overhead, but good interactive response, especially with slower devices.
Schedulers assigned through this option take precedence over {option}config.hardware.block.defaultScheduler and {option}config.hardware.block.defaultSchedulerRotational but may be overridden by other udev rules.

documents.title: Option: hardware.bluetooth.disabledPlugins
documents.content: Built-in plugins to disable

documents.title: Option: hardware.bluetooth.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable support for Bluetooth.

documents.title: Option: hardware.bluetooth.hsphfpd.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable support for hsphfpd[-prototype] implementation.

documents.title: Option: hardware.bluetooth.input
documents.content: Set configuration for the input service (/etc/bluetooth/input.conf). See https://github.com/bluez/bluez/blob/master/profiles/input/input.conf for full list of options.

documents.title: Option: hardware.bluetooth.network
documents.content: Set configuration for the network service (/etc/bluetooth/network.conf). See https://github.com/bluez/bluez/blob/master/profiles/network/network.conf for full list of options.

documents.title: Option: hardware.bluetooth.package
documents.content: The bluez package to use.

documents.title: Option: hardware.bluetooth.powerOnBoot
documents.content: Whether to power up the default Bluetooth controller on boot.

documents.title: Option: hardware.bluetooth.settings
documents.content: Set configuration for system-wide bluetooth (/etc/bluetooth/main.conf). See https://github.com/bluez/bluez/blob/master/src/main.conf for full list of options.

documents.title: Option: hardware.brillo.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable brillo in userspace. This will allow brightness control from users in the video group .

documents.title: Option: hardware.bumblebee.connectDisplay
documents.content:

documents.title: Option: hardware.display.edid.linuxhw
documents.content:
Exposes EDID files from users-sourced database at https://github.com/linuxhw/EDID
Attribute names will be mapped to EDID filenames <NAME>.bin.
Attribute values are lists of awk regexp patterns that (together) must match exactly one line in either of:
AnalogDisplay.md
DigitalDisplay.md

There is no universal way of locating your device config, but here are some practical tips:
locate your device:

find your model number (second column)
locate manufacturer (first column) and go through the list manually

narrow down results using other columns until there is only one left:

Name column
production date (Made column)
resolution Res
screen diagonal (Inch column)
as a last resort use ID from the last column

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.branch
documents.content:
The branch of the NVIDIA driver to use.
Note: if {option}hardware.nvidia.package is set, it overrides this option.
Commonly interesting branches for end users:
production, new_feature, beta: NVIDIA's official production / new feature / beta release branches.
stable: The default; the highest stable version.
latest: Whichever is newer of production and new_feature.
bleeding_edge: Whichever is newer of latest and beta.
legacy_580: The long-lived 580 series (LTSB), for GPUs that newer driver branches no longer support (often Maxwell through Volta; roughly GeForce GTX 9xx through 10xx, plus rare Volta cards like TITAN V).
vulkan_beta: The Vulkan developer beta driver, for users interested in testing new Vulkan features.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.dynamicBoost.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable dynamic Boost balances power between the CPU and the GPU for improved performance on supported laptops using the nvidia-powerd daemon. For more information, see the NVIDIA docs, on Chapter 23. Dynamic Boost on Linux .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.enabled
documents.content: True if NVIDIA support is enabled

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.forceFullCompositionPipeline
documents.content: Whether to enable forcefully the full composition pipeline. This sometimes fixes screen tearing issues. This has been reported to reduce the performance of some OpenGL applications and may produce issues in WebGL. It also drastically increases the time the driver needs to clock down after load .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.gsp.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the GPU System Processor (GSP) on the video card .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.modesetting.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable kernel modesetting when using the NVIDIA proprietary driver.
Enabling this fixes screen tearing when using Optimus via PRIME (see {option}hardware.nvidia.prime.sync.enable. This is not enabled by default because it is not officially supported by NVIDIA and would not work with SLI.
Enabling this and using version 545 or newer of the proprietary NVIDIA driver causes it to provide its own framebuffer device, which can cause Wayland compositors to work when they otherwise wouldn't. .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.moduleParams
documents.content: Additional parameters to pass to the NVIDIA kernel module.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.nvidiaPersistenced
documents.content: Whether to enable nvidia-persistenced a update for NVIDIA GPU headless mode, i.e. It ensures all GPUs stay awake even during headless mode .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.nvidiaSettings
documents.content: Whether to enable nvidia-settings, NVIDIA's GUI configuration tool .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.open
documents.content: Whether to enable the open source NVIDIA kernel module.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.package
documents.content:
The NVIDIA driver package to use.
Prefer using {option}hardware.nvidia.branch when possible.
If you set this option, it is recommended to pick a package from config.boot.kernelPackages.nvidiaPackages so the driver build matches your configured kernel.
For custom versions, you can use nvidiaPackages.mkDriver; see pkgs/os-specific/linux/nvidia-x11/default.nix for examples.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.powerManagement.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable experimental power management through systemd. For more information, see the NVIDIA docs, on Chapter 21. Configuring Power Management Support .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.powerManagement.finegrained
documents.content: Whether to enable experimental power management of PRIME offload. For more information, see the NVIDIA docs, on Chapter 22. PCI-Express Runtime D3 (RTD3) Power Management .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.powerManagement.kernelSuspendNotifier
documents.content: Whether to enable NVIDIA driver support for kernel suspend notifiers, which allows the driver to be notified of suspend and resume events by the kernel, rather than relying on systemd services. Requires NVIDIA driver version 595 or newer, and the open source kernel modules. .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.allowExternalGpu
documents.content: Whether to enable configuring X to allow external NVIDIA GPUs when using Prime [Reverse] sync optimus .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.amdgpuBusId
documents.content:
Bus ID of the AMD APU. You can find it using lspci; for example if lspci shows the AMD APU at "0001:02:03.4", set this option to "PCI:2@1:3:4".
lspci might omit the PCI domain (0001 in above example) if it is zero. In which case, use "@0" instead.
Please be aware that this option takes decimal address while lspci reports hexadecimal address. So for device at domain "10000", use "@65536".

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.intelBusId
documents.content:
Bus ID of the Intel GPU. You can find it using lspci; for example if lspci shows the Intel GPU at "0001:02:03.4", set this option to "PCI:2@1:3:4".
lspci might omit the PCI domain (0001 in above example) if it is zero. In which case, use "@0" instead.
Please be aware that this option takes decimal address while lspci reports hexadecimal address. So for device at domain "10000", use "@65536".

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.nvidiaBusId
documents.content:
Bus ID of the NVIDIA GPU. You can find it using lspci; for example if lspci shows the NVIDIA GPU at "0001:02:03.4", set this option to "PCI:2@1:3:4".
lspci might omit the PCI domain (0001 in above example) if it is zero. In which case, use "@0" instead.
Please be aware that this option takes decimal address while lspci reports hexadecimal address. So for device at domain "10000", use "@65536".

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.offload.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable render offload support using the NVIDIA proprietary driver via PRIME.
If this is enabled, then the bus IDs of the NVIDIA and Intel/AMD GPUs have to be specified ({option}hardware.nvidia.prime.nvidiaBusId and {option}hardware.nvidia.prime.intelBusId or {option}hardware.nvidia.prime.amdgpuBusId) .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.offload.enableOffloadCmd
documents.content:
Whether to enable adding a nvidia-offload convenience script to {option}environment.systemPackages for offloading programs to an nvidia device. To work, you must also enable {option}hardware.nvidia.prime.offload.enable or {option}hardware.nvidia.prime.reverseSync.enable.
Example usage: nvidia-offload sauerbraten_client
This script can be renamed with {option}hardware.nvidia.prime.offload.enableOffloadCmd. .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.offload.offloadCmdMainProgram
documents.content: Specifies the CLI name of the {option}hardware.nvidia.prime.offload.enableOffloadCmd convenience script for offloading programs to an nvidia device.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.reverseSync.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable NVIDIA Optimus support using the NVIDIA proprietary driver via reverse PRIME. If enabled, the Intel/AMD GPU will be used for all rendering, while enabling output to displays attached only to the NVIDIA GPU without a multiplexer.
Warning: This feature is relatively new, depending on your system this might work poorly. AMD support, especially so. See: https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/the-all-new-outputsink-feature-aka-reverse-prime/129828
Note that this option only has any effect if the "nvidia" driver is specified in {option}services.xserver.videoDrivers, and it should preferably be the only driver there.
If this is enabled, then the bus IDs of the NVIDIA and Intel/AMD GPUs have to be specified ({option}hardware.nvidia.prime.nvidiaBusId and {option}hardware.nvidia.prime.intelBusId or {option}hardware.nvidia.prime.amdgpuBusId).
If you enable this, you may want to also enable kernel modesetting for the NVIDIA driver ({option}hardware.nvidia.modesetting.enable) in order to prevent tearing.
Note that this configuration will only be successful when a display manager for which the {option}services.xserver.displayManager.setupCommands option is supported is used .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.reverseSync.setupCommands.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable configure the display manager to be able to use the outputs attached to the NVIDIA GPU. Disable in order to configure the NVIDIA GPU outputs manually using xrandr. Note that this configuration will only be successful when a display manager for which the {option}services.xserver.displayManager.setupCommands option is supported is used .

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.sync.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable NVIDIA Optimus support using the NVIDIA proprietary driver via PRIME. If enabled, the NVIDIA GPU will be always on and used for all rendering, while enabling output to displays attached only to the integrated Intel/AMD GPU without a multiplexer.
Note that this option only has any effect if the "nvidia" driver is specified in {option}services.xserver.videoDrivers, and it should preferably be the only driver there.
If this is enabled, then the bus IDs of the NVIDIA and Intel/AMD GPUs have to be specified ({option}hardware.nvidia.prime.nvidiaBusId and {option}hardware.nvidia.prime.intelBusId or {option}hardware.nvidia.prime.amdgpuBusId).
If you enable this, you may want to also enable kernel modesetting for the NVIDIA driver ({option}hardware.nvidia.modesetting.enable) in order to prevent tearing.
Note that this configuration will only be successful when a display manager for which the {option}services.xserver.displayManager.setupCommands option is supported is used .

When enabled, will automatically register the "dsseries" SANE backend.
This supports the Brother DSmobile scanner series, including the DS-620, DS-720D, DS-820W, and DS-920DW scanners.

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.draghys
documents.content: The drag hysteresis controls how hard it is to drag with z-axis pressed.

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.drift_time
documents.content:
This parameter controls the period of time to test for a 'hands off' condition (i.e. when no force is applied) before a drift (noise) calibration occurs.
IBM Trackpoints have a feature to compensate for drift by recalibrating themselves periodically. By default, if for 0.5 seconds there is no change in position, it's used as the new zero. This duration is too low. Often, the calibration happens when the trackpoint is in fact being used.

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.emulateWheel

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.enable

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.ext_dev

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.fakeButtons
documents.content: Switch to "bare" PS/2 mouse support in case Trackpoint buttons are not recognized properly. This can happen for example on models like the L430, T450, T450s, on which the Trackpoint buttons are actually a part of the Synaptics touchpad.

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.inertia

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.mindrag

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.press_to_select

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.reach

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.sensitivity

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.skipback

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.speed

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.thresh

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.upthresh

documents.title: Option: hardware.trackpoint.ztime

documents.title: Option: hardware.tuxedo-drivers.enable

Whether to enable The tuxedo-drivers driver enables access to the following on TUXEDO notebooks:
Driver for Fn-keys
SysFS control of brightness/color/mode for most TUXEDO keyboards
Hardware I/O driver for TUXEDO Control Center

For more inforation it is best to check at the source code description: https://gitlab.com/tuxedocomputers/development/packages/tuxedo-drivers .

documents.title: Option: hardware.tuxedo-drivers.settings.charging-priority
documents.content:
These options manage the trade-off between battery charging and CPU performance when the USB-C power supply cannot provide sufficient power for both simultaneously:
charge_battery prioritizes battery charging (driver default)
performance prioritizes maximum CPU performance

documents.title: Option: hardware.tuxedo-drivers.settings.charging-profile
documents.content:
The maximum charge level to help reduce battery wear:
high_capacity charges to 100% (driver default)
balanced charges to 90%
stationary charges to 80% (maximum lifespan)

Note: Regardless of the configured charging profile, the operating system will always report the battery as being charged to 100%.

documents.title: Option: hardware.tuxedo-drivers.settings.fn-lock
documents.content:
Enables or disables the laptop keyboard's Function (Fn) lock at boot.
When set to true, the Fn lock is enabled, allowing the function keys (F1–F12) to control brightness, volume etc.
