documents.content:
Controller-specific quirk flags, keyed by MAC address. Flags are combined as a bitmask to address compatibility issues with specific controllers.
The value is a sum of individual flag values. For example, to apply flags 1, 2, and 4, use 7 (1 + 2 + 4). To apply flags 2, 4, and 32, use 38 (2 + 4 + 32).
See https://github.com/atar-axis/xpadneo/blob/master/docs/CONFIGURATION.md for available quirk flags and their values.

documents.title: Option: hardware.xpadneo.rumbleAttenuation
documents.content:
Force feedback attenuation settings. Higher values reduce rumble strength.
See https://github.com/atar-axis/xpadneo/blob/master/docs/CONFIGURATION.md for more information.

documents.title: Option: hardware.xpadneo.rumbleAttenuation.overall
documents.content: Overall force feedback attenuation as a percentage. 0 means full rumble, 100 means no rumble. Applies to both main and trigger rumble.

documents.title: Option: hardware.xpadneo.rumbleAttenuation.triggers
documents.content: Extra attenuation for trigger rumble as a percentage, applied on top of {option}overall. For example, overall = 50 and triggers = 50 results in 50% main rumble and 25% trigger rumble. Set to 100 to disable trigger rumble while keeping main rumble. null means no extra trigger attenuation.

documents.title: Option: hardware.xpadneo.settings
documents.content:
Kernel module parameters for hid_xpadneo. These are passed directly to the module via modprobe.
See https://github.com/atar-axis/xpadneo/blob/master/docs/CONFIGURATION.md for available parameters and their values.

documents.title: Option: i18n.defaultCharset
documents.content: The default locale character set.

documents.title: Option: i18n.defaultLocale
documents.content: The default locale. It determines the language for program messages, the format for dates and times, sort order, and so on. Setting the default character set is done via {option}i18n.defaultCharset.

documents.title: Option: i18n.extraLocaleSettings
documents.content:
A set of additional system-wide locale settings other than LANG which can be configured with {option}i18n.defaultLocale. Note that the /UTF-8 suffix used in {option}i18n.extraLocales indicates a character set, and it must not be added manually here. To use a non-UTF-8 character set such as ISO-XXXX-8, the {option}i18n.localeCharsets can be used.
Note that if the LANGUAGE key is used in this option, it is ignored when computing the locales required to be installed, because the possible values of this key are more diverse and flexible then the others.

documents.title: Option: i18n.extraLocales
documents.content: Additional locales that the system should support, besides the ones configured with {option}i18n.defaultLocale and {option}i18n.extraLocaleSettings. Set this to "all" to install all available locales.

documents.title: Option: i18n.glibcLocales
documents.content:
Customized pkg.glibcLocales package.
Changing this option can disable handling of i18n.defaultLocale and supportedLocale.

documents.title: Option: i18n.imperativeLocale
documents.content:
Whether to enable imperative locale and keyboard management via localectl.
When enabled, locale and keyboard settings can be changed at runtime using localectl set-locale and localectl set-keymap. When disabled (the default), these settings are managed declaratively through {option}i18n.defaultLocale, {option}i18n.extraLocaleSettings, and {option}console.keyMap. .

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable an additional input method type.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.enableGtk2
documents.content: Whether to enable Gtk2 support.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.enableGtk3
documents.content: Whether to enable Gtk3 support.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.enabled
documents.content: Deprecated - use type and enable = true instead

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.fcitx5.addons
documents.content: Enabled Fcitx5 addons.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.fcitx5.ignoreUserConfig
documents.content: Ignore the user configures. Warning: When this is enabled, the user config files are totally ignored and the user dict can't be saved and loaded.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.fcitx5.quickPhrase
documents.content: Quick phrases.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.fcitx5.quickPhraseFiles
documents.content: Quick phrase files.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.fcitx5.settings.addons
documents.content: The addon configures in conf folder in ini format with global sections. Each item is written to the corresponding file.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.fcitx5.settings.globalOptions
documents.content: The global options in config file in ini format.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.fcitx5.settings.inputMethod
documents.content: The input method configure in profile file in ini format.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.fcitx5.waylandFrontend
documents.content: Use the Wayland input method frontend. See Using Fcitx 5 on Wayland.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.ibus.engines
documents.content: Enabled IBus engines. Available engines are: anthy, bamboo, cangjie, chewing, hangul, libpinyin, libthai, m17n, mozc, mozc-ut, pinyin, rime, table, table-chinese, table-others, typing-booster, typing-booster-unwrapped, uniemoji.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.ibus.panel
documents.content: Replace the IBus panel with another panel.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.ibus.waylandFrontend
documents.content: Use the Wayland input method frontend. This doesn't set GTK_IM_MODULE and QT_IM_MODULE environment variables. See Using Fcitx 5 on Wayland.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.kime.daemonModules
documents.content: List of enabled daemon modules

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.kime.extraConfig
documents.content: extra kime configuration. Refer to https://github.com/Riey/kime/blob/v3.1.1/docs/CONFIGURATION.md for details on supported values.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.kime.iconColor
documents.content: Color of the indicator icon

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.type
documents.content:
Select the enabled input method. Input methods is a software to input symbols that are not available on standard input devices.
Input methods are specially used to input Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters.
Currently the following input methods are available in NixOS:
ibus: The intelligent input bus, extra input engines can be added using i18n.inputMethod.ibus.engines.
fcitx5: The next generation of fcitx, addons (including engines, dictionaries, skins) can be added using i18n.inputMethod.fcitx5.addons.
nabi: A Korean input method based on XIM. Nabi doesn't support Qt 5.
uim: The universal input method, is a library with a XIM bridge. uim mainly support Chinese, Japanese and Korean.
hime: An extremely easy-to-use input method framework.
kime: Koream IME.

documents.title: Option: i18n.inputMethod.uim.toolbar
documents.content: selected UIM toolbar.

documents.title: Option: i18n.localeCharsets
documents.content:
Per each {option}i18n.extraLocaleSettings, choose the character set to use for it. Essentially defaults to UTF-8 for all of them.
Note that for a locale category that uses the C locale, setting a character set to it via this setting is ignored.

documents.title: Option: image.modules
documents.content: image-specific NixOS Modules used for system.build.images.

documents.title: Option: lib
documents.content: This option allows modules to define helper functions, constants, etc.

documents.title: Option: location.latitude
documents.content: Your current latitude, between -90.0 and 90.0. Must be provided along with longitude.

documents.title: Option: location.longitude
documents.content: Your current longitude, between between -180.0 and 180.0. Must be provided along with latitude.

documents.title: Option: location.provider
documents.content: The location provider to use for determining your location. If set to manual you must also provide latitude/longitude.

documents.title: Option: meta.maintainers
documents.content:
List of maintainers of each module. This option should be defined at most once per module.
The option value is not a list of maintainers, but an attribute set that maps module file names to lists of maintainers.

documents.title: Option: meta.teams
documents.content: List of team maintainers of each module. This option should be defined at most once per module.

documents.title: Option: networking.bonds
documents.content: This option allows you to define bond devices that aggregate multiple, underlying networking interfaces together. The value of this option is an attribute set. Each attribute specifies a bond, with the attribute name specifying the name of the bond's network interface

documents.title: Option: networking.bonds.<name>.driverOptions
documents.content: Options for the bonding driver. Documentation can be found in https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/networking/bonding.txt

documents.title: Option: networking.bonds.<name>.interfaces
documents.content: The interfaces to bond together

documents.title: Option: networking.bonds.<name>.lacp_rate
documents.content: DEPRECATED, use driverOptions. Option specifying the rate in which we'll ask our link partner to transmit LACPDU packets in 802.3ad mode.

documents.title: Option: networking.bonds.<name>.miimon
documents.content: DEPRECATED, use driverOptions. Miimon is the number of millisecond in between each round of polling by the device driver for failed links. By default polling is not enabled and the driver is trusted to properly detect and handle failure scenarios.

documents.title: Option: networking.bonds.<name>.mode
documents.content: DEPRECATED, use driverOptions. The mode which the bond will be running. The default mode for the bonding driver is balance-rr, optimizing for throughput. More information about valid modes can be found at https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/networking/bonding.txt

documents.title: Option: networking.bonds.<name>.xmit_hash_policy
documents.content: DEPRECATED, use driverOptions. Selects the transmit hash policy to use for slave selection in balance-xor, 802.3ad, and tlb modes.

documents.title: Option: networking.bridges
documents.content: This option allows you to define Ethernet bridge devices that connect physical networks together. The value of this option is an attribute set. Each attribute specifies a bridge, with the attribute name specifying the name of the bridge's network interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.bridges.<name>.interfaces
documents.content: The physical network interfaces connected by the bridge.

documents.title: Option: networking.bridges.<name>.rstp
documents.content: Whether the bridge interface should enable rstp.

documents.title: Option: networking.defaultGateway
documents.content: The default gateway. It can be left empty if it is auto-detected through DHCP. It can be specified as a string or an option set along with a network interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.defaultGateway.address
documents.content: The default gateway address.

documents.title: Option: networking.defaultGateway.interface
documents.content: The default gateway interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.defaultGateway.metric
documents.content: The default gateway metric/preference.

documents.title: Option: networking.defaultGateway.source
documents.content: The default source address.

documents.title: Option: networking.defaultGateway6
documents.content: The default ipv6 gateway. It can be left empty if it is auto-detected through DHCP. It can be specified as a string or an option set along with a network interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.defaultGateway6.address
documents.content: The default gateway address.

documents.title: Option: networking.defaultGateway6.interface
documents.content: The default gateway interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.defaultGateway6.metric
documents.content: The default gateway metric/preference.

documents.title: Option: networking.defaultGateway6.source
documents.content: The default source address.

documents.title: Option: networking.defaultGatewayWindowSize
documents.content: The window size of the default gateway. It limits maximal data bursts that TCP peers are allowed to send to us.

documents.title: Option: networking.dhcpcd.IPv6rs
documents.content: Force enable or disable solicitation and receipt of IPv6 Router Advertisements. This is required, for example, when using a static unique local IPv6 address (ULA) and global IPv6 address auto-configuration with SLAAC.

documents.title: Option: networking.dhcpcd.allowInterfaces
documents.content: Enable the DHCP client for any interface whose name matches any of the shell glob patterns in this list. Any interface not explicitly matched by this pattern will be denied. This pattern only applies when non-null.

documents.title: Option: networking.dhcpcd.allowSetuid
documents.content: Whether to relax the security sandbox to allow running setuid binaries (e.g. sudo) in the dhcpcd hooks.

documents.title: Option: networking.dhcpcd.denyInterfaces
documents.content: Disable the DHCP client for any interface whose name matches any of the shell glob patterns in this list. The purpose of this option is to blacklist virtual interfaces such as those created by Xen, libvirt, LXC, etc.

documents.title: Option: networking.dhcpcd.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable dhcpcd for device configuration. This is mainly to explicitly disable dhcpcd (for example when using networkd).

documents.title: Option: networking.dhcpcd.extraConfig
documents.content: Literal string to append to the config file generated for dhcpcd.

documents.title: Option: networking.dhcpcd.persistent
documents.content: Whether to leave interfaces configured on dhcpcd daemon shutdown. Set to true if you have your root or store mounted over the network or this machine accepts SSH connections through DHCP interfaces and clients should be notified when it shuts down.

documents.title: Option: networking.dhcpcd.runHook
documents.content:
Shell code that will be run after all other hooks. See man dhcpcd-run-hooks for details on what is possible.
::: {.note} To use sudo or similar tools in your script you may have to set:
In addition, as most of the filesystem is inaccessible to dhcpcd by default, you may want to define some exceptions, e.g.
:::

documents.title: Option: networking.dhcpcd.setHostname
documents.content:
Whether to set the machine hostname based on the information received from the DHCP server.
::: {.note} The hostname will be changed only if the current one is the empty string, localhost or nixos.
Polkit () is also required. :::

documents.title: Option: networking.dhcpcd.wait
documents.content: This option specifies when the dhcpcd service will fork to background. If set to "background", dhcpcd will fork to background immediately. If set to "ipv4" or "ipv6", dhcpcd will wait for the corresponding IP address to be assigned. If set to "any", dhcpcd will wait for any type (IPv4 or IPv6) to be assigned. If set to "both", dhcpcd will wait for both an IPv4 and an IPv6 address before forking. The option "if-carrier-up" is equivalent to "any" if either ethernet is plugged or WiFi is powered, and to "background" otherwise.

documents.title: Option: networking.domain
documents.content:
The system domain name. Used to populate the {option}fqdn value.
::: {.warning} The domain name is not configured for DNS resolution purposes, see {option}search instead. :::

documents.title: Option: networking.enableB43Firmware
documents.content: Turn on this option if you want firmware for the NICs supported by the b43 module.

documents.title: Option: networking.enableIPv6
documents.content: Whether to enable support for IPv6.

documents.title: Option: networking.enableIntel2200BGFirmware
documents.content: Turn on this option if you want firmware for the Intel PRO/Wireless 2200BG to be loaded automatically. This is required if you want to use this device.

documents.title: Option: networking.extraHosts
documents.content: Additional verbatim entries to be appended to {file}/etc/hosts. For adding hosts from derivation results, use {option}networking.hostFiles instead.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.allowPing
documents.content: Whether to respond to incoming ICMPv4 echo requests ("pings"). ICMPv6 pings are always allowed because the larger address space of IPv6 makes network scanning much less effective.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.allowedTCPPortRanges
documents.content: A range of TCP ports on which incoming connections are accepted.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.allowedTCPPorts
documents.content: List of TCP ports on which incoming connections are accepted.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.allowedUDPPortRanges
documents.content: Range of open UDP ports.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.allowedUDPPorts
documents.content: List of open UDP ports.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.autoLoadConntrackHelpers
documents.content:
Whether to auto-load connection-tracking helpers. See the description at networking.firewall.connectionTrackingModules
(needs kernel 3.5+)

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.backend
documents.content: Underlying implementation for the firewall service.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.checkReversePath
documents.content:
Performs a reverse path filter test on a packet. If a reply to the packet would not be sent via the same interface that the packet arrived on, it is refused.
If using asymmetric routing or other complicated routing, set this option to loose mode or disable it and setup your own counter-measures.
This option can be either true (or "strict"), "loose" (only drop the packet if the source address is not reachable via any interface) or false.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.connectionTrackingModules
documents.content:
List of connection-tracking helpers that are auto-loaded. The complete list of possible values is given in the example.
As helpers can pose as a security risk, it is advised to set this to an empty list and disable the setting networking.firewall.autoLoadConntrackHelpers unless you know what you are doing. Connection tracking is disabled by default.
Loading of helpers is recommended to be done through the CT target. More info: https://home.regit.org/netfilter-en/secure-use-of-helpers/

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the firewall. This is a simple stateful firewall that blocks connection attempts to unauthorised TCP or UDP ports on this machine.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.extraCommands
documents.content:
Additional shell commands executed as part of the firewall initialisation script. These are executed just before the final "reject" firewall rule is added, so they can be used to allow packets that would otherwise be refused.
This option only works with the iptables based firewall.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.extraForwardRules
documents.content:
Additional nftables rules to be appended to the forward-allow chain.
This option only works with the nftables based firewall.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.extraInputRules
documents.content:
Additional nftables rules to be appended to the input-allow chain.
This option only works with the nftables based firewall.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.extraPackages
documents.content: Additional packages to be included in the environment of the system as well as the path of networking.firewall.extraCommands.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.extraReversePathFilterRules
documents.content:
Additional nftables rules to be appended to the rpfilter-allow chain.
This option only works with the nftables based firewall.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.extraStopCommands
documents.content:
Additional shell commands executed as part of the firewall shutdown script. These are executed just after the removal of the NixOS input rule, or if the service enters a failed state.
This option only works with the iptables based firewall.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.filterForward
documents.content:
Enable filtering in IP forwarding.
This option only works with the nftables based firewall.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.interfaces
documents.content: Interface-specific open ports.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.interfaces.<name>.allowedTCPPortRanges
documents.content: A range of TCP ports on which incoming connections are accepted.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.interfaces.<name>.allowedTCPPorts
documents.content: List of TCP ports on which incoming connections are accepted.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.interfaces.<name>.allowedUDPPortRanges
documents.content: Range of open UDP ports.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.interfaces.<name>.allowedUDPPorts
documents.content: List of open UDP ports.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.logRefusedConnections
documents.content: Whether to log rejected or dropped incoming connections. Note: The logs are found in the kernel logs, i.e. dmesg or journalctl -k.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.logRefusedPackets
documents.content: Whether to log all rejected or dropped incoming packets. This tends to give a lot of log messages, so it's mostly useful for debugging. Note: The logs are found in the kernel logs, i.e. dmesg or journalctl -k.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.logRefusedUnicastsOnly
documents.content: If {option}networking.firewall.logRefusedPackets and this option are enabled, then only log packets specifically directed at this machine, i.e., not broadcasts or multicasts.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.logReversePathDrops
documents.content: Logs dropped packets failing the reverse path filter test if the option networking.firewall.checkReversePath is enabled.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.package
documents.content: The package to use for running the firewall service.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.pingLimit
documents.content:
If pings are allowed, this allows setting rate limits on them.
For the iptables based firewall, it should be set like "--limit 1/minute --limit-burst 5".
For the nftables based firewall, it should be set like "2/second" or "1/minute burst 5 packets".

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.rejectPackets
documents.content: If set, refused packets are rejected rather than dropped (ignored). This means that an ICMP "port unreachable" error message is sent back to the client (or a TCP RST packet in case of an existing connection). Rejecting packets makes port scanning somewhat easier.

documents.title: Option: networking.firewall.trustedInterfaces
documents.content: Traffic coming in from these interfaces will be accepted unconditionally. Traffic from the loopback (lo) interface will always be accepted.

documents.title: Option: networking.fooOverUDP
documents.content: This option allows you to configure Foo Over UDP and Generic UDP Encapsulation endpoints. See {manpage}ip-fou(8) for details.

documents.title: Option: networking.fooOverUDP.<name>.local
documents.content: Local address (and optionally device) to bind to using the given port.

documents.title: Option: networking.fooOverUDP.<name>.local.address
documents.content: Local address to bind to. The address must be available when the FOU endpoint is created, using the scripted network setup this can be achieved either by setting dev or adding dependency information to systemd.services.<name>-fou-encap; it isn't supported when using networkd.

documents.title: Option: networking.fooOverUDP.<name>.local.dev
documents.content: Network device to bind to.

documents.title: Option: networking.fooOverUDP.<name>.port
documents.content: Local port of the encapsulation UDP socket.

documents.title: Option: networking.fooOverUDP.<name>.protocol
documents.content: Protocol number of the encapsulated packets. Specifying null (the default) creates a GUE endpoint, specifying a protocol number will create a FOU endpoint.

documents.title: Option: networking.fqdn
documents.content:
The fully qualified domain name (FQDN) of this host. By default, it is the result of combining networking.hostName and networking.domain.
Using this option will result in an evaluation error if the hostname is empty or no domain is specified.
Modules that accept a mere networking.hostName but prefer a fully qualified domain name may use networking.fqdnOrHostName instead.

documents.title: Option: networking.fqdnOrHostName
documents.content:
Either the fully qualified domain name (FQDN), or just the host name if it does not exist.
This is a convenience option for modules to read instead of fqdn when a mere hostName is also an acceptable value; this option does not throw an error when domain or fqdn is unset.

documents.title: Option: networking.getaddrinfo.enable
documents.content:
Enables custom address sorting configuration for {manpage}getaddrinfo(3) according to RFC 3484.
This option generates a {file}/etc/gai.conf file to override the default address sorting tables, as described in {manpage}gai.conf(5).
This setting is only applicable when using the GNU C Library (glibc). It has no effect with other libc implementations.

documents.title: Option: networking.getaddrinfo.label
documents.content:
Adds entries to the label table, as described in section 2.1 of RFC 3484.
If any label entries are provided, the glibc’s default label table is ignored.

documents.title: Option: networking.getaddrinfo.precedence
documents.content:
Similar to {option}networking.getaddrinfo.label, but this option defines entries for the precedence table instead.
See sections 2.1 and 10.3 of RFC 3484 for details.
Providing any value will disable the glibc's default precedence table.

documents.title: Option: networking.getaddrinfo.reload
documents.content:
Determines whether a process should detect changes to the configuration file since it was last read.
If enabled, the file is re-read automatically. This may cause issues in multithreaded applications and is generally discouraged.

documents.title: Option: networking.getaddrinfo.scopev4
documents.content:
Adds custom rules to the IPv4 scope table.
By default, the scope IDs described in section 3.2 of RFC 6724 are used.
Modifying these values is rarely necessary.

documents.title: Option: networking.greTunnels
documents.content: This option allows you to define Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) tunnels.

documents.title: Option: networking.greTunnels.<name>.dev
documents.content: The underlying network device on which the tunnel resides.

documents.title: Option: networking.greTunnels.<name>.local
documents.content: The address of the local endpoint which the remote side should send packets to.

documents.title: Option: networking.greTunnels.<name>.remote
documents.content: The address of the remote endpoint to forward traffic over.

documents.title: Option: networking.greTunnels.<name>.ttl
documents.content: The time-to-live/hoplimit of the connection to the remote tunnel endpoint.

documents.title: Option: networking.greTunnels.<name>.type
documents.content: Whether the tunnel routes layer 2 (tap) or layer 3 (tun) traffic.

documents.title: Option: networking.hostFiles
documents.content: Files that should be concatenated together to form {file}/etc/hosts.

documents.title: Option: networking.hostId
documents.content:
The 32-bit host ID of the machine, formatted as 8 hexadecimal characters.
You should try to make this ID unique among your machines. You can generate a random 32-bit ID using the following commands:
head -c 8 /etc/machine-id
(this derives it from the machine-id that systemd generates) or
head -c4 /dev/urandom | od -A none -t x4
The primary use case is to ensure when using ZFS that a pool isn't imported accidentally on a wrong machine.

documents.title: Option: networking.hostName
documents.content:
The name of the machine. Leave it empty if you want to obtain it from a DHCP server (if using DHCP). The hostname must be a valid DNS label (see RFC 1035 section 2.3.1: "Preferred name syntax", RFC 1123 section 2.1: "Host Names and Numbers") and as such must not contain the domain part. This means that the hostname must start with a letter or digit, end with a letter or digit, and have as interior characters only letters, digits, and hyphen. The maximum length is 63 characters. Additionally it is recommended to only use lower-case characters. If (e.g. for legacy reasons) a FQDN is required as the Linux kernel network node hostname (uname --nodename) the option boot.kernel.sysctl."kernel.hostname" can be used as a workaround (but the 64 character limit still applies).
WARNING: Do not use underscores (_) or you may run into unexpected issues.

documents.title: Option: networking.hosts
documents.content: Locally defined maps of hostnames to IP addresses.

documents.title: Option: networking.ifstate.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable networking using IfState.

documents.title: Option: networking.ifstate.package
documents.content: The ifstate package to use.

documents.title: Option: networking.ifstate.settings
documents.content: Content of IfState's configuration file. See https://ifstate.net/2.2/schema/ for details.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces
documents.content:
The configuration for each network interface.
Please note that {option}systemd.network.netdevs has more features and is better maintained. When building new things, it is advised to use that instead.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv4.addresses
documents.content: List of IPv4 addresses that will be statically assigned to the interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv4.addresses.*.address
documents.content: IPv4 address of the interface. Leave empty to configure the interface using DHCP.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv4.addresses.*.prefixLength
documents.content: Subnet mask of the interface, specified as the number of bits in the prefix (24).

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv4.routes
documents.content:
List of extra IPv4 static routes that will be assigned to the interface.
::: {.warning} If the route type is the default unicast, then the scope is set differently depending on the value of {option}networking.useNetworkd: the script-based backend sets it to link, while networkd sets it to global. :::
If you want consistency between the two implementations, set the scope of the route manually with networking.interfaces.eth0.ipv4.routes = [{ options.scope = "global"; }] for example.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv4.routes.*.address
documents.content: IPv4 address of the network.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv4.routes.*.options
documents.content: Other route options. See the symbol OPTIONS in the {manpage}ip-route(8) manual page for the details. You may also specify metric, src, protocol, scope, from and table, which are technically not route options, in the sense used in the manual.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv4.routes.*.prefixLength
documents.content: Subnet mask of the network, specified as the number of bits in the prefix (24).

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv4.routes.*.type
documents.content:
Type of the route. See the Route types section in the {manpage}ip-route(8) manual page for the details.
Note that prohibit, blackhole, unreachable, and throw cannot be configured per device, so they are not available here. Similarly, nat hasn't been supported since kernel 2.6.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv4.routes.*.via
documents.content: IPv4 address of the next hop.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv6.addresses
documents.content: List of IPv6 addresses that will be statically assigned to the interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv6.addresses.*.address
documents.content: IPv6 address of the interface. Leave empty to configure the interface using DHCP.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv6.addresses.*.prefixLength
documents.content: Subnet mask of the interface, specified as the number of bits in the prefix (64).

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv6.routes
documents.content: List of extra IPv6 static routes that will be assigned to the interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv6.routes.*.address
documents.content: IPv6 address of the network.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv6.routes.*.options
documents.content: Other route options. See the symbol OPTIONS in the {manpage}ip-route(8) manual page for the details. You may also specify metric, src, protocol, scope, from and table, which are technically not route options, in the sense used in the manual.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv6.routes.*.prefixLength
documents.content: Subnet mask of the network, specified as the number of bits in the prefix (64).

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv6.routes.*.type
documents.content:
Type of the route. See the Route types section in the {manpage}ip-route(8) manual page for the details.
Note that prohibit, blackhole, unreachable, and throw cannot be configured per device, so they are not available here. Similarly, nat hasn't been supported since kernel 2.6.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv6.routes.*.via
documents.content: IPv6 address of the next hop.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.macAddress
documents.content: MAC address of the interface. Leave empty to use the default.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.mtu
documents.content: MTU size for packets leaving the interface. Leave empty to use the default.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.name
documents.content: Name of the interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.proxyARP
documents.content:
Turn on proxy_arp for this device. This is mainly useful for creating pseudo-bridges between a real interface and a virtual network such as VPN or a virtual machine for interfaces that don't support real bridging (most wlan interfaces). As ARP proxying acts slightly above the link-layer, below-ip traffic isn't bridged, so things like DHCP won't work. The advantage above using NAT lies in the fact that no IP addresses are shared, so all hosts are reachable/routeable.
WARNING: turns on ip-routing, so if you have multiple interfaces, you should think of the consequence and setup firewall rules to limit this.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.tempAddress
Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.useDHCP
documents.content: Whether this interface should be configured with DHCP. Overrides the default set by {option}networking.useDHCP. If null (the default), DHCP is enabled if the interface has no IPv4 addresses configured with {option}networking.interfaces.<name>.ipv4.addresses, and disabled otherwise.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.virtual
documents.content: Whether this interface is virtual and should be created by tunctl. This is mainly useful for creating bridges between a host and a virtual network such as VPN or a virtual machine.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.virtualOwner
documents.content: In case of a virtual device, the user who owns it. null will not set owner, allowing access to any user.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.virtualType
documents.content: The type of interface to create. The default is TUN for an interface name starting with "tun", otherwise TAP.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.wakeOnLan.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable wol on this interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.interfaces.<name>.wakeOnLan.policy
documents.content:
The Wake-on-LAN policy to set for the device.
The options are
phy: Wake on PHY activity
unicast: Wake on unicast messages
multicast: Wake on multicast messages
broadcast: Wake on broadcast messages
arp: Wake on ARP
magic: Wake on receipt of a magic packet

documents.title: Option: networking.ipips
documents.content:
This option allows you to define interfaces encapsulating IP packets within IP packets; which should be automatically created.
For example, this allows you to create 4in6 (RFC 2473) or IP within IP (RFC 2003) tunnels.

documents.title: Option: networking.ipips.<name>.dev
documents.content: The underlying network device on which the tunnel resides.

documents.title: Option: networking.ipips.<name>.encapsulation.limit
documents.content: For an IPv6-based tunnel, the maximum number of nested encapsulation to allow. 0 means no nesting, "none" unlimited.

documents.title: Option: networking.ipips.<name>.encapsulation.type
Option: networking.ipips.<name>.local
documents.content: The address of the local endpoint which the remote side should send packets to.

documents.title: Option: networking.ipips.<name>.remote
documents.content: The address of the remote endpoint to forward traffic over.

documents.title: Option: networking.ipips.<name>.ttl
documents.content: The time-to-live of the connection to the remote tunnel endpoint.

documents.title: Option: networking.iproute2.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable copying IP route configuration files.

documents.title: Option: networking.iproute2.rttablesExtraConfig
documents.content: Verbatim lines to add to /etc/iproute2/rt_tables

documents.title: Option: networking.ipvlans
documents.content: This option allows you to define ipvlan interfaces which should be automatically created.

documents.title: Option: networking.ipvlans.<name>.flags
documents.content: The flags of the ipvlan device.

documents.title: Option: networking.ipvlans.<name>.interface
documents.content: The interface the ipvlan will transmit packets through.

documents.title: Option: networking.ipvlans.<name>.mode
documents.content: The mode of the interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.jool.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable Jool, an Open Source implementation of IPv4/IPv6 translation on Linux.
Jool can perform stateless IP/ICMP translation (SIIT) or stateful NAT64, analogous to the IPv4 NAPT. Refer to the upstream documentation for the supported modes of translation and how to configure them.
Enabling this option will install the Jool kernel module and the command line tools for controlling it.

documents.title: Option: networking.jool.nat64
documents.content:
Definitions of NAT64 instances of Jool. See the documentation for the available options. Also check out the tutorial for an introduction to NAT64 and how to troubleshoot the setup.
The attribute name defines the name of the instance, with the main one being default: this can be accessed from the command line without specifying the name with -i.
::: {.note} Instances created imperatively from the command line will not interfere with the NixOS instances, provided the respective pool4 addresses and port ranges are not overlapping. :::
::: {.warning} Changes to an instance performed via jool -i <name> are applied correctly but will be lost after restarting the respective jool-nat64-<name>.service. :::

documents.title: Option: networking.jool.nat64.<name>.framework
documents.content: The framework to use for attaching Jool's translation to the exist kernel packet processing rules. See the documentation for the differences between the two options.

documents.title: Option: networking.jool.nat64.<name>.global.pool6
documents.content: The prefix used for embedding IPv4 into IPv6 addresses. Defaults to the well-known NAT64 prefix, defined by RFC 6052.

documents.title: Option: networking.jool.siit
documents.content:
Definitions of SIIT instances of Jool. See the documentation for the available options. Also check out the tutorial for an introduction to SIIT and how to troubleshoot the setup.
The attribute name defines the name of the instance, with the main one being default: this can be accessed from the command line without specifying the name with -i.
::: {.note} Instances created imperatively from the command line will not interfere with the NixOS instances, provided the respective EAMT addresses and port ranges are not overlapping. :::
::: {.warning} Changes to an instance performed via jool -i <name> are applied correctly but will be lost after restarting the respective jool-siit-<name>.service. :::

documents.title: Option: networking.jool.siit.<name>.framework
documents.content: The framework to use for attaching Jool's translation to the exist kernel packet processing rules. See the documentation for the differences between the two options.

documents.title: Option: networking.localCommands
documents.content: Shell commands to be executed after all the network interfaces have been created, but not necessarily fully configured.

documents.title: Option: networking.macvlans
documents.content: This option allows you to define macvlan interfaces which should be automatically created.

documents.title: Option: networking.macvlans.<name>.interface
documents.content: The interface the macvlan will transmit packets through.

documents.title: Option: networking.macvlans.<name>.mode
documents.content: The mode of the macvlan device.

documents.title: Option: networking.modemmanager.enable
documents.content: Whether to use ModemManager to manage modem devices. This is usually used by some higher layer manager such as NetworkManager but can be used standalone especially if using a modem for non-IP connectivity (e.g. GPS).

documents.title: Option: networking.modemmanager.fccUnlockScripts
documents.content: List of FCC unlock scripts to enable on the system, behaving as described in https://modemmanager.org/docs/modemmanager/fcc-unlock/#integration-with-third-party-fcc-unlock-tools.

documents.title: Option: networking.modemmanager.fccUnlockScripts.*.id
documents.content: vid:pid of either the PCI or USB vendor and product ID

documents.title: Option: networking.modemmanager.fccUnlockScripts.*.path
documents.content: Path to the unlock script

documents.title: Option: networking.modemmanager.package
documents.content: The modemmanager package to use.

documents.title: Option: networking.nameservers
documents.content: The list of nameservers. It can be left empty if it is auto-detected through DHCP.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.dmzHost
documents.content: The local IP address to which all traffic that does not match any forwarding rule is forwarded.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Network Address Translation (NAT). A properly configured firewall or a trusted L2 on all network interfaces is required to prevent unauthorized access to the internal network.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.enableIPv6
documents.content: Whether to enable IPv6 NAT.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.externalIP
documents.content: The public IP address to which packets from the local network are to be rewritten. If this is left empty, the IP address associated with the external interface will be used. Only connections made to this IP address will be forwarded to the internal network when using forwardPorts.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.externalIPv6
documents.content: The public IPv6 address to which packets from the local network are to be rewritten. If this is left empty, the IP address associated with the external interface will be used. Only connections made to this IP address will be forwarded to the internal network when using forwardPorts.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.externalInterface
documents.content: The name of the external network interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.extraCommands
documents.content:
Additional shell commands executed as part of the nat initialisation script.
This option is incompatible with the nftables based nat module.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.extraStopCommands
documents.content:
Additional shell commands executed as part of the nat teardown script.
This option is incompatible with the nftables based nat module.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.forwardPorts
documents.content: List of forwarded ports from the external interface to internal destinations by using DNAT. Destination can be IPv6 if IPv6 NAT is enabled.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.forwardPorts.*.destination
documents.content: Forward connection to destination ip:port (or [ipv6]:port); to specify a port range, use ip:start-end

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.forwardPorts.*.loopbackIPs
documents.content: Public IPs for NAT reflection; for connections to loopbackip:sourcePort from the host itself and from other hosts behind NAT

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.forwardPorts.*.proto
documents.content: Protocol of forwarded connection

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.forwardPorts.*.sourcePort
documents.content: Source port of the external interface; to specify a port range, use a string with a colon (e.g. "60000:61000")

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.internalIPs
documents.content: The IP address ranges for which to perform NAT. Packets coming from these addresses (on any interface) and destined for the external interface will be rewritten.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.internalIPv6s
documents.content: The IPv6 address ranges for which to perform NAT. Packets coming from these addresses (on any interface) and destined for the external interface will be rewritten.

documents.title: Option: networking.nat.internalInterfaces
documents.content: The interfaces for which to perform NAT. Packets coming from these interface and destined for the external interface will be rewritten.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.appendNameservers
documents.content: A list of name servers that should be appended to the ones configured in NetworkManager or received by DHCP.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.connectionConfig
documents.content: Configuration for the [connection] section of NetworkManager.conf. Refer to https://developer.gnome.org/NetworkManager/stable/NetworkManager.conf.html#id-1.2.3.11 or {manpage}NetworkManager.conf(5) for more information.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.dhcp
documents.content: Which program (or internal library) should be used for DHCP.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.dispatcherScripts
documents.content: A list of scripts which will be executed in response to network events.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.dispatcherScripts.*.source
documents.content: Path to the hook script.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.dispatcherScripts.*.type
documents.content: Dispatcher hook type. Look up the hooks described at https://developer.gnome.org/NetworkManager/stable/NetworkManager.html and choose the type depending on the output folder. You should then filter the event type (e.g., "up"/"down") from within your script.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.dns
documents.content:
Set the DNS ({file}resolv.conf) processing mode.
A description of these modes can be found in the main section of https://developer.gnome.org/NetworkManager/stable/NetworkManager.conf.html or in {manpage}NetworkManager.conf(5).

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.enable
documents.content: Whether to use NetworkManager to obtain an IP address and other configuration for all network interfaces that are not manually configured. If enabled, a group networkmanager will be created. Add all users that should have permission to change network settings to this group.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.environmentFiles
documents.content: Files to load as environment file. Environment variables from this file will be substituted into the static configuration file using envsubst.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.profiles
documents.content: Declaratively define NetworkManager profiles. You can find information about the generated file format here and here. You current profiles which are most likely stored in /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections and there is a tool to convert them to the needed nix code. If you add a new ad-hoc connection via a GUI or nmtui or anything similar it should just work together with the declarative ones. And if you edit a declarative profile NetworkManager will move it to the persistent storage and treat it like a ad-hoc one, but there will be two profiles as soon as the systemd unit from this option runs again which can be confusing since NetworkManager tools will start displaying two profiles with the same name and probably a bit different settings depending on what you edited. A profile won't be deleted even if it's removed from the config until the system reboots because that's when NetworkManager clears it's temp directory. If networking.resolvconf.enable is true, attributes affecting the name resolution (such as ignore-auto-dns) may not end up changing /etc/resolv.conf as expected when other name services (for example networking.dhcpcd) are enabled. Run resolvconf -l in the terminal to see what each service produces.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.profiles.<name>.connection.id
documents.content: This is the name that will be displayed by NetworkManager and GUIs.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.profiles.<name>.connection.type
documents.content: The connection type defines the connection kind, like vpn, wireguard, gsm, wifi and more.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.secrets.entries
documents.content:
A list of secrets to provide to NetworkManager by reading their values from configured files.
Note that NetworkManager should be configured to read secrets from a secret agent. This can be done for example through the networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.profiles options.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.secrets.entries.*.file
documents.content: file from which the secret value is read

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.secrets.entries.*.key
documents.content: key in the setting section for which this entry provides a value

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.secrets.entries.*.matchId
documents.content:
connection id used by NetworkManager. Often displayed as name in GUIs.
NetworkManager describes this as a human readable unique identifier for the connection, like "Work Wi-Fi" or "T-Mobile 3G".

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.secrets.entries.*.matchIface
documents.content: interface name of the NetworkManager connection

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.secrets.entries.*.matchSetting
documents.content: name of the setting section for which secrets are requested

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.secrets.entries.*.matchType
documents.content:
NetworkManager connection type
The NetworkManager configuration settings reference roughly corresponds to connection types. More might be available on your system depending on the installed plugins.
https://networkmanager.dev/docs/api/latest/ch01.html

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.secrets.entries.*.matchUuid
documents.content:
UUID of the connection profile
UUIDs are assigned once on connection creation and should never change as long as the connection still applies to the same network.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.secrets.entries.*.trim
documents.content: whether leading and trailing whitespace should be stripped from the files content before being passed to NetworkManager

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ensureProfiles.secrets.package
documents.content: The nm-file-secret-agent package to use.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.ethernet.macAddress
documents.content:
Set the MAC address of the interface.
"XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX": MAC address of the interface
"permanent": Use the permanent MAC address of the device
"preserve": Don’t change the MAC address of the device upon activation
"random": Generate a randomized value upon each connect
"stable": Generate a stable, hashed MAC address

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.insertNameservers
documents.content: A list of name servers that should be inserted before the ones configured in NetworkManager or received by DHCP.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.logLevel
documents.content: Set the default logging verbosity level.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.package
documents.content: The networkmanager package to use.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.plugins
documents.content:
List of plugin packages to install.
See https://search.nixos.org/packages?query=networkmanager- for available plugin packages. and https://networkmanager.dev/docs/vpn/ for an overview over builtin and external plugins and their support status.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.settings
documents.content: Configuration added to the generated NetworkManager.conf, note that you can overwrite settings with this. Refer to https://developer.gnome.org/NetworkManager/stable/NetworkManager.conf.html or {manpage}NetworkManager.conf(5) for more information.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.unmanaged
documents.content: List of interfaces that will not be managed by NetworkManager. Interface name can be specified here, but if you need more fidelity, refer to https://developer.gnome.org/NetworkManager/stable/NetworkManager.conf.html#device-spec or the "Device List Format" Appendix of {manpage}NetworkManager.conf(5).

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.wifi.backend
documents.content: Specify the Wi-Fi backend used for the device. Currently supported are {option}wpa_supplicant or {option}iwd (experimental).

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.wifi.macAddress
documents.content:
Set the MAC address of the interface.
"XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX": MAC address of the interface
"permanent": Use the permanent MAC address of the device
"preserve": Don’t change the MAC address of the device upon activation
"random": Generate a randomized value upon each connect
"stable": Generate a stable, hashed MAC address
"stable-ssid": Generate a stable MAC addressed based on Wi-Fi network

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.wifi.powersave
documents.content: Whether to enable Wi-Fi power saving.

documents.title: Option: networking.networkmanager.wifi.scanRandMacAddress
documents.content: Whether to enable MAC address randomization of a Wi-Fi device during scanning.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.checkRuleset
documents.content: Run nft check on the ruleset to spot syntax errors during build. Because this is executed in a sandbox, the check might fail if it requires access to any environmental factors or paths outside the Nix store. To circumvent this, the ruleset file can be edited using the preCheckRuleset option to work in the sandbox environment.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.checkRulesetRedirects
documents.content: Set of paths that should be intercepted and rewritten while checking the ruleset using pkgs.buildPackages.libredirect.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable nftables and use nftables based firewall if enabled. nftables is a Linux-based packet filtering framework intended to replace frameworks like iptables.
Note that if you have Docker enabled you will not be able to use nftables without intervention. Docker uses iptables internally to setup NAT for containers. This module disables the ip_tables kernel module, however Docker automatically loads the module. Please see https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/issues/24318#issuecomment-289216273 for more information.
There are other programs that use iptables internally too, such as libvirt. For information on how the two firewalls interact, see https://wiki.nftables.org/wiki-nftables/index.php/Troubleshooting#Question_4._How_do_nftables_and_iptables_interact_when_used_on_the_same_system.3F.
Some network configurations may prevent VMs from having network access, see https://wiki.nixos.org/wiki/Networking#Virtualization.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.extraDeletions
documents.content: Extra deletion commands to be run on every firewall start, reload and after stopping the firewall.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.flattenRulesetFile
documents.content:
Use builtins.readFile rather than include to handle {option}networking.nftables.rulesetFile. It is useful when you want to apply {option}networking.nftables.preCheckRuleset to {option}networking.nftables.rulesetFile.
::: {.note} It is expected that {option}networking.nftables.rulesetFile can be accessed from the build sandbox. :::

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.flushRuleset
documents.content: Whether to enable flushing the entire ruleset on each reload.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.preCheckRuleset
documents.content: This script gets run before the ruleset is checked. It can be used to create additional files needed for the ruleset check to work, or modify the ruleset for cases the build environment cannot cover.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.ruleset
documents.content:
The ruleset to be used with nftables. Should be in a format that can be loaded using "/bin/nft -f". The ruleset is updated atomically. Note that if the tables should be cleaned first, either:
networking.nftables.flushRuleset = true; needs to be set (flushes all tables)
networking.nftables.extraDeletions needs to be set
or networking.nftables.tables can be used, which will clean up the table automatically

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.rulesetFile
documents.content: The ruleset file to be used with nftables. Should be in a format that can be loaded using "nft -f". The ruleset is updated atomically.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.tables
documents.content: Tables to be added to ruleset. Tables will be added together with delete statements to clean up the table before every update.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.tables.<name>.content
documents.content: The table content.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.tables.<name>.enable
documents.content: Enable this table.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.tables.<name>.family
documents.content: Table family.

documents.title: Option: networking.nftables.tables.<name>.name
documents.content: Table name.

documents.title: Option: networking.openconnect.interfaces
documents.content: OpenConnect interfaces.

documents.title: Option: networking.openconnect.interfaces.<name>.autoStart
documents.content: Whether this VPN connection should be started automatically.

documents.title: Option: networking.openconnect.interfaces.<name>.certificate
documents.content: Certificate to authenticate with.

documents.title: Option: networking.openconnect.interfaces.<name>.extraOptions
documents.content: Extra config to be appended to the interface config. It should contain long-format options as would be accepted on the command line by openconnect (see https://www.infradead.org/openconnect/manual.html). documents.title: Option: networking.openconnect.interfaces.<name>.gateway
documents.content: Gateway server to connect to.

documents.title: Option: networking.openconnect.interfaces.<name>.passwordFile
documents.content: File containing the password to authenticate with. This is passed to openconnect via the --passwd-on-stdin option.

documents.title: Option: networking.openconnect.interfaces.<name>.privateKey
documents.content: Private key to authenticate with.

documents.title: Option: networking.openconnect.interfaces.<name>.protocol
documents.content: Protocol to use.

documents.title: Option: networking.openconnect.interfaces.<name>.user
documents.content: Username to authenticate with.

documents.title: Option: networking.openconnect.package
documents.content: The openconnect package to use.

documents.title: Option: networking.proxy.allProxy
documents.content: This option specifies the all_proxy environment variable.

documents.title: Option: networking.proxy.default
documents.content: This option specifies the default value for httpProxy, httpsProxy, ftpProxy and rsyncProxy.

documents.title: Option: networking.proxy.ftpProxy
documents.content: This option specifies the ftp_proxy environment variable.

documents.title: Option: networking.proxy.httpProxy
documents.content: This option specifies the http_proxy environment variable.

documents.title: Option: networking.proxy.httpsProxy
documents.content: This option specifies the https_proxy environment variable.

documents.title: Option: networking.proxy.noProxy
documents.content: This option specifies the no_proxy environment variable. If a default proxy is used and noProxy is null, then noProxy will be set to 127.0.0.1,localhost.

documents.title: Option: networking.proxy.rsyncProxy
documents.content: This option specifies the rsync_proxy environment variable.

documents.title: Option: networking.resolvconf.dnsExtensionMechanism
documents.content: Enable the edns0 option in {file}resolv.conf. With that option set, glibc supports use of the extension mechanisms for DNS (EDNS) specified in RFC 2671. The most popular user of that feature is DNSSEC, which does not work without it.

documents.title: Option: networking.resolvconf.dnsSingleRequest
documents.content: Recent versions of glibc will issue both ipv4 (A) and ipv6 (AAAA) address queries at the same time, from the same port. Sometimes upstream routers will systemically drop the ipv4 queries. The symptom of this problem is that 'getent hosts example.com' only returns ipv6 (or perhaps only ipv4) addresses. The workaround for this is to specify the option 'single-request' in /etc/resolv.conf. This option enables that.

documents.title: Option: networking.resolvconf.enable
documents.content: Whether DNS configuration is managed by resolvconf.

documents.title: Option: networking.resolvconf.extraConfig
documents.content: Extra configuration to append to {file}resolvconf.conf.

documents.title: Option: networking.resolvconf.extraOptions
documents.content: Set the options in {file}/etc/resolv.conf.

documents.title: Option: networking.resolvconf.package
documents.content:
The package that provides the system-wide resolvconf command. Defaults to openresolv if this module is enabled. Otherwise, can be used by other modules (for example {option}services.resolved) to provide a compatibility layer.
This option generally shouldn't be set by the user.

documents.title: Option: networking.resolvconf.useLocalResolver
documents.content: Use local DNS server for resolving.

documents.title: Option: networking.rxe.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable RDMA over converged ethernet.

documents.title: Option: networking.rxe.interfaces
documents.content: Enable RDMA on the listed interfaces. The corresponding virtual RDMA interfaces will be named rxe_<interface>. UDP port 4791 must be open on the respective ethernet interfaces.

documents.title: Option: networking.search
documents.content: The list of domain search paths that are considered for resolving hostnames with fewer dots than configured in the ndots option, which defaults to 1 if unset.

documents.title: Option: networking.sits
documents.content: This option allows you to define interfaces encapsulating IPv6 packets within IPv4 packets; which should be automatically created.

documents.title: Option: networking.sits.<name>.dev
documents.content: The underlying network device on which the tunnel resides.

documents.title: Option: networking.sits.<name>.encapsulation
documents.content: Configures the type of encapsulation.

documents.title: Option: networking.sits.<name>.encapsulation.port
documents.content: Destination port when using UDP encapsulation.

documents.title: Option: networking.sits.<name>.encapsulation.sourcePort
documents.content: Source port when using UDP encapsulation. Will be chosen automatically by the kernel if unset.

documents.title: Option: networking.sits.<name>.encapsulation.type
Option: networking.sits.<name>.local
documents.content: The address of the local endpoint which the remote side should send packets to.

documents.title: Option: networking.sits.<name>.remote
documents.content: The address of the remote endpoint to forward traffic over.

documents.title: Option: networking.sits.<name>.ttl
documents.content: The time-to-live of the connection to the remote tunnel endpoint.

documents.title: Option: networking.stevenblack.block
documents.content: Additional blocklist extensions.

documents.title: Option: networking.stevenblack.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the stevenblack hosts file blocklist.

documents.title: Option: networking.stevenblack.package
documents.content: The stevenblack-blocklist package to use.

documents.title: Option: networking.stevenblack.whitelist
documents.content: Domains to exclude from blocking.

documents.title: Option: networking.supplicant
documents.content:
Interfaces for which to start {command}wpa_supplicant. The supplicant is used to scan for and associate with wireless networks, or to authenticate with 802.1x capable network switches.
The value of this option is an attribute set. Each attribute configures a {command}wpa_supplicant service, where the attribute name specifies the name of the interface that {command}wpa_supplicant operates on. The attribute name can be a space separated list of interfaces. The attribute names WLAN, LAN and DBUS have a special meaning. WLAN and LAN are configurations for universal {command}wpa_supplicant service that is started for each WLAN interface or for each LAN interface, respectively. DBUS defines a device-unrelated {command}wpa_supplicant service that can be accessed through D-Bus.

documents.title: Option: networking.supplicant.<name>.bridge
documents.content: Name of the bridge interface that wpa_supplicant should listen at.

documents.title: Option: networking.supplicant.<name>.configFile.path
documents.content: External {file}wpa_supplicant.conf configuration file. The configuration options defined declaratively within networking.supplicant have precedence over options defined in configFile.

documents.title: Option: networking.supplicant.<name>.configFile.writable
documents.content: Whether the configuration file at configFile.path should be written to by wpa_supplicant.

documents.title: Option: networking.supplicant.<name>.driver
documents.content: Force a specific wpa_supplicant driver.

documents.title: Option: networking.supplicant.<name>.extraCmdArgs
documents.content: Command line arguments to add when executing wpa_supplicant.

documents.title: Option: networking.supplicant.<name>.extraConf
documents.content: Configuration options for {file}wpa_supplicant.conf. Options defined here have precedence over options in configFile. NOTE: Do not write sensitive data into extraConf as it will be world-readable in the nix-store. For sensitive information use the configFile instead.

documents.title: Option: networking.supplicant.<name>.userControlled.enable
documents.content: Allow normal users to control wpa_supplicant through wpa_gui or wpa_cli. This is useful for laptop users that switch networks a lot and don't want to depend on a large package such as NetworkManager just to pick nearby access points.

documents.title: Option: networking.supplicant.<name>.userControlled.group
documents.content: Members of this group can control wpa_supplicant.

documents.title: Option: networking.supplicant.<name>.userControlled.socketDir
documents.content: Directory of sockets for controlling wpa_supplicant.

documents.title: Option: networking.tcpcrypt.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable opportunistic TCP encryption. If the other end speaks Tcpcrypt, then your traffic will be encrypted; otherwise it will be sent in clear text. Thus, Tcpcrypt alone provides no guarantees -- it is best effort. If, however, a Tcpcrypt connection is successful and any attackers that exist are passive, then Tcpcrypt guarantees privacy.

documents.title: Option: networking.tempAddresses
Option: networking.timeServers
documents.content: The set of NTP servers from which to synchronise.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.addr
documents.content: Virtual shared IP address.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.advBase
documents.content: Advertisement frequency in seconds.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.advSkew
documents.content: Advertisement skew in seconds.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.deadratio
documents.content: Ratio to consider a host as dead.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.downscript
documents.content: Command to run after become backup, the interface name, virtual address and optional extra parameters are passed as arguments.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable ucarp, userspace implementation of CARP.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.extraParam
documents.content: Extra parameter to pass to the up/down scripts.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.ignoreIfState
documents.content: Ignore interface state, e.g., down or no carrier.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.interface
documents.content: Network interface to bind to.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.neutral
documents.content: Do not run downscript at start if the host is the backup.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.noMcast
documents.content: Use broadcast instead of multicast advertisements.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.package
documents.content: The ucarp package to use. Please note that the default package, pkgs.ucarp, has not received any upstream updates for a long time and can be considered as unmaintained.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.passwordFile
documents.content: File containing shared password between CARP hosts.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.preempt
documents.content: Enable preemptive failover. Thus, this host becomes the CARP master as soon as possible.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.shutdown
documents.content: Call downscript at exit.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.srcIp
documents.content: Source (real) IP address of this host.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.upscript
documents.content: Command to run after become master, the interface name, virtual address and optional extra parameters are passed as arguments.

documents.title: Option: networking.ucarp.vhId
documents.content: Virtual IP identifier shared between CARP hosts.

documents.title: Option: networking.useDHCP
documents.content: Whether to use DHCP to obtain an IP address and other configuration for all network interfaces that do not have any manually configured IPv4 addresses.

documents.title: Option: networking.useHostResolvConf
documents.content: In containers, whether to use the {file}resolv.conf supplied by the host.

documents.title: Option: networking.useNetworkd
documents.content: Whether we should use networkd as the network configuration backend or the legacy script based system. Note that this option is experimental, enable at your own risk.

documents.title: Option: networking.usePredictableInterfaceNames
documents.content: Whether to assign predictable names to network interfaces. If enabled, interfaces are assigned names that contain topology information (e.g. wlp3s0) and thus should be stable across reboots. If disabled, names depend on the order in which interfaces are discovered by the kernel, which may change randomly across reboots; for instance, you may find eth0 and eth1 flipping unpredictably.

documents.title: Option: networking.vlans
documents.content: This option allows you to define vlan devices that tag packets on top of a physical interface. The value of this option is an attribute set. Each attribute specifies a vlan, with the name specifying the name of the vlan interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.vlans.<name>.id
documents.content: The vlan identifier

documents.title: Option: networking.vlans.<name>.interface
documents.content: The interface the vlan will transmit packets through.

documents.title: Option: networking.vswitches
documents.content: This option allows you to define Open vSwitches that connect physical networks together. The value of this option is an attribute set. Each attribute specifies a vswitch, with the attribute name specifying the name of the vswitch's network interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.vswitches.<name>.controllers
documents.content: Specify the controller targets. For the allowed options see man 8 ovs-vsctl.

documents.title: Option: networking.vswitches.<name>.extraOvsctlCmds
documents.content: Commands to manipulate the Open vSwitch database. Every line executed with ovs-vsctl. All commands are bundled together with the operations for adding the interfaces into one atomic operation.

documents.title: Option: networking.vswitches.<name>.interfaces
documents.content: The physical network interfaces connected by the vSwitch.

documents.title: Option: networking.vswitches.<name>.interfaces.<name>.name
documents.content: Name of the interface

documents.title: Option: networking.vswitches.<name>.interfaces.<name>.type
documents.content: Openvswitch type to assign to interface

documents.title: Option: networking.vswitches.<name>.interfaces.<name>.vlan
documents.content: Vlan tag to apply to interface

documents.title: Option: networking.vswitches.<name>.openFlowRules
documents.content: OpenFlow rules to insert into the Open vSwitch. All openFlowRules are loaded with ovs-ofctl within one atomic operation.

documents.title: Option: networking.vswitches.<name>.openFlowVersion
documents.content: Version of OpenFlow protocol to use when communicating with the switch internally (e.g. with openFlowRules).

documents.title: Option: networking.vswitches.<name>.supportedOpenFlowVersions
documents.content: Supported versions to enable on this switch.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces
documents.content: Wireguard interfaces.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.address
documents.content: The IP addresses of the interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.autostart
documents.content: Whether to bring up this interface automatically during boot.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.configFile
documents.content: wg-quick .conf file, describing the interface. Using this option can be a useful means of configuring WireGuard if one has an existing .conf file. This overrides any other configuration interface configuration options. See wg-quick manpage for more details.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.dns
documents.content: The IP addresses of DNS servers to configure.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.extraOptions
documents.content: Extra options to append to the interface section. Can be used to define AmneziaWG-specific options.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.generatePrivateKeyFile
documents.content: Automatically generate a private key with {command}wg genkey, at the privateKeyFile location.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.listenPort
documents.content: 16-bit port for listening. Optional; if not specified, automatically generated based on interface name.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.mtu
documents.content: If not specified, the MTU is automatically determined from the endpoint addresses or the system default route, which is usually a sane choice. However, to manually specify an MTU to override this automatic discovery, this value may be specified explicitly.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.peers
documents.content: Peers linked to the interface.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.peers.*.allowedIPs
documents.content: List of IP (v4 or v6) addresses with CIDR masks from which this peer is allowed to send incoming traffic and to which outgoing traffic for this peer is directed. The catch-all 0.0.0.0/0 may be specified for matching all IPv4 addresses, and ::/0 may be specified for matching all IPv6 addresses.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.peers.*.endpoint
documents.content: Endpoint IP or hostname of the peer, followed by a colon, and then a port number of the peer.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.peers.*.persistentKeepalive
documents.content: This is optional and is by default off, because most users will not need it. It represents, in seconds, between 1 and 65535 inclusive, how often to send an authenticated empty packet to the peer, for the purpose of keeping a stateful firewall or NAT mapping valid persistently. For example, if the interface very rarely sends traffic, but it might at anytime receive traffic from a peer, and it is behind NAT, the interface might benefit from having a persistent keepalive interval of 25 seconds; however, most users will not need this.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.peers.*.presharedKey
documents.content:
Base64 preshared key generated by {command}wg genpsk. Optional, and may be omitted. This option adds an additional layer of symmetric-key cryptography to be mixed into the already existing public-key cryptography, for post-quantum resistance.
Warning: Consider using presharedKeyFile instead if you do not want to store the key in the world-readable Nix store.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.peers.*.presharedKeyFile
documents.content: File pointing to preshared key as generated by {command}wg genpsk. Optional, and may be omitted. This option adds an additional layer of symmetric-key cryptography to be mixed into the already existing public-key cryptography, for post-quantum resistance.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.peers.*.publicKey
documents.content: The base64 public key to the peer.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.postDown
documents.content: Command called after the interface is taken down.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.postUp
documents.content: Commands called after the interface setup.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.preDown
documents.content: Command called before the interface is taken down.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.preUp
documents.content: Commands called at the start of the interface setup.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.privateKey
documents.content:
Base64 private key generated by {command}wg genkey.
Warning: Consider using privateKeyFile instead if you do not want to store the key in the world-readable Nix store.

documents.title: Option: networking.wg-quick.interfaces.<name>.privateKeyFile
documents.content: Private key file as generated by {command}wg genkey.
