Configuration for Nix, see https://nixos.org/manual/nix/stable/command-ref/conf-file.html or {manpage}nix.conf(5) for available options. The value declared here will be translated directly to the key-value pairs Nix expects.
You can use {command}nix-instantiate --eval --strict '<nixpkgs/nixos>' -A config.nix.settings to view the current value. By default it is empty.
Nix configurations defined under {option}nix.* will be translated and applied to this option. In addition, configuration specified in {option}nix.extraOptions will be appended verbatim to the resulting config file.

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.allowed-users
documents.content: A list of names of users (separated by whitespace) that are allowed to connect to the Nix daemon. As with {option}nix.settings.trusted-users, you can specify groups by prefixing them with @. Also, you can allow all users by specifying *. The default is *. Note that trusted users are always allowed to connect.

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.auto-optimise-store
documents.content: If set to true, Nix automatically detects files in the store that have identical contents, and replaces them with hard links to a single copy. This saves disk space. If set to false (the default), you can still run nix-store --optimise to get rid of duplicate files.

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.cores
documents.content: This option defines the maximum number of concurrent tasks during one build. It affects, e.g., -j option for make. The special value 0 means that the builder should use all available CPU cores in the system. Some builds may become non-deterministic with this option; use with care! Packages will only be affected if enableParallelBuilding is set for them.

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.extra-sandbox-paths
documents.content: Directories from the host filesystem to be included in the sandbox.

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.max-jobs
documents.content: This option defines the maximum number of jobs that Nix will try to build in parallel. The default is auto, which means it will use all available logical cores. It is recommend to set it to the total number of logical cores in your system (e.g., 16 for two CPUs with 4 cores each and hyper-threading).

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.require-sigs
documents.content: If enabled (the default), Nix will only download binaries from binary caches if they are cryptographically signed with any of the keys listed in {option}nix.settings.trusted-public-keys. If disabled, signatures are neither required nor checked, so it's strongly recommended that you use only trustworthy caches and https to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.sandbox
documents.content:
If set, Nix will perform builds in a sandboxed environment that it will set up automatically for each build. This prevents impurities in builds by disallowing access to dependencies outside of the Nix store by using network and mount namespaces in a chroot environment.
This is enabled by default even though it has a possible performance impact due to the initial setup time of a sandbox for each build. It doesn't affect derivation hashes, so changing this option will not trigger a rebuild of packages.
When set to "relaxed", this option permits derivations that set __noChroot = true; to run outside of the sandboxed environment. Exercise caution when using this mode of operation! It is intended to be a quick hack when building with packages that are not easily setup to be built reproducibly.

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.substituters
documents.content:
List of binary cache URLs used to obtain pre-built binaries of Nix packages.
By default https://cache.nixos.org/ is added.

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.system-features
documents.content: The set of features supported by the machine. Derivations can express dependencies on system features through the requiredSystemFeatures attribute.

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.trusted-public-keys
documents.content: List of public keys used to sign binary caches. If {option}nix.settings.trusted-public-keys is enabled, then Nix will use a binary from a binary cache if and only if it is signed by any of the keys listed here. By default, only the key for cache.nixos.org is included.

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.trusted-substituters
documents.content: List of binary cache URLs that non-root users can use (in addition to those specified using {option}nix.settings.substituters) by passing --option binary-caches to Nix commands.

documents.title: Option: nix.settings.trusted-users
documents.content: A list of names of users that have additional rights when connecting to the Nix daemon, such as the ability to specify additional binary caches, or to import unsigned NARs. You can also specify groups by prefixing them with @; for instance, @wheel means all users in the wheel group.

documents.title: Option: nix.sshServe.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable serving the Nix store as a remote store via SSH.

documents.title: Option: nix.sshServe.keys
documents.content: A list of SSH public keys allowed to access the binary cache via SSH.

documents.title: Option: nix.sshServe.protocol
documents.content: The specific Nix-over-SSH protocol to use.

documents.title: Option: nix.sshServe.trusted
documents.content: Whether to add nix-ssh to the nix.settings.trusted-users

documents.title: Option: nix.sshServe.write
documents.content: Whether to enable writing to the Nix store as a remote store via SSH. Note: by default, the sshServe user is named nix-ssh and is not a trusted-user. nix-ssh should be added to the {option}nix.sshServe.trusted option in most use cases, such as allowing remote building of derivations to anonymous people based on ssh key

documents.title: Option: nixops.enableDeprecatedAutoLuks
documents.content: Whether to enable the deprecated NixOps AutoLuks module.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.buildPlatform
documents.content:
Specifies the platform on which NixOS should be built. By default, NixOS is built on the system where it runs, but you can change where it's built. Setting this option will cause NixOS to be cross-compiled.
For instance, if you're doing distributed multi-platform deployment, or if you're building machines, you can set this to match your development system and/or build farm.
Ignored when nixpkgs.pkgs is set.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.config
documents.content:
Global configuration for Nixpkgs. The complete list of Nixpkgs configuration options is in the Nixpkgs manual section on global configuration.
Ignored when {option}nixpkgs.pkgs is set.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.crossSystem
documents.content:
Systems with a recently generated hardware-configuration.nix may instead specify only {option}nixpkgs.buildPlatform, or fall back to removing the {option}nixpkgs.hostPlatform line from the generated config.
Specifies the platform for which NixOS should be built. Specify this only if it is different from nixpkgs.localSystem, the platform on which NixOS should be built. In other words, specify this to cross-compile NixOS. Otherwise it should be set as null, the default. See its description in the Nixpkgs manual for more details.
Ignored when nixpkgs.pkgs or hostPlatform is set.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.flake.setFlakeRegistry
documents.content:
Whether to pin nixpkgs in the system-wide flake registry (/etc/nix/registry.json) to the store path of the sources of nixpkgs used to build the NixOS system.
This is on by default for NixOS configurations built with flakes.
This option makes {command}nix run nixpkgs#hello reuse dependencies from the system, avoid refetching nixpkgs, and have a consistent result every time.
Note that this option makes the NixOS closure depend on the nixpkgs sources, which may add undesired closure size if the system will not have any nix commands run on it.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.flake.setNixPath
documents.content:
Whether to set {env}NIX_PATH to include nixpkgs=flake:nixpkgs such that <nixpkgs> lookups receive the version of nixpkgs that the system was built with, in concert with {option}nixpkgs.flake.setFlakeRegistry.
This is on by default for NixOS configurations built with flakes.
This makes {command}nix-build '<nixpkgs>' -A hello work out of the box on flake systems.
Note that this option makes the NixOS closure depend on the nixpkgs sources, which may add undesired closure size if the system will not have any nix commands run on it.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.flake.source
documents.content:
The path to the nixpkgs sources used to build the system. This is automatically set up to be the store path of the nixpkgs flake used to build the system if using nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem, and is otherwise null by default.
This can also be optionally set if the NixOS system is not built with a flake but still uses pinned sources: set this to the store path for the nixpkgs sources used to build the system, as may be obtained by fetchTarball, for example.
Note: the name of the store path must be "source" due to https://github.com/NixOS/nix/issues/7075.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.hostPlatform
documents.content:
Specifies the platform where the NixOS configuration will run.
To cross-compile, set also nixpkgs.buildPlatform.
Ignored when nixpkgs.pkgs is set.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.localSystem
documents.content:
Systems with a recently generated hardware-configuration.nix do not need to specify this option, unless cross-compiling, in which case you should set only {option}nixpkgs.buildPlatform.
If this is somehow not feasible, you may fall back to removing the {option}nixpkgs.hostPlatform line from the generated config and use the old options.
Specifies the platform on which NixOS should be built. When nixpkgs.crossSystem is unset, it also specifies the platform for which NixOS should be built. If this option is unset, it defaults to the platform type of the machine where evaluation happens. Specifying this option is useful when doing distributed multi-platform deployment, or when building virtual machines. See its description in the Nixpkgs manual for more details.
Ignored when nixpkgs.pkgs or hostPlatform is set.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.overlays
documents.content:
List of overlays to apply to Nixpkgs. This option allows modifying the Nixpkgs package set accessed through the pkgs module argument.
For details, see the Overlays chapter in the Nixpkgs manual.
If the {option}nixpkgs.pkgs option is set, overlays specified using nixpkgs.overlays will be applied after the overlays that were already included in nixpkgs.pkgs.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.pkgs
documents.content:
If set, the pkgs argument to all NixOS modules is the value of this option, extended with nixpkgs.overlays, if that is also set. Either nixpkgs.crossSystem or nixpkgs.localSystem will be used in an assertion to check that the NixOS and Nixpkgs architectures match. Any other options in nixpkgs.*, notably config, will be ignored.
If unset, the pkgs argument to all NixOS modules is determined as shown in the default value for this option.
The default value imports the Nixpkgs source files relative to the location of this NixOS module, because NixOS and Nixpkgs are distributed together for consistency, so the nixos in the default value is in fact a relative path. The config, overlays, localSystem, and crossSystem come from this option's siblings.
This option can be used by applications like NixOps to increase the performance of evaluation, or to create packages that depend on a container that should be built with the exact same evaluation of Nixpkgs, for example. Applications like this should set their default value using lib.mkDefault, so user-provided configuration can override it without using lib.
Note that using a distinct version of Nixpkgs with NixOS may be an unexpected source of problems. Use this option with care.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.system
documents.content:
This option does not need to be specified for NixOS configurations with a recently generated hardware-configuration.nix.
Specifies the Nix platform type on which NixOS should be built. It is better to specify nixpkgs.localSystem instead.
is the same as
See nixpkgs.localSystem for more information.
Ignored when nixpkgs.pkgs, nixpkgs.localSystem or nixpkgs.hostPlatform is set.

documents.title: Option: openstack.zfs.datasets
documents.content:
Datasets to create under the tank and boot zpools.
NOTE: This option is used only at image creation time, and does not attempt to declaratively create or manage datasets on an existing system.

documents.title: Option: openstack.zfs.datasets.<name>.mount
documents.content: Where to mount this dataset.

documents.title: Option: openstack.zfs.datasets.<name>.properties
documents.content: Properties to set on this dataset.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable support for Power Devices, such as Uninterruptible Power Supplies, Power Distribution Units and Solar Controllers .

documents.title: Option: power.ups.maxStartDelay
documents.content: This can be set as a global variable above your first UPS definition and it can also be set in a UPS section. This value controls how long upsdrvctl will wait for the driver to finish starting. This keeps your system from getting stuck due to a broken driver or UPS.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.mode
documents.content:
The MODE determines which part of the NUT is to be started, and which configuration files must be modified.
The values of MODE can be:
none: NUT is not configured, or use the Integrated Power Management, or use some external system to startup NUT components. So nothing is to be started.
standalone: This mode address a local only configuration, with 1 UPS protecting the local system. This implies to start the 3 NUT layers (driver, upsd and upsmon) and the matching configuration files. This mode can also address UPS redundancy.
netserver: same as for the standalone configuration, but also need some more ACLs and possibly a specific LISTEN directive in upsd.conf. Since this MODE is opened to the network, a special care should be applied to security concerns.
netclient: this mode only requires upsmon.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.openFirewall
documents.content: Open ports in the firewall for upsd.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.package
documents.content: The nut package to use.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.schedulerRules
documents.content: File which contains the rules to handle UPS events.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.ups
documents.content: This is where you configure all the UPSes that this system will be monitoring directly. These are usually attached to serial ports, but USB devices are also supported.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.ups.<name>.description
documents.content: Description of the UPS.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.ups.<name>.directives
documents.content: List of configuration directives for this UPS.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.ups.<name>.driver
documents.content: Specify the program to run to talk to this UPS. apcsmart, bestups, and sec are some examples.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.ups.<name>.maxStartDelay
documents.content: This can be set as a global variable above your first UPS definition and it can also be set in a UPS section. This value controls how long upsdrvctl will wait for the driver to finish starting. This keeps your system from getting stuck due to a broken driver or UPS.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.ups.<name>.port
documents.content: The serial port to which your UPS is connected. /dev/ttyS0 is usually the first port on Linux boxes, for example.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.ups.<name>.shutdownOrder
documents.content: When you have multiple UPSes on your system, you usually need to turn them off in a certain order. upsdrvctl shuts down all the 0s, then the 1s, 2s, and so on. To exclude a UPS from the shutdown sequence, set this to -1.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.ups.<name>.summary
documents.content: Lines which would be added inside ups.conf for handling this UPS.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsd
documents.content: Options for the upsd.conf configuration file.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsd.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable upsd.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsd.extraConfig
documents.content: Additional lines to add to upsd.conf.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsd.listen
documents.content: Address of the interface for upsd to listen on. See man upsd for details`.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsd.listen.*.address
documents.content: Address of the interface for upsd to listen on. See man upsd.conf for details.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsd.listen.*.port
documents.content: TCP port for upsd to listen on. See man upsd.conf for details.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsmon
documents.content: Options for the upsmon.conf configuration file.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsmon.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable upsmon.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsmon.group
documents.content: Group for the default nutmon user. If the default user is created and this is not specified, a default group will be created.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsmon.monitor
documents.content: Set of UPS to monitor. See man upsmon.conf for details.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsmon.monitor.<name>.passwordFile
documents.content: The full path to a file containing the password from upsd.users for accessing this UPS. The password file is read on service start. See upsmon.conf for details.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsmon.monitor.<name>.powerValue
documents.content: Number of power supplies that the UPS feeds on this system. See upsmon.conf for details.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsmon.monitor.<name>.system
documents.content: Identifier of the UPS to monitor, in this form: <upsname>[@<hostname>[:<port>]] See upsmon.conf for details.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsmon.monitor.<name>.type
documents.content: The relationship with upsd. See upsmon.conf for details.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsmon.monitor.<name>.user
documents.content: Username from upsd.users for accessing this UPS. See upsmon.conf for details.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsmon.settings
documents.content: Additional settings to add to upsmon.conf.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.upsmon.user
documents.content: User to run upsmon as. upsmon.conf will have its owner set to this user. If not specified, a default user will be created.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.users
documents.content: Users that can access upsd. See man upsd.users.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.users.<name>.actions
documents.content: Allow the user to do certain things with upsd. See man upsd.users for details.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.users.<name>.instcmds
documents.content: Let the user initiate specific instant commands. Use "ALL" to grant all commands automatically. For the full list of what your UPS supports, use "upscmd -l". See man upsd.users for details.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.users.<name>.passwordFile
documents.content: The full path to a file that contains the user's (clear text) password. The password file is read on service start.

documents.title: Option: power.ups.users.<name>.upsmon
documents.content: Add the necessary actions for a upsmon process to work. See man upsd.users for details.

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.bootCommands
documents.content: Commands executed only once after initial boot. These commands are executed before powerUpCommands.

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.cpuFreqGovernor
documents.content:
Configure the governor used to regulate the frequency of the available CPUs. By default, the kernel configures the performance governor, although this may be overwritten in your hardware-configuration.nix file.
Often used values: "ondemand", "powersave", "performance"

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.cpufreq.max
documents.content: The maximum frequency the CPU will use. Defaults to the maximum possible.

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.cpufreq.min
documents.content: The minimum frequency the CPU will use.

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable power management. This includes support for suspend-to-RAM and powersave features on laptops.

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.powerDownCommands
documents.content: Commands executed when the machine powers down. That is, they're executed both when the system shuts down and when it goes to suspend or hibernation.

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.powerUpCommands
documents.content: Commands executed when the machine powers up. That is, they're executed both when the system first boots and when it resumes from suspend or hibernation.

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.powertop.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable powertop auto tuning on startup.

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.powertop.postStart
documents.content:
Shell commands executed after powertop is started.
This can be used to workaround problematic configurations. For example, you can retrigger an udev rule to disable power saving on unsupported USB devices:

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.powertop.preStart
documents.content: Shell commands executed before powertop is started.

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.resumeCommands
documents.content: Commands executed after the system resumes from suspend-to-RAM.

documents.title: Option: powerManagement.scsiLinkPolicy
documents.content:
SCSI link power management policy. The kernel default is "max_performance".
"med_power_with_dipm" is supported by kernel versions 4.15 and newer.

documents.title: Option: programs._1password-gui.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the 1Password GUI application.

documents.title: Option: programs._1password-gui.polkitPolicyOwners
documents.content: A list of users who should be able to integrate 1Password with polkit-based authentication mechanisms.

documents.title: Option: programs._1password.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the 1Password CLI tool.

documents.title: Option: programs._1password.package
documents.content: The 1Password CLI package to use.

documents.title: Option: programs.alvr.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable ALVR, the VR desktop streamer.

documents.title: Option: programs.alvr.openFirewall
documents.content: Whether to open the default ports in the firewall for the ALVR server.

documents.title: Option: programs.alvr.package
documents.content: The alvr package to use.

documents.title: Option: programs.amnezia-vpn.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable The AmneziaVPN client.

documents.title: Option: programs.amnezia-vpn.package
documents.content: The amnezia-vpn package to use.

documents.title: Option: programs.appgate-sdp.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the AppGate SDP VPN client.

documents.title: Option: programs.appimage.binfmt
documents.content: Whether to enable binfmt registration to run appimages via appimage-run seamlessly.

documents.title: Option: programs.arp-scan.enable

documents.title: Option: programs.atop.atopRotateTimer.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the atop-rotate timer, which restarts the atop service daily to make sure the data files are rotate.

documents.title: Option: programs.atop.atopService.enable

documents.title: Option: programs.atop.atopgpu.enable
documents.content: Whether to install and enable the atopgpud daemon to get information about NVIDIA gpus.

documents.title: Option: programs.atop.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Atop, a tool for monitoring system resources.

documents.title: Option: programs.atop.netatop.enable
documents.content: Whether to install and enable the netatop kernel module. Note: this sets the kernel taint flag "O" for loading out-of-tree modules.

documents.title: Option: programs.atop.netatop.package
documents.content: Which package to use for netatop.

documents.title: Option: programs.atop.package
documents.content: The atop package to use.

documents.title: Option: programs.atop.settings
documents.content: Parameters to be written to {file}/etc/atoprc.

documents.title: Option: programs.atop.setuidWrapper.enable
documents.content: Whether to install a setuid wrapper for Atop. This is required to use some of the features as non-root user (e.g.: ipc information, netatop, atopgpu). Atop tries to drop the root privileges shortly after starting.

documents.title: Option: programs.atuin.daemon.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the Atuin daemon.

documents.title: Option: programs.atuin.daemon.logLevel
documents.content: Log level for the Atuin daemon.

documents.title: Option: programs.atuin.enable

documents.title: Option: programs.pay-respects.aiIntegration
documents.content:
Whether to enable pay-respects' LLM integration. When there is no rule for a given error, pay-respects can query an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint for command corrections.
If this is set to false, all LLM-related features are disabled.
If this is set to true, the default OpenAI endpoint will be used, using upstream's API key. This default API key may be rate-limited.
You can also set a custom API endpoint, large language model and locale for command corrections. Simply access the aiIntegration.url, aiIntegration.model and aiIntegration.locale options, as described in the example.
Take a look at the services.ollama NixOS module if you wish to host a local large language model for pay-respects.

For all of these methods, you can set a custom secret API key by using the _PR_AI_API_KEY environment variable.

strict - Each connection will be done via chained proxies all proxies chained in the order as they appear in the list all proxies must be online to play in chain otherwise EINTR is returned to the app.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.forwardX11
documents.content: Whether to request X11 forwarding on outgoing connections by default. If set to null, the option is not set at all. This is useful for running graphical programs on the remote machine and have them display to your local X11 server. Historically, this value has depended on the value used by the local sshd daemon, but there really isn't a relation between the two. Note: there are some security risks to forwarding an X11 connection. NixOS's X server is built with the SECURITY extension, which prevents some obvious attacks. To enable or disable forwarding on a per-connection basis, see the -X and -x options to ssh. The -Y option to ssh enables trusted forwarding, which bypasses the SECURITY extension.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.hostKeyAlgorithms
documents.content: Specifies the host key algorithms that the client wants to use in order of preference.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.kexAlgorithms

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts
documents.content: The set of system-wide known SSH hosts. To make simple setups more convenient the name of an attribute in this set is used as a host name for the entry. This behaviour can be disabled by setting hostNames explicitly. You can use extraHostNames to add additional host names without disabling this default.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts.<name>.certAuthority
documents.content: This public key is an SSH certificate authority, rather than an individual host's key.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts.<name>.extraHostNames
documents.content: A list of additional host names and/or IP numbers used for accessing the host's ssh service. This list is ignored if hostNames is set explicitly.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts.<name>.hostNames
documents.content: A list of host names and/or IP numbers used for accessing the host's ssh service. This list includes the name of the containing knownHosts attribute by default for convenience. If you wish to configure multiple host keys for the same host use multiple knownHosts entries with different attribute names and the same hostNames list.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts.<name>.publicKey
documents.content: The public key data for the host. You can fetch a public key from a running SSH server with the {command}ssh-keyscan command. The public key should not include any host names, only the key type and the key itself.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts.<name>.publicKeyFile
documents.content: The path to the public key file for the host. The public key file is read at build time and saved in the Nix store. You can fetch a public key file from a running SSH server with the {command}ssh-keyscan command. The content of the file should follow the same format as described for the publicKey option. Only a single key is supported. If a host has multiple keys, use {option}programs.ssh.knownHostsFiles instead.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHostsFiles
documents.content: Files containing SSH host keys to set as global known hosts. /etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts (which is generated by {option}programs.ssh.knownHosts) is always included.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.macs
documents.content: Specifies the MAC (message authentication code) algorithms in order of preference. The MAC algorithm is used for data integrity protection.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.package

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.pubkeyAcceptedKeyTypes

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.setXAuthLocation

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.startAgent

documents.title: Option: programs.starship.transientPrompt.enable
documents.content:

This option only works with fish, as bash requires a custom configuration involving Ble.sh, which can be enabled with programs.bash.blesh.enable, but not configured using NixOS .

documents.title: Option: programs.starship.transientPrompt.left
documents.content:
Fish code composing the body of the starship_transient_prompt_func function. The output of this code will become the left side of the transient prompt.
Not setting this option (or setting it to null) will prevent the starship_transient_prompt_func function from being generated. By default, the left prompt is a bold-green '❯' character.

documents.title: Option: programs.tsmClient.servers
documents.content: Server definitions ("stanzas") for the client system-options file. The name of each entry will be used for the internal servername by default. Each attribute will be transformed into a line with a key-value pair within the server's stanza. Integers as values will be canonically turned into strings. The boolean value true will be turned into a line with just the attribute's name. The value null will not generate a line. A list as values generates an entry for each value, according to the rules above.

Caution: If this option is enabled and the server forces to renew the password (e.g. on first connection), a random password will be generated and stored .

Setting this option to false does not mean that software OpenGL won't work; it may still work depending on your system configuration.
This option is also intended to generate warnings if you are using some configuration that's incompatible with using headless software OpenGL in TurboVNC.

documents.title: Option: programs.uwsm.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable uwsm, which wraps standalone Wayland compositors with a set of Systemd units on the fly. This essentially binds the wayland compositor into graphical-session-pre.target, graphical-session.target, xdg-desktop-autostart.target.
This is useful for Wayland compositors like Hyprland, Sway, Wayfire, etc. that do not start these targets and services on their own.
::: {.note} You must configure waylandCompositors suboptions as well so that UWSM knows which compositors to manage.
Additionally, this by default uses dbus-broker as the dbus implementation for better compatibility. If you dislike this behavior you can set services.dbus.implementation = lib.mkForce "dbus" in your configuration. :::
If you are having trouble starting a service that depends on graphical-session.target, while using a WM, enabling this option might help .

documents.title: Option: programs.zsh.autosuggestions.strategy
documents.content:
ZSH_AUTOSUGGEST_STRATEGY is an array that specifies how suggestions should be generated. The strategies in the array are tried successively until a suggestion is found. There are currently three built-in strategies to choose from:
history: Chooses the most recent match from history.
completion: Chooses a suggestion based on what tab-completion would suggest. (requires zpty module)
match_prev_cmd: Like history, but chooses the most recent match whose preceding history item matches the most recently executed command. Note that this strategy won't work as expected with ZSH options that don't preserve the history order such as HIST_IGNORE_ALL_DUPS or HIST_EXPIRE_DUPS_FIRST.

documents.title: Option: security.allowSimultaneousMultithreading
documents.content:
Whether to allow SMT/hyperthreading. Disabling SMT means that only physical CPU cores will be usable at runtime, potentially at significant performance cost.
The primary motivation for disabling SMT is to mitigate the risk of leaking data between threads running on the same CPU core (due to e.g., shared caches). This attack vector is unproven.
Disabling SMT is a supplement to the L1 data cache flushing mitigation (see ) versus malicious VM guests (SMT could "bring back" previously flushed data).

documents.title: Option: security.allowUserNamespaces
documents.content:
Whether to allow creation of user namespaces.
The motivation for disabling user namespaces is the potential presence of code paths where the kernel's permission checking logic fails to account for namespacing, instead permitting a namespaced process to act outside the namespace with the same privileges as it would have inside it. This is particularly damaging in the common case of running as root within the namespace.
When user namespace creation is disallowed, attempting to create a user namespace fails with "no space left on device" (ENOSPC). root may re-enable user namespace creation at runtime.

documents.title: Option: security.apparmor.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable the AppArmor Mandatory Access Control system.
If you're enabling this module on a running system, note that a reboot will be required to activate AppArmor in the kernel.
Also, beware that enabling this module privileges stability over security by not trying to kill unconfined but newly confinable running processes by default, though it would be needed because AppArmor can only confine new or already confined processes of an executable. This killing would for instance be necessary when upgrading to a NixOS revision introducing for the first time an AppArmor profile for the executable of a running process.
Enable if you want this service to do such killing by sending a SIGTERM to those running processes.

documents.title: Option: security.apparmor.enableCache
documents.content:
Whether to enable caching of AppArmor policies in /var/cache/apparmor/.
Beware that AppArmor policies almost always contain Nix store paths, and thus produce at each change of these paths a new cached version accumulating in the cache.

documents.title: Option: security.apparmor.includes
documents.content: List of paths to be added to AppArmor's searched paths when resolving include directives.

documents.title: Option: security.apparmor.killUnconfinedConfinables
documents.content:
Whether to enable killing of processes which have an AppArmor profile enabled (in ) but are not confined (because AppArmor can only confine new processes).
This is only sending a gracious SIGTERM signal to the processes, not a SIGKILL.
Beware that due to a current limitation of AppArmor, only profiles with exact paths (and no name) can enable such kills.
