documents.title: Option: security.auditd.plugins.<name>.active
documents.content: Whether to enable Whether to enable this plugin.

documents.title: Option: security.auditd.plugins.<name>.args
documents.content: This allows you to pass arguments to the child program. Generally plugins do not take arguments and have their own config file that instructs them how they should be configured.

documents.title: Option: security.auditd.plugins.<name>.direction
documents.content:
The option is dictated by the plugin. In or out are the only choices. You cannot make a plugin operate in a way it wasn't designed just by changing this option. This option is to give a clue to the event dispatcher about which direction events flow.
::: {.note} Inbound events are not supported yet. :::

documents.title: Option: security.auditd.plugins.<name>.format
documents.content: Binary passes the data exactly as the audit event dispatcher gets it from the audit daemon. The string option tells the dispatcher to completely change the event into a string suitable for parsing with the audit parsing library.

documents.title: Option: security.auditd.plugins.<name>.path
documents.content: This is the absolute path to the plugin executable.

documents.title: Option: security.auditd.plugins.<name>.settings
documents.content: Plugin-specific config file to link to /etc/audit/.conf

documents.title: Option: security.auditd.plugins.<name>.type
documents.content: This tells the dispatcher how the plugin wants to be run. There is only one valid option, always, which means the plugin is external and should always be run. The default is always since there are no more builtin plugins.

documents.title: Option: security.auditd.settings
documents.content: auditd configuration file contents. See {auditd.conf} for supported values.

documents.title: Option: security.auditd.settings.admin_space_left
documents.content: This is a numeric value in mebibytes (MiB) that tells the audit daemon when to perform a configurable action because the system is running low on disk space. This should be considered the last chance to do something before running out of disk space. The numeric value for this parameter should be lower than the number for {option}space_left. You may also append a percent sign (e.g. 1%) to the number to have the audit daemon calculate the number based on the disk partition size.

documents.title: Option: security.auditd.settings.space_left
documents.content:
If the free space in the filesystem containing log_file drops below this value, the audit daemon takes the action specified by {option}space_left_action. If the value of {option}space_left is specified as a whole number, it is interpreted as an absolute size in mebibytes (MiB). If the value is specified as a number between 1 and 99 followed by a percentage sign (e.g., 5%), the audit daemon calculates the absolute size in megabytes based on the size of the filesystem containing {option}log_file. (E.g., if the filesystem containing {option}log_file is 2 gibibytes in size, and {option}space_left is set to 25%, then the audit daemon sets {option}space_left to approximately 500 mebibytes.
::: {.note} This calculation is performed when the audit daemon starts, so if you resize the filesystem containing {option}log_file while the audit daemon is running, you should send the audit daemon SIGHUP to re-read the configuration file and recalculate the correct per‐ centage. :::

documents.title: Option: security.chromiumSuidSandbox.enable
documents.content:
Whether to install the Chromium SUID sandbox which is an executable that Chromium may use in order to achieve sandboxing.
If you get the error "The SUID sandbox helper binary was found, but is not configured correctly.", turning this on might help.
Also, if the URL chrome://sandbox tells you that "You are not adequately sandboxed!", turning this on might resolve the issue.

documents.title: Option: security.dhparams.defaultBitSize
documents.content: This allows to override the default bit size for all of the Diffie-Hellman parameters set in {option}security.dhparams.params.

documents.title: Option: security.dhparams.enable
documents.content: Whether to generate new DH params and clean up old DH params.

documents.title: Option: security.dhparams.params
documents.content:
Diffie-Hellman parameters to generate.
The value is the size (in bits) of the DH params to generate. The generated DH params path can be found in config.security.dhparams.params.«name».path.
::: {.note} The name of the DH params is taken as being the name of the service it serves and the params will be generated before the said service is started. :::
::: {.warning} If you are removing all dhparams from this list, you have to leave {option}security.dhparams.enable for at least one activation in order to have them be cleaned up. This also means if you rollback to a version without any dhparams the existing ones won't be cleaned up. Of course this only applies if {option}security.dhparams.stateful is true. :::
::: {.note} For module implementers: It's recommended to not set a specific bit size here, so that users can easily override this by setting {option}security.dhparams.defaultBitSize. :::

documents.title: Option: security.dhparams.params.<name>.bits
documents.content: The bit size for the prime that is used during a Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

documents.title: Option: security.dhparams.params.<name>.path
documents.content: The resulting path of the generated Diffie-Hellman parameters file for other services to reference. This could be either a store path or a file inside the directory specified by {option}security.dhparams.path.

documents.title: Option: security.dhparams.path
documents.content: Path to the directory in which Diffie-Hellman parameters will be stored. This only is relevant if {option}security.dhparams.stateful is true.

documents.title: Option: security.dhparams.stateful
documents.content:
Whether generation of Diffie-Hellman parameters should be stateful or not. If this is enabled, PEM-encoded files for Diffie-Hellman parameters are placed in the directory specified by {option}security.dhparams.path. Otherwise the files are created within the Nix store.
::: {.note} If this is false the resulting store path will be non-deterministic and will be rebuilt every time the openssl package changes. :::

documents.title: Option: security.doas.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the {command}doas command, which allows non-root users to execute commands as root.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraConfig
documents.content: Extra configuration text appended to {file}doas.conf. Be aware that this option cannot be used to override the behaviour allowing passwordless operation for root.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraRules
documents.content: Define specific rules to be set in the {file}/etc/doas.conf file. More specific rules should come after more general ones in order to yield the expected behavior. You can use mkBefore and/or mkAfter to ensure this is the case when configuration options are merged. Be aware that this option cannot be used to override the behaviour allowing passwordless operation for root.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraRules.*.args
documents.content: Arguments that must be provided to the command. When set to [], the command must be run without any arguments.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraRules.*.cmd
documents.content:
The command the user is allowed to run. When set to null (the default), all commands are allowed.
NOTE: It is best practice to specify absolute paths. If a relative path is specified, only a restricted PATH will be searched.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraRules.*.groups
documents.content: The groups / GIDs this rule should apply for.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraRules.*.keepEnv
documents.content: If true, environment variables other than those listed in {manpage}doas(1) are kept when creating the environment for the new process.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraRules.*.noLog
documents.content: If true, successful executions will not be logged to {manpage}syslogd(8).

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraRules.*.noPass
documents.content: If true, the user is not required to enter a password.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraRules.*.persist
documents.content: If true, do not ask for a password again for some time after the user successfully authenticates.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraRules.*.runAs
documents.content:
Which user or group the specified command is allowed to run as. When set to null (the default), all users are allowed.
A user can be specified using just the username: "foo". It is also possible to only allow running as a specific group with ":bar".

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraRules.*.setEnv
documents.content:
Keep or set the specified variables. Variables may also be removed with a leading '-' or set using variable=value. If the first character of value is a '$', the value to be set is taken from the existing environment variable of the indicated name. This option is processed after the default environment has been created.
NOTE: All rules have setenv { SSH_AUTH_SOCK } by default. To prevent SSH_AUTH_SOCK from being inherited, add "-SSH_AUTH_SOCK" anywhere in this list.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.extraRules.*.users
documents.content: The usernames / UIDs this rule should apply for.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.package
documents.content: The doas package to use.

documents.title: Option: security.doas.wheelNeedsPassword
documents.content: Whether users of the wheel group must provide a password to run commands as super user via {command}doas.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.acceptEnvFactor
documents.content:
Look for factor selection or passcode in the $DUO_PASSCODE environment variable before prompting the user for input.
When $DUO_PASSCODE is non-empty, it will override autopush. The SSH client will need SendEnv DUO_PASSCODE in its configuration, and the SSH server will similarly need AcceptEnv DUO_PASSCODE.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.allowTcpForwarding
documents.content: By default, when SSH forwarding, enabling Duo Security will disable TCP forwarding. By enabling this, you potentially undermine some of the SSH based login security. Note this is not needed if you use PAM.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.autopush
documents.content: If true, Duo Unix will automatically send a push login request to the user’s phone, falling back on a phone call if push is unavailable. If false, the user will be prompted to choose an authentication method. When configured with autopush = yes, we recommend setting prompts = 1.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.failmode
documents.content: On service or configuration errors that prevent Duo authentication, fail "safe" (allow access) or "secure" (deny access). The default is "safe".

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.fallbackLocalIP
documents.content:
Duo Unix reports the IP address of the authorizing user, for the purposes of authorization and whitelisting. If Duo Unix cannot detect the IP address of the client, setting fallbackLocalIP = yes will cause Duo Unix to send the IP address of the server it is running on.
If you are using IP whitelisting, enabling this option could cause unauthorized logins if the local IP is listed in the whitelist.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.groups
documents.content: If specified, Duo authentication is required only for users whose primary group or supplementary group list matches one of the space-separated pattern lists. Refer to https://duo.com/docs/duounix for details.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.host
documents.content: Duo API hostname.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.integrationKey
documents.content: Integration key.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.motd
documents.content: Print the contents of /etc/motd to screen after a successful login.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.pam.enable
documents.content: If enabled, protect logins with Duo Security using PAM support.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.prompts
documents.content:
If a user fails to authenticate with a second factor, Duo Unix will prompt the user to authenticate again. This option sets the maximum number of prompts that Duo Unix will display before denying access. Must be 1, 2, or 3. Default is 3.
For example, when prompts = 1, the user will have to successfully authenticate on the first prompt, whereas if prompts = 2, if the user enters incorrect information at the initial prompt, he/she will be prompted to authenticate again.
When configured with autopush = true, we recommend setting prompts = 1.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.pushinfo
documents.content: Include information such as the command to be executed in the Duo Push message.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.secretKeyFile
documents.content: A file containing your secret key. The security of your Duo application is tied to the security of your secret key.

documents.title: Option: security.duosec.ssh.enable
documents.content: If enabled, protect SSH logins with Duo Security.

documents.title: Option: security.enableWrappers
documents.content: Whether to enable SUID/SGID wrappers.

documents.title: Option: security.forcePageTableIsolation
documents.content:
Whether to force-enable the Page Table Isolation (PTI) Linux kernel feature even on CPU models that claim to be safe from Meltdown.
This hardening feature is most beneficial to systems that run untrusted workloads that rely on address space isolation for security.

documents.title: Option: security.googleOsLogin.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable Google OS Login.
The OS Login package enables the following components: AuthorizedKeysCommand to query valid SSH keys from the user's OS Login profile during ssh authentication phase. NSS Module to provide user and group information PAM Module for the sshd service, providing authorization and authentication support, allowing the system to use data stored in Google Cloud IAM permissions to control both, the ability to log into an instance, and to perform operations as root (sudo).

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.basedn
documents.content: Base DN to use when performing LDAP operations.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.cacheCredentials
documents.content: Whether to cache credentials.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.certificate
documents.content:
IPA server CA certificate.
Use nix-prefetch-url http://$server/ipa/config/ca.crt to obtain the file and the hash.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.chromiumSupport
documents.content: Whether to whitelist the FreeIPA domain in Chromium.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.domain
documents.content: Domain of the IPA server.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.dyndns.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable FreeIPA automatic hostname updates.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.dyndns.interface
documents.content: Network interface to perform hostname updates through.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable FreeIPA domain integration.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.ifpAllowedUids
documents.content: A list of users allowed to access the ifp dbus interface.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.ipaHostname
documents.content: Fully-qualified hostname used to identify this host in the IPA domain.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.offlinePasswords
documents.content: Whether to store offline passwords when the server is down.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.realm
documents.content: Kerberos realm.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.server
documents.content: IPA Server hostname.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.shells
documents.content:
List of shells which binaries should be installed to /bin/.
FreeIPA typicly configures somesthing like /bin/bash into the users shell attribute.

documents.title: Option: security.ipa.useAsTimeserver
documents.content: Whether to add the IPA server to the timeserver.

documents.title: Option: security.isolate.boxRoot
documents.content: All sandboxes are created under this directory. To avoid symlink attacks, this directory and all its ancestors must be writeable only by root.

documents.title: Option: security.isolate.cgRoot
documents.content: Control group which subgroups are placed under. Either an explicit path to a subdirectory in cgroupfs, or "auto:file" to read the path from "file", where it is put by isolate-cg-helper.

documents.title: Option: security.isolate.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Sandbox for securely executing untrusted programs .

documents.title: Option: security.isolate.extraConfig
documents.content: Extra configuration to append to the configuration file.

documents.title: Option: security.isolate.firstGid
documents.content: Start of block of GIDs reserved for sandboxes.

documents.title: Option: security.isolate.firstUid
documents.content: Start of block of UIDs reserved for sandboxes.

documents.title: Option: security.isolate.lockRoot
documents.content: Directory where lock files are created.

documents.title: Option: security.isolate.numBoxes
documents.content: Number of UIDs and GIDs to reserve, starting from {option}firstUid and {option}firstGid.

documents.title: Option: security.isolate.package
documents.content: The isolate-unwrapped package to use.

documents.title: Option: security.isolate.restrictedInit
documents.content: If true, only root can create sandboxes.

documents.title: Option: security.krb5.enable
documents.content: Enable and configure Kerberos utilities

documents.title: Option: security.krb5.package
documents.content: The krb5 package to use.

documents.title: Option: security.krb5.settings
documents.content: Structured contents of the {file}krb5.conf file. See {manpage}krb5.conf(5) for details about configuration.

documents.title: Option: security.krb5.settings.include
documents.content: Files to include in the Kerberos configuration.

documents.title: Option: security.krb5.settings.includedir
documents.content: Directories containing files to include in the Kerberos configuration.

documents.title: Option: security.krb5.settings.module
documents.content: Modules to obtain Kerberos configuration from.

documents.title: Option: security.lockKernelModules
documents.content: Disable kernel module loading once the system is fully initialised. Module loading is disabled until the next reboot. Problems caused by delayed module loading can be fixed by adding the module(s) in question to {option}boot.kernelModules.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.chfnRestrict
documents.content: Use chfn SUID to allow non-root users to change their account GECOS information.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.package
documents.content: The shadow package to use.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings
documents.content: Config options for the /etc/login.defs file, that defines the site-specific configuration for the shadow password suite. See {manpage}login.defs(5) man page for available options.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.DEFAULT_HOME
documents.content: Indicate if login is allowed if we can't cd to the home directory.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.ENCRYPT_METHOD
documents.content: This defines the system default encryption algorithm for encrypting passwords.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.GID_MAX
documents.content: Range of group IDs used for the creation of regular groups by useradd, groupadd, or newusers.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.GID_MIN
documents.content: Range of group IDs used for the creation of regular groups by useradd, groupadd, or newusers.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.SYS_GID_MAX
documents.content: Range of group IDs used for the creation of system groups by useradd, groupadd, or newusers

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.SYS_GID_MIN
documents.content: Range of group IDs used for the creation of system groups by useradd, groupadd, or newusers

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.SYS_UID_MAX
documents.content: Range of user IDs used for the creation of system users by useradd or newusers.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.SYS_UID_MIN
documents.content: Range of user IDs used for the creation of system users by useradd or newusers.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.TTYGROUP
documents.content: The terminal permissions: the login tty will be owned by the TTYGROUP group, and the permissions will be set to TTYPERM

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.TTYPERM
documents.content: The terminal permissions: the login tty will be owned by the TTYGROUP group, and the permissions will be set to TTYPERM

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.UID_MAX
documents.content: Range of user IDs used for the creation of regular users by useradd or newusers.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.UID_MIN
documents.content: Range of user IDs used for the creation of regular users by useradd or newusers.

documents.title: Option: security.loginDefs.settings.UMASK
documents.content: The file mode creation mask is initialized to this value.

documents.title: Option: security.lsm
documents.content: A list of the LSMs to initialize in order.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.dp9ik.authserver
documents.content: This controls the hostname for the 9front authentication server that users will be authenticated against.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.dp9ik.control
documents.content: This option sets the pam "control" used for this module.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.dp9ik.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable the dp9ik pam module provided by tlsclient.
If set, users can be authenticated against the 9front authentication server given in {option}security.pam.dp9ik.authserver .

documents.title: Option: security.pam.enableFscrypt
documents.content:
Whether to enable fscrypt, to automatically unlock directories with the user's login password.
This also enables a service at security.pam.services.fscrypt which is used by fscrypt to verify the user's password when setting up a new protector. If you use something other than pam_unix to verify user passwords, please remember to adjust this PAM service .

documents.title: Option: security.pam.enableOTPW
documents.content: Whether to enable the OTPW (one-time password) PAM module.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.enableUMask
documents.content: Whether to enable the umask PAM module.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.howdy.control
documents.content: This option sets the PAM "control" used for this module.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.howdy.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable the Howdy PAM module.
If set, users can be authenticated using Howdy, the Windows Hello™-style facial authentication service.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.krb5.enable
documents.content:
Enables Kerberos PAM modules (pam-krb5, pam-ccreds).
If set, users can authenticate with their Kerberos password. This requires a valid Kerberos configuration (security.krb5.enable should be set to true).
Note that the Kerberos PAM modules are not necessary when using SSS to handle Kerberos authentication.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.loginLimits
documents.content:
Define resource limits that should apply to users or groups. Each item in the list should be an attribute set with a {var}domain, {var}type, {var}item, and {var}value attribute. The syntax and semantics of these attributes must be that described in {manpage}limits.conf(5).
Note that these limits do not apply to systemd services, whose limits can be changed via {option}systemd.settings.Manager instead.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.loginLimits.*.domain
documents.content: Username, groupname, or wildcard this limit applies to

documents.title: Option: security.pam.loginLimits.*.item
documents.content: Item this limit applies to

documents.title: Option: security.pam.loginLimits.*.type
documents.content: Type of this limit

documents.title: Option: security.pam.loginLimits.*.value
documents.content: Value of this limit

documents.title: Option: security.pam.makeHomeDir.skelDirectory
documents.content: Path to skeleton directory whose contents are copied to home directories newly created by pam_mkhomedir.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.makeHomeDir.umask
documents.content: The user file mode creation mask to use on home directories newly created by pam_mkhomedir.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.additionalSearchPaths
documents.content: Additional programs to include in the search path of pam_mount. Useful for example if you want to use some FUSE filesystems like bindfs.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.createMountPoints
documents.content: Create mountpoints for volumes if they do not exist.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.cryptMountOptions
documents.content: Global mount options that apply to every crypt volume. You can define volume-specific options in the volume definitions.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.debugLevel
documents.content: Sets the Debug-Level. 0 disables debugging, 1 enables pam_mount tracing, and 2 additionally enables tracing in mount.crypt. The default is 0. For more information, visit https://pam-mount.sourceforge.net/pam_mount.conf.5.html.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.enable
documents.content: Enable PAM mount system to mount filesystems on user login.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.extraVolumes
documents.content: List of volume definitions for pam_mount. For more information, visit https://pam-mount.sourceforge.net/pam_mount.conf.5.html.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.fuseMountOptions
documents.content: Global mount options that apply to every FUSE volume. You can define volume-specific options in the volume definitions.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.logoutHup
documents.content: Kill remaining processes after logout by sending a SIGHUP.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.logoutKill
documents.content: Kill remaining processes after logout by sending a SIGKILL.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.logoutTerm
documents.content: Kill remaining processes after logout by sending a SIGTERM.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.logoutWait
documents.content: Amount of microseconds to wait until killing remaining processes after final logout. For more information, visit https://pam-mount.sourceforge.net/pam_mount.conf.5.html.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.mount.removeCreatedMountPoints
documents.content: Remove mountpoints created by pam_mount after logout. This only affects mountpoints that have been created by pam_mount in the same session.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.oath.digits
documents.content: Specify the lib.length of the one-time password in number of digits.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.oath.enable
documents.content: Enable the OATH (one-time password) PAM module.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.oath.usersFile
documents.content: Set the path to file where the user's credentials are stored. This file must not be world readable!

documents.title: Option: security.pam.oath.window
documents.content: Specify the number of one-time passwords to check in order to accommodate for situations where the system and the client are slightly out of sync (iteration for HOTP or time steps for TOTP).

documents.title: Option: security.pam.p11.control
documents.content:
This option sets pam "control". If you want to have multi factor authentication, use "required". If you want to use the PKCS#11 device instead of the regular password, use "sufficient".
Read {manpage}pam.conf(5) for better understanding of this option.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.p11.enable
documents.content:
Enables P11 PAM (pam_p11) module.
If set, users can log in with SSH keys and PKCS#11 tokens.
More information can be found here.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.package
documents.content: The pam package to use.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.rssh.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable authenticating using a signature performed by the ssh-agent.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.rssh.settings
documents.content:
Options to pass to the pam_rssh module. Refer to https://github.com/z4yx/pam_rssh/blob/main/README.md#optional-arguments for supported values.
Boolean values render just the key if true, and nothing if false. Null values are ignored. All other values are rendered as key-value pairs.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.rssh.settings.auth_key_file
documents.content:
Path to file with trusted public keys in OpenSSH's authorized_keys format. The following variables are expanded to the respective PAM items:
service: PAM_SERVICE, the service name,
user: PAM_USER, the username of the entity under whose identity service will be given,
tty: PAM_TTY, the terminal name,
rhost: PAM_RHOST, the requesting hostname, and
ruser: PAM_RUSER, the requesting entity.

These PAM items are explained in {manpage}pam_get_item(3).
Variables may be specified as $var, ${var} or ${var:defaultValue}.
::: {.note} Specifying user-writeable files here results in an insecure configuration: a malicious process can then edit such an authorized_keys file and bypass the ssh-agent-based authentication.
This option is ignored if {option}security.pam.rssh.settings.authorized_keys_command is set.
If both this option and {option}security.pam.rssh.settings.authorized_keys_command are unset, the keys will be read from ${HOME}/.ssh/authorized_keys, which should be considered insecure.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services
documents.content: This option defines the PAM services. A service typically corresponds to a program that uses PAM, e.g. {command}login or {command}passwd. Each attribute of this set defines a PAM service, with the attribute name defining the name of the service.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.allowNullPassword
documents.content: Whether to allow logging into accounts that have no password set (i.e., have an empty password field in {file}/etc/passwd or {file}/etc/group). This does not enable logging into disabled accounts (i.e., that have the password field set to !). Note that regardless of what the pam_unix documentation says, accounts with hashed empty passwords are always allowed to log in.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.duoSecurity.enable
documents.content: If set, use the Duo Security pam module pam_duo for authentication. Requires configuration of {option}security.duosec options.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable this PAM service.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.enableAppArmor
documents.content: Enable support for attaching AppArmor profiles at the user/group level, e.g., as part of a role based access control scheme.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.enableGnomeKeyring
documents.content: If enabled, pam_gnome_keyring will attempt to automatically unlock the user's default Gnome keyring upon login. If the user login password does not match their keyring password, Gnome Keyring will prompt separately after login.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.enableUMask
documents.content: If enabled, the pam_umask module will be loaded.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.failDelay.delay
documents.content: The delay time (in microseconds) on failure.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.failDelay.enable
documents.content: If enabled, this will replace the FAIL_DELAY setting from login.defs. Change the delay on failure per-application.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.forwardXAuth
documents.content: Whether X authentication keys should be passed from the calling user to the target user (e.g. for {command}su)

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.fprintAuth
documents.content: If set, fingerprint reader will be used (if exists and your fingerprints are enrolled).

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.gnupg.enable
documents.content: If enabled, pam_gnupg will attempt to automatically unlock the user's GPG keys with the login password via {command}gpg-agent. The keygrips of all keys to be unlocked should be written to {file}~/.pam-gnupg, and can be queried with {command}gpg -K --with-keygrip. Presetting passphrases must be enabled by adding allow-preset-passphrase in {file}~/.gnupg/gpg-agent.conf.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.gnupg.noAutostart
documents.content: Don't start {command}gpg-agent if it is not running. Useful in conjunction with starting {command}gpg-agent as a systemd user service.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.gnupg.storeOnly
documents.content: Don't send the password immediately after login, but store for PAM session.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.googleAuthenticator.allowNullOTP
documents.content: Whether to allow login for accounts that have no OTP set (i.e., accounts with no OTP configured or no existing {file}~/.google_authenticator).

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.googleAuthenticator.enable
documents.content: If set, users with enabled Google Authenticator (created {file}~/.google_authenticator) will be required to provide Google Authenticator token to log in.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.googleAuthenticator.forwardPass
documents.content: The authentication provides a single field requiring the user's password followed by the one-time password (OTP).

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.googleOsLoginAccountVerification
documents.content: If set, will use the Google OS Login PAM modules (pam_oslogin_login, pam_oslogin_admin) to verify possible OS Login users and set sudoers configuration accordingly. This only makes sense to enable for the sshd PAM service.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.googleOsLoginAuthentication
documents.content: If set, will use the pam_oslogin_login's user authentication methods to authenticate users using 2FA. This only makes sense to enable for the sshd PAM service.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.howdy.control
documents.content: This option sets the PAM "control" used for this module.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.howdy.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable the Howdy PAM module.
If set, users can be authenticated using Howdy, the Windows Hello™-style facial authentication service.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.kwallet.enable
documents.content: If enabled, pam_wallet will attempt to automatically unlock the user's default KDE wallet upon login. If the user has no wallet named "kdewallet", or the login password does not match their wallet password, KDE will prompt separately after login.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.kwallet.forceRun
documents.content: The force_run option is used to tell the PAM module for KWallet to forcefully run even if no graphical session (such as a GUI display manager) is detected. This is useful for when you are starting an X Session or a Wayland Session from a TTY. If you intend to log-in from a TTY, it is recommended that you enable this option and ensure that plasma-kwallet-pam.service is started by graphical-session.target.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.kwallet.package
documents.content: The kwallet-pam package to use.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.lastlog.enable
documents.content: Whether to update {file}/var/log/wtmp.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.lastlog.silent
documents.content: Whether to suppress the message showing the last login date.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.limits
documents.content: Attribute set describing resource limits. Defaults to the value of {option}security.pam.loginLimits. The meaning of the values is explained in {manpage}limits.conf(5).

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.limits.*.domain
documents.content: Username, groupname, or wildcard this limit applies to

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.limits.*.item
documents.content: Item this limit applies to

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.limits.*.type
documents.content: Type of this limit

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.limits.*.value
documents.content: Value of this limit

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.logFailures
documents.content: Whether to log authentication failures in {file}/var/log/faillog.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.makeHomeDir
documents.content: Whether to try to create home directories for users with $HOMEs pointing to nonexistent locations on session login.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.mysqlAuth
documents.content: If set, the pam_mysql module will be used to authenticate users against a MySQL/MariaDB database.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.name
documents.content: Name of the PAM service.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.nodelay
documents.content: Whether the delay after typing a wrong password should be disabled.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.oathAuth
documents.content: If set, the OATH Toolkit will be used.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.otpwAuth
documents.content: If set, the OTPW system will be used (if {file}~/.otpw exists).

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.p11Auth
documents.content: If set, keys listed in {file}~/.ssh/authorized_keys and {file}~/.eid/authorized_certificates can be used to log in with the associated PKCS#11 tokens.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.pamMount
documents.content: Enable PAM mount (pam_mount) system to mount filesystems on user login.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.requireWheel
documents.content: Whether to permit root access only to members of group wheel.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.rootOK
documents.content: If set, root doesn't need to authenticate (e.g. for the {command}useradd service).

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.rssh
documents.content: If set, the calling user's SSH agent is used to authenticate against the configured keys. This module works in a manner similar to pam_ssh_agent_auth, but supports a wider range of SSH key types, including those protected by security keys (FIDO2).

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.setEnvironment
documents.content: Whether the service should set the environment variables listed in {option}environment.sessionVariables using pam_env.so.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.setLoginUid
documents.content: Set the login uid of the process ({file}/proc/self/loginuid) for auditing purposes. The login uid is only set by ‘entry points’ like {command}login and {command}sshd, not by commands like {command}sudo.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.showMotd
documents.content: Whether to show the message of the day.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.slurm.adopt.enable
documents.content: If set, it prevents users from logging into nodes if they have no jobs in the node. It also tracks any other spawned processes for accounting and ensures complete job cleanup when a job is completed for any successful connection. Spawned processes get "adopted" as external steps into the current job. As such, those steps get integrated with Slurm accounting and control group facilities.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.slurm.adopt.settings
documents.content:
Slurm Adopt Settings. More information is available at:
https://slurm.schedmd.com/pam_slurm_adopt.html

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.slurm.adopt.settings.action_adopt_failure
documents.content: What to do if the process is unable to be adopted into a job. allow matches the upstream default which is only really suitable for testing; production systems will want deny as a default.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.slurm.adopt.settings.action_generic_failure
documents.content: Catch all for failures related to kernel issues or slurmd access. Ignore falls through to the next PAM module, allowing the connection to go through without adoption.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.slurm.adopt.settings.action_no_jobs
documents.content: What to do if no jobs from the user are found, deny or ignore (pass along to next PAM module).

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.slurm.adopt.settings.action_unknown
documents.content: If the user has jobs, attach them to the newest job. Allow the connection through without adoption.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.slurm.adopt.settings.disable_x11
documents.content: Disable or enable x11 sessions. '0' means the adopted connection has Slurm X11 forwarding with DISPLAY overwritten using X11 tunnel endpoint details.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.slurm.adopt.settings.join_container
documents.content: Attach to a container created by job_container/tmpfs

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.slurm.adopt.settings.nodename
documents.content: Set this only when the Slurm NodeName for this machine differs from hostname -s. If unset, pam_slurm_adopt uses the host short name.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.slurm.enable
documents.content: If set, ONLY prevents users from logging into nodes if they have no jobs in the node. This module is a legacy implementation with functionality limited to login restrictions.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.sshAgentAuth
documents.content: If set, the calling user's SSH agent is used to authenticate against the keys in the calling user's {file}~/.ssh/authorized_keys. This is useful for {command}sudo on password-less remote systems.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.sssdStrictAccess
documents.content: enforce sssd access control

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.startSession
documents.content: If set, the service will register a new session with systemd's login manager. For local sessions, this will give the user access to audio devices, CD-ROM drives. In the default PolicyKit configuration, it also allows the user to reboot the system.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.text
documents.content: Contents of the PAM service file.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.ttyAudit.disablePattern
documents.content: For each user matching one of comma-separated glob patterns, disable TTY auditing

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.ttyAudit.enable
documents.content: Enable or disable TTY auditing for specified users

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.ttyAudit.enablePattern
documents.content: For each user matching one of comma-separated glob patterns, enable TTY auditing

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.ttyAudit.openOnly
documents.content: Set the TTY audit flag when opening the session, but do not restore it when closing the session. Using this option is necessary for some services that don't fork() to run the authenticated session, such as sudo.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.u2f.control
documents.content:
This option sets pam "control". If you want to have multi factor authentication, use "required". If you want to use U2F device instead of regular password, use "sufficient".
Read {manpage}pam.conf(5) for better understanding of this option.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.u2f.enable
documents.content: If set, users listed in {file}$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/Yubico/u2f_keys (or {file}$HOME/.config/Yubico/u2f_keys if XDG variable is not set) are able to log in with the associated U2F key. Path can be changed using {option}security.pam.u2f.authFile option.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.unixAuth
documents.content: Whether users can log in with passwords defined in {file}/etc/shadow.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.usshAuth
documents.content:
If set, users with an SSH certificate containing an authorized principal in their SSH agent are able to log in. Specific options are controlled using the {option}security.pam.ussh options.
Note that the {option}security.pam.ussh.enable must also be set for this option to take effect.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.yubicoAuth
documents.content: If set, users listed in {file}~/.yubico/authorized_yubikeys are able to log in with the associated Yubikey tokens.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.services.<name>.zfs
documents.content: Enable unlocking and mounting of encrypted ZFS home dataset at login.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.sshAgentAuth.authorizedKeysFiles
documents.content:
A list of paths to files in OpenSSH's authorized_keys format, containing the keys that will be trusted by the pam_ssh_agent_auth module.
The following patterns are expanded when interpreting the path:
%f and %H respectively expand to the fully-qualified and short hostname ;
%u expands to the username ;
~ or %h expands to the user's home directory.

::: {.note} Specifying user-writeable files here result in an insecure configuration: a malicious process can then edit such an authorized_keys file and bypass the ssh-agent-based authentication.
See issue #31611 :::

documents.title: Option: security.pam.sshAgentAuth.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable authenticating using a signature performed by the ssh-agent. This allows using SSH keys exclusively, instead of passwords, for instance on remote machines .

documents.title: Option: security.pam.u2f.control
documents.content:
This option sets pam "control". If you want to have multi factor authentication, use "required". If you want to use U2F device instead of regular password, use "sufficient".
Read {manpage}pam.conf(5) for better understanding of this option.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.u2f.enable
documents.content:
Enables U2F PAM (pam-u2f) module.
If set, users listed in {file}$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/Yubico/u2f_keys (or {file}$HOME/.config/Yubico/u2f_keys if XDG variable is not set) are able to log in with the associated U2F key. The path can be changed using {option}security.pam.u2f.authFile option.
File format is:
This file can be generated using {command}pamu2fcfg command.
More information can be found here.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.u2f.settings
documents.content:
Options to pass to the PAM module.
Boolean values render just the key if true, and nothing if false. Null values are ignored. All other values are rendered as key-value pairs.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.u2f.settings.appid
documents.content:
By default pam-u2f module sets the application ID to pam://$HOSTNAME.
When using {command}pamu2fcfg, you can specify your application ID with the -i flag.
More information can be found here

documents.title: Option: security.pam.u2f.settings.authfile
documents.content:
By default pam-u2f module reads the keys from {file}$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/Yubico/u2f_keys (or {file}$HOME/.config/Yubico/u2f_keys if XDG variable is not set).
If you want to change auth file locations or centralize database (for example use {file}/etc/u2f-mappings) you can set this option.
File format is: username:first_keyHandle,first_public_key: second_keyHandle,second_public_key This file can be generated using {command}pamu2fcfg command.
More information can be found here.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.u2f.settings.cue
documents.content:
By default pam-u2f module does not inform user that he needs to use the u2f device, it just waits without a prompt.
If you set this option to true, cue option is added to pam-u2f module and reminder message will be displayed.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.u2f.settings.debug
documents.content: Debug output to stderr.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.u2f.settings.interactive
documents.content: Set to prompt a message and wait before testing the presence of a U2F device. Recommended if your device doesn’t have a tactile trigger.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.u2f.settings.origin
documents.content:
By default pam-u2f module sets the origin to pam://$HOSTNAME. Setting origin to an host independent value will allow you to reuse credentials across machines
When using {command}pamu2fcfg, you can specify your application ID with the -o flag.
More information can be found here

documents.title: Option: security.pam.ussh.authorizedPrincipals
documents.content:
Comma-separated list of authorized principals to permit; if the user presents a certificate with one of these principals, then they will be authorized.
Note that pam-ussh also requires that the certificate contain a principal matching the user's username. The principals from this list are in addition to those principals.
Mutually exclusive with authorizedPrincipalsFile.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.ussh.authorizedPrincipalsFile
documents.content:
Path to a list of principals; if the user presents a certificate with one of these principals, then they will be authorized.
Note that pam-ussh also requires that the certificate contain a principal matching the user's username. The principals from this file are in addition to those principals.
Mutually exclusive with authorizedPrincipals.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.ussh.caFile
documents.content:
By default pam-ussh reads the trusted user CA keys from {file}/etc/ssh/trusted_user_ca.
This should be set the same as your TrustedUserCAKeys option for sshd.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.ussh.control
documents.content:
This option sets pam "control". If you want to have multi factor authentication, use "required". If you want to use the SSH certificate instead of the regular password, use "sufficient".
Read {manpage}pam.conf(5) for better understanding of this option.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.ussh.enable
documents.content:
Enables Uber's USSH PAM (pam-ussh) module.
This is similar to pam-ssh-agent, except that the presence of a CA-signed SSH key with a valid principal is checked instead.
Note that this module must both be enabled using this option and on a per-PAM-service level as well (using usshAuth).
More information can be found here.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.ussh.group
documents.content: If set, then the authenticating user must be a member of this group to use this module.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.yubico.challengeResponsePath
documents.content:
If not null, set the path used by yubico pam module where the challenge expected response is stored.
More information can be found here.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.yubico.control
documents.content:
This option sets pam "control". If you want to have multi factor authentication, use "required". If you want to use Yubikey instead of regular password, use "sufficient".
Read {manpage}pam.conf(5) for better understanding of this option.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.yubico.debug
documents.content: Debug output to stderr.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.yubico.enable
documents.content:
Enables Yubico PAM (yubico-pam) module.
If set, users listed in {file}~/.yubico/authorized_yubikeys are able to log in with the associated Yubikey tokens.
The file must have only one line: username:yubikey_token_id1:yubikey_token_id2 More information can be found here.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.yubico.id
documents.content: client id

documents.title: Option: security.pam.yubico.mode
documents.content:
Mode of operation.
Use "client" for online validation with a YubiKey validation service such as the YubiCloud.
Use "challenge-response" for offline validation using YubiKeys with HMAC-SHA-1 Challenge-Response configurations. See the man-page {manpage}ykpamcfg(1) for further details on how to configure offline Challenge-Response validation.
More information can be found here.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.zfs.enable
documents.content: Enable unlocking and mounting of encrypted ZFS home dataset at login.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.zfs.homes
documents.content: Prefix of home datasets. This value will be concatenated with "/" + <username> in order to determine the home dataset to unlock.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.zfs.mountRecursively
documents.content: Mount child datasets of home dataset.

documents.title: Option: security.pam.zfs.noUnmount
documents.content: Do not unmount home dataset on logout.

documents.title: Option: security.pki.caBundle
documents.content: (Read-only) the path to the final bundle of certificate authorities as a single file.

documents.title: Option: security.pki.caCertificateBlacklist
documents.content: A list of blacklisted CA certificate names that won't be imported from the Mozilla Trust Store into {file}/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt. Use the names from that file.

documents.title: Option: security.pki.certificateFiles
documents.content: A list of files containing trusted root certificates in PEM format. These are concatenated to form {file}/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, which is used by many programs that use OpenSSL, such as {command}curl and {command}git.

documents.title: Option: security.pki.certificates
documents.content: A list of trusted root certificates in PEM format.

documents.title: Option: security.pki.useCompatibleBundle
documents.content:
Whether to enable usage of a compatibility bundle.
Such a bundle consists exclusively of BEGIN CERTIFICATE and no BEGIN TRUSTED CERTIFICATE, which is an OpenSSL specific PEM format.
It is known to be incompatible with certain software stacks.
Nevertheless, enabling this will strip all additional trust rules provided by the certificates themselves. This can have security consequences depending on your usecases .

documents.title: Option: security.please.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable please, a Sudo clone which allows a users to execute a command or edit a file as another user .

documents.title: Option: security.please.package
documents.content: The please package to use.

documents.title: Option: security.please.settings
documents.content: Please configuration. Refer to https://github.com/edneville/please/blob/master/please.ini.md for details.

documents.title: Option: security.please.wheelNeedsPassword
documents.content: Whether users of the wheel group must provide a password to run commands or edit files with {command}please and {command}pleaseedit respectively.

documents.title: Option: security.polkit.adminIdentities
documents.content: Specifies which users are considered “administrators”, for those actions that require the user to authenticate as an administrator (i.e. have an auth_admin value). By default, this is all users in the wheel group.

documents.title: Option: security.polkit.debug
documents.content: Whether to enable debug logs from polkit. This is required in order to see log messages from rule definitions.

documents.title: Option: security.polkit.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable polkit.

documents.title: Option: security.polkit.extraConfig
documents.content: Any polkit rules to be added to config (in JavaScript ;-). See: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/polkit/docs/latest/polkit.8.html#polkit-rules

documents.title: Option: security.polkit.package
documents.content: The polkit package to use.

documents.title: Option: security.protectKernelImage
documents.content: Whether to prevent replacing the running kernel image.

documents.title: Option: security.rtkit.args
documents.content: Command-line options for rtkit-daemon.

documents.title: Option: security.rtkit.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the RealtimeKit system service, which hands out realtime scheduling priority to user processes on demand. For example, PulseAudio and PipeWire use this to acquire realtime priority.

documents.title: Option: security.rtkit.package
documents.content: The rtkit package to use.

documents.title: Option: security.run0.enableSudoAlias
documents.content: Whether to enable make {command}sudo an alias to {command}run0..

documents.title: Option: security.run0.wheelNeedsPassword
documents.content: Whether users of the wheel group must provide a password to run commands as super user via {command}run0.

documents.title: Option: security.shadow.enable
documents.content:
Enable the shadow authentication suite, which provides critical programs such as su, login, passwd.
Note: This is currently experimental. Only disable this if you're confident that you can recover your system if it breaks.

documents.title: Option: security.shadow.su.package
documents.content: The su package to use. This can be overridden by other modules (e.g. sudo-rs) to provide an alternative su implementation.

documents.title: Option: security.soteria.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable Soteria, a Polkit authentication agent for any desktop environment.
::: {.note} You should only enable this if you are on a Desktop Environment that does not provide a graphical polkit authentication agent, or you are on a standalone window manager or Wayland compositor. :::

documents.title: Option: security.soteria.package
documents.content: The soteria package to use.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.configFile
documents.content: This string contains the contents of the {file}sudoers file.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.defaultOptions
documents.content: Options used for the default rules, granting root and the wheel group permission to run any command as any user.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable a memory-safe implementation of the {command}sudo command, which allows non-root users to execute commands as root .

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.execWheelOnly
documents.content: Only allow members of the wheel group to execute sudo by setting the executable's permissions accordingly. This prevents users that are not members of wheel from exploiting vulnerabilities in sudo such as CVE-2021-3156.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.extraConfig
documents.content: Extra configuration text appended to {file}sudoers.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.extraRules
documents.content: Define specific rules to be in the {file}sudoers file. More specific rules should come after more general ones in order to yield the expected behavior. You can use lib.mkBefore/lib.mkAfter to ensure this is the case when configuration options are merged.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.extraRules.*.commands
documents.content: The commands for which the rule should apply.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.extraRules.*.groups
documents.content: The groups / GIDs this rule should apply for.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.extraRules.*.host
documents.content: For what host this rule should apply.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.extraRules.*.runAs
documents.content:
Under which user/group the specified command is allowed to run.
A user can be specified using just the username: "foo". It is also possible to specify a user/group combination using "foo:bar" or to only allow running as a specific group with ":bar".

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.extraRules.*.users
documents.content: The usernames / UIDs this rule should apply for.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.package
documents.content: The sudo-rs package to use.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo-rs.wheelNeedsPassword
documents.content: Whether users of the wheel group must provide a password to run commands as super user via {command}sudo.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo.configFile
documents.content: This string contains the contents of the {file}sudoers file.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo.defaultOptions
documents.content: Options used for the default rules, granting root and the wheel group permission to run any command as any user.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the {command}sudo command, which allows non-root users to execute commands as root.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo.execWheelOnly
documents.content: Only allow members of the wheel group to execute sudo by setting the executable's permissions accordingly. This prevents users that are not members of wheel from exploiting vulnerabilities in sudo such as CVE-2021-3156.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo.extraConfig
documents.content: Extra configuration text appended to {file}sudoers.

documents.title: Option: security.sudo.extraRules
documents.content: Define specific rules to be in the {file}sudoers file. More specific rules should come after more general ones in order to yield the expected behavior. You can use mkBefore/mkAfter to ensure this is the case when configuration options are merged.

documents.title: Option: security.tpm2.fapi.ekCertLess
documents.content:
A switch to disable Endorsement Key (EK) certificate verification.
A value of null indicates that the generated fapi config file does not contain a ek_cert_less key. The effect of not having that key at all is the same as setting its value to false.
A value of false means that the tss2 cli will not work if there is no EK Cert installed, or if the installed EK Cert can't be validated.
A value of true means that the tss2 cli will work even if there's no EK cert installed.

documents.title: Option: security.tpm2.fapi.ekFingerprint
documents.content:
The fingerprint of the endorsement key.
A value of null means that you have chosen not to specify the expected fingerprint of the EK. You can still have an endorsement key, it just won't get checked to see if it's fingerprint matches a particular value before being used.

documents.title: Option: security.virtualisation.flushL1DataCache
documents.content:
Whether the hypervisor should flush the L1 data cache before entering guests. See also .
null: uses the kernel default
"never": disables L1 data cache flushing entirely. May be appropriate if all guests are trusted.
"cond": flushes L1 data cache only for pre-determined code paths. May leak information about the host address space layout.
"always": flushes L1 data cache every time the hypervisor enters the guest. May incur significant performance cost.

documents.title: Option: security.wrappers
documents.content: This option effectively allows adding setuid/setgid bits, capabilities, changing file ownership and permissions of a program without directly modifying it. This works by creating a wrapper program in a directory (not configurable), which is then added to the shell PATH.

documents.title: Option: security.wrappers.<name>.capabilities
documents.content:
A comma-separated list of capability clauses to be given to the wrapper program. The format for capability clauses is described in the “TEXTUAL REPRESENTATION” section of the {manpage}cap_from_text(3) manual page. For a list of capabilities supported by the system, check the {manpage}capabilities(7) manual page.
::: {.note} cap_setpcap, which is required for the wrapper program to be able to raise caps into the Ambient set is NOT raised to the Ambient set so that the real program cannot modify its own capabilities!! This may be too restrictive for cases in which the real program needs cap_setpcap but it at least leans on the side security paranoid vs. too relaxed. :::

documents.content: Whether to enable the HTTP/3 protocol. This requires activating the QUIC transport protocol services.nginx.virtualHosts.<name>.quic = true;. documents.title: Option: services.alloy.configPath
documents.content:
Alloy configuration file/directory path.
We default to /etc/alloy here, and expect the user to configure a configuration file via environment.etc."alloy/config.alloy".
This allows config reload, contrary to specifying a store path.
All .alloy files in the same directory (ignoring subdirs) are also honored and are added to systemd.services.alloy.reloadTriggers to enable config reload during nixos-rebuild switch.
This can also point to another directory containing *.alloy files, or a single Alloy file in the Nix store (at the cost of reload).
Component names must be unique across all Alloy configuration files, and configuration blocks must not be repeated.
Alloy will continue to run if subsequent reloads of the configuration file fail, potentially marking components as unhealthy depending on the nature of the failure. When this happens, Alloy will continue functioning in the last valid state.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.hostname
documents.content: The hostname to serve Anuko Time Tracker on.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx
documents.content: With this option, you can customize the Nginx virtualHost settings.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.acmeFallbackHost
documents.content:
Host which to proxy requests to if ACME challenge is not found. Useful if you want multiple hosts to be able to verify the same domain name.
With this option, you could request certificates for the present domain with an ACME client that is running on another host, which you would specify here.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.acmeRoot
documents.content: Directory for the ACME challenge, which is public. Don't put certs or keys in here. Set to null to inherit from config.security.acme.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.addSSL
documents.content: Whether to enable HTTPS in addition to plain HTTP. This will set defaults for listen to listen on all interfaces on the respective default ports (80, 443).

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.basicAuth
documents.content:
Basic Auth protection for a vhost.
WARNING: This is implemented to store the password in plain text in the Nix store.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.basicAuthFile
documents.content: Basic Auth password file for a vhost. Can be created by running {command}nix-shell --packages apacheHttpd --run 'htpasswd -B -c FILENAME USERNAME'.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.default
documents.content: Makes this vhost the default.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.enableACME
documents.content: Whether to ask Let's Encrypt to sign a certificate for this vhost. Alternately, you can use an existing certificate through {option}useACMEHost.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.extraConfig
documents.content: These lines go to the end of the vhost verbatim.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.forceSSL
documents.content: Whether to add a separate nginx server block that redirects (defaults to 301, configurable with redirectCode) all plain HTTP traffic to HTTPS. This will set defaults for listen to listen on all interfaces on the respective default ports (80, 443), where the non-SSL listens are used for the redirect vhosts.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.globalRedirect
documents.content: If set, all requests for this host are redirected (defaults to 301, configurable with redirectCode) to the given hostname.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.http2
documents.content: Whether to enable the HTTP/2 protocol. Note that (as of writing) due to nginx's implementation, to disable HTTP/2 you have to disable it on all vhosts that use a given IP address / port. If there is one server block configured to enable http2, then it is enabled for all server blocks on this IP. See https://stackoverflow.com/a/39466948/263061.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.http3
documents.content: Whether to enable the HTTP/3 protocol. This requires activating the QUIC transport protocol services.nginx.virtualHosts.<name>.quic = true;. Note that HTTP/3 support is experimental and not yet recommended for production. Read more at https://quic.nginx.org/ HTTP/3 availability must be manually advertised, preferably in each location block.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.http3_hq
documents.content: Whether to enable the HTTP/0.9 protocol negotiation used in QUIC interoperability tests. This requires activating the QUIC transport protocol services.nginx.virtualHosts.<name>.quic = true;. Note that special application protocol support is experimental and not yet recommended for production. Read more at https://quic.nginx.org/

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.kTLS
documents.content: Whether to enable kTLS support. Implementing TLS in the kernel (kTLS) improves performance by significantly reducing the need for copying operations between user space and the kernel. Required Nginx version 1.21.4 or later.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.listen
documents.content:
Listen addresses and ports for this virtual host. IPv6 addresses must be enclosed in square brackets. Note: this option overrides addSSL and onlySSL.
If you only want to set the addresses manually and not the ports, take a look at listenAddresses.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.listen.*.addr
documents.content: Listen address.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.listen.*.extraParameters
documents.content: Extra parameters of this listen directive.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.listen.*.port
documents.content: Port number to listen on. If unset and the listen address is not a socket then nginx defaults to 80.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.listen.*.proxyProtocol
documents.content: Enable PROXY protocol.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.listen.*.ssl
documents.content: Enable SSL.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.listenAddresses
documents.content:
Listen addresses for this virtual host. Compared to listen this only sets the addresses and the ports are chosen automatically.
Note: This option overrides networking.enableIPv6

documents.content: Declarative location config

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.locations.<name>.basicAuth
documents.content:
Basic Auth protection for a vhost.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.locations.<name>.priority
documents.content: Order of this location block in relation to the others in the vhost. The semantics are the same as with lib.mkOrder. Smaller values have a greater priority.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.locations.<name>.proxyPass

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.locations.<name>.proxyWebsockets
documents.content: Whether to support proxying websocket connections with HTTP/1.1.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.locations.<name>.recommendedProxySettings
documents.content: Enable recommended proxy settings.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.locations.<name>.recommendedUwsgiSettings
documents.content: Enable recommended uwsgi settings.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.locations.<name>.return

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.locations.<name>.root

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.locations.<name>.uwsgiPass

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.onlySSL
documents.content: Whether to enable HTTPS and reject plain HTTP connections. This will set defaults for listen to listen on all interfaces on port 443.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.quic
documents.content: Whether to enable the QUIC transport protocol. Note that QUIC support is experimental and not yet recommended for production. Read more at https://quic.nginx.org/

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.redirectCode
documents.content: HTTP status used by globalRedirect and forceSSL. Possible usecases include temporary (302, 307) redirects, keeping the request method and body (307, 308), or explicitly resetting the method to GET (303). See https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Redirections.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.rejectSSL
documents.content: Whether to listen for and reject all HTTPS connections to this vhost. Useful in default server blocks to avoid serving the certificate for another vhost. Uses the ssl_reject_handshake directive available in nginx versions 1.19.4 and above.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.reuseport
documents.content: Create an individual listening socket . It is required to specify only once on one of the hosts.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.root

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.serverName

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.nginx.useACMEHost
documents.content: A host of an existing Let's Encrypt certificate to use. This is useful if you have many subdomains and want to avoid hitting the rate limit. Alternately, you can generate a certificate through {option}enableACME. Note that this option does not create any certificates, nor it does add subdomains to existing ones – you will need to create them manually using .

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.settings.reportFooter

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.settings.weekendStartDay
documents.content: This option defines which days are highlighted with weekend color. 6 means Saturday. For Saudi Arabia, etc. set it to 4 for Thursday and Friday to be weekend days.

documents.title: Option: services.anuko-time-tracker.user

documents.title: Option: services.apache-kafka.formatLogDirsIgnoreFormatted

documents.title: Option: services.apache-kafka.settings
documents.content:
Kafka broker configuration {file}server.properties.
Note that .properties files contain mappings from string to string. Keys with dots are NOT represented by nested attrs in these settings, but instead as quoted strings (ie. settings."broker.id", NOT settings.broker.id).

documents.title: Option: services.apache-kafka.settings."broker.id"
documents.content: Broker ID. -1 or null to auto-allocate in zookeeper mode.

documents.title: Option: services.apache-kafka.settings."log.dirs"

documents.title: Option: services.apache-kafka.settings.listeners

documents.title: Option: services.apcupsd.configText
documents.content: Contents of the runtime configuration file, apcupsd.conf. The default settings makes apcupsd autodetect USB UPSes, limit network access to localhost and shutdown the system when the battery level is below 50 percent, or when the UPS has calculated that it has 5 minutes or less of remaining power-on time. See man apcupsd.conf for details.

documents.title: Option: services.apcupsd.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the APC UPS daemon. apcupsd monitors your UPS and permits orderly shutdown of your computer in the event of a power failure. User manual: http://www.apcupsd.com/manual/manual.html. Note that apcupsd runs as root (to allow shutdown of computer). You can check the status of your UPS with the "apcaccess" command.

documents.title: Option: services.apcupsd.hooks
documents.content:
Each attribute in this option names an apcupsd event and the string value it contains will be executed in a shell, in response to that event (prior to the default action). See "man apccontrol" for the list of events and what they represent.
A hook script can stop apccontrol from doing its default action by exiting with value 99. Do not do this unless you know what you're doing.

documents.title: Option: services.arbtt.enable

documents.title: Option: services.arbtt.logFile

documents.title: Option: services.arbtt.package
documents.content: The arbtt package to use.

documents.title: Option: services.arbtt.sampleRate
documents.content: The sampling interval in seconds.

documents.title: Option: services.archisteamfarm.bots
