documents.title: Option: users.extraUsers.<name>.hashedPassword
documents.content:
Specifies the hashed password for the user.
The {option}initialHashedPassword, {option}hashedPassword, {option}initialPassword, {option}password and {option}hashedPasswordFile options all control what password is set for the user.
In a system where is false, typically only one of {option}hashedPassword, {option}password, or {option}hashedPasswordFile will be set.
In a system where or is true, typically only one of {option}initialPassword, {option}initialHashedPassword, or {option}hashedPasswordFile will be set.
If the option {option}users.mutableUsers is true, the password defined in one of the above password options will only be set when the user is created for the first time. After that, you are free to change the password with the ordinary user management commands. If {option}users.mutableUsers is false, you cannot change user passwords, they will always be set according to the password options.
If none of the password options are set, then no password is assigned to the user, and the user will not be able to do password-based logins.
If multiple of these password options are set at the same time then a specific order of precedence is followed, which can lead to surprising results. The order of precedence differs depending on whether the {option}users.mutableUsers option is set.
If the option {option}users.mutableUsers is false, then the order of precedence is as shown below, where values on the left are overridden by values on the right: {option}initialHashedPassword -> {option}hashedPassword -> {option}initialPassword -> {option}password -> {option}hashedPasswordFile
If the option {option}users.mutableUsers is true, then the order of precedence is as shown below, where values on the left are overridden by values on the right: {option}initialHashedPassword -> {option}initialPassword -> {option}hashedPassword -> {option}password -> {option}hashedPasswordFile
To generate a hashed password run mkpasswd.
If set to an empty string (""), this user will be able to log in without being asked for a password (but not via remote services such as SSH, or indirectly via {command}su or {command}sudo). This should only be used for e.g. bootable live systems. Note: this is different from setting an empty password, which can be achieved using {option}users.users.<name?>.password.
If set to null (default) this user will not be able to log in using a password (i.e. via {command}login command).

documents.content:
Specifies the initial hashed password for the user, i.e. the hashed password assigned if the user does not already exist. If {option}users.mutableUsers is true, the password can be changed subsequently using the {command}passwd command. Otherwise, it's equivalent to setting the {option}hashedPassword option.
The {option}initialHashedPassword, {option}hashedPassword, {option}initialPassword, {option}password and {option}hashedPasswordFile options all control what password is set for the user.
In a system where is false, typically only one of {option}hashedPassword, {option}password, or {option}hashedPasswordFile will be set.
In a system where or is true, typically only one of {option}initialPassword, {option}initialHashedPassword, or {option}hashedPasswordFile will be set.
If the option {option}users.mutableUsers is true, the password defined in one of the above password options will only be set when the user is created for the first time. After that, you are free to change the password with the ordinary user management commands. documents.title: Option: users.extraUsers.<name>.isNormalUser
documents.content: Indicates whether this is an account for a “real” user. This automatically sets {option}group to users, {option}createHome to true, {option}home to {file}/home/«username», {option}useDefaultShell to true, and {option}isSystemUser to false. Exactly one of isNormalUser and isSystemUser must be true.

documents.title: Option: users.extraUsers.<name>.isSystemUser
documents.content: Indicates if the user is a system user or not. This option only has an effect if {option}uid is {option}null, in which case it determines whether the user's UID is allocated in the range for system users (below 1000) or in the range for normal users (starting at 1000). documents.title: Option: users.extraUsers.<name>.linger
documents.content:
Whether to enable or disable lingering for this user. Without lingering, user units will not be started until the user logs in, and may be stopped on logout depending on the settings in {file}logind.conf.
By default, NixOS will not manage lingering, new users will default to not lingering, and lingering can be configured imperatively using loginctl enable-linger or loginctl disable-linger. Setting this option to true or false is the declarative equivalent of running loginctl enable-linger or loginctl disable-linger respectively.

documents.title: Option: users.extraUsers.<name>.name
documents.content: The name of the user account. If undefined, the name of the attribute set will be used.

documents.title: Option: users.extraUsers.<name>.openssh.authorizedKeys.keyFiles
documents.content: A list of files each containing one OpenSSH public key that should be added to the user's authorized keys. documents.title: Option: users.extraUsers.<name>.openssh.authorizedPrincipals

documents.title: Option: users.extraUsers.<name>.packages

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.base
documents.content: The distinguished name of the search base.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.bind.distinguishedName
documents.content: The distinguished name to bind to the LDAP server with. If this is not specified, an anonymous bind will be done.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.bind.passwordFile
documents.content: The path to a file containing the credentials to use when binding to the LDAP server (if not binding anonymously).

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.bind.policy
documents.content: Specifies the policy to use for reconnecting to an unavailable LDAP server. The default is hard_open, which reconnects if opening the connection to the directory server failed. By contrast, hard_init reconnects if initializing the connection failed. Initializing may not actually contact the directory server, and it is possible that a malformed configuration file will trigger reconnection. If soft is specified, then nss_ldap will return immediately on server failure. All hard reconnect policies block with exponential backoff before retrying.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.bind.timeLimit
documents.content: Specifies the time limit (in seconds) to use when connecting to the directory server. This is distinct from the time limit specified in {option}users.ldap.timeLimit and affects the initial server connection only.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.daemon.enable
documents.content: Whether to let the nslcd daemon (nss-pam-ldapd) handle the LDAP lookups for NSS and PAM. This can improve performance, and if you need to bind to the LDAP server with a password, it increases security, since only the nslcd user needs to have access to the bindpw file, not everyone that uses NSS and/or PAM. If this option is enabled, a local nscd user is created automatically, and the nslcd service is started automatically when the network get up.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.daemon.extraConfig
documents.content: Extra configuration options that will be added verbatim at the end of the nslcd configuration file ({manpage}nslcd.conf(5)).

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.daemon.rootpwmoddn
documents.content: The distinguished name to use to bind to the LDAP server when the root user tries to modify a user's password.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.daemon.rootpwmodpwFile
documents.content: The path to a file containing the credentials with which to bind to the LDAP server if the root user tries to change a user's password.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable authentication against an LDAP server.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.extraConfig
documents.content: Extra configuration options that will be added verbatim at the end of the ldap configuration file ({manpage}ldap.conf(5)). If {option}users.ldap.daemon is enabled, this configuration will not be used. In that case, use {option}users.ldap.daemon.extraConfig instead.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.loginPam

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.nsswitch
documents.content: Whether to include lookup against LDAP in NSS.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.server
documents.content: The URL of the LDAP server.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.timeLimit
documents.content: Specifies the time limit (in seconds) to use when performing searches. A value of zero (0), which is the default, is to wait indefinitely for searches to be completed.

documents.title: Option: users.ldap.useTLS
documents.content: If enabled, use TLS (encryption) over an LDAP (port 389) connection. The alternative is to specify an LDAPS server (port 636) in {option}users.ldap.server or to forego security.

documents.title: Option: users.manageLingering
documents.content: Whether to manage whether users linger or not.

documents.title: Option: users.motd

documents.title: Option: users.motdFile
documents.content: A file containing the message of the day shown to users when they log in.

documents.title: Option: users.mutableUsers
documents.content:
If set to true, you are free to add new users and groups to the system with the ordinary useradd and groupadd commands. On system activation, the existing contents of the /etc/passwd and /etc/group files will be merged with the contents generated from the users.users and users.groups options. The initial password for a user will be set according to users.users, but existing passwords will not be changed.
::: {.warning} If set to false, the contents of the user and group files will simply be replaced on system activation. This also holds for the user passwords; all changed passwords will be reset according to the users.users configuration on activation. :::

documents.title: Option: users.mysql.pam.passwordColumn
documents.content: The name of the column that contains a (encrypted) password string.

documents.title: Option: users.mysql.pam.passwordCrypt
documents.content:
The method to encrypt the user's password:
0 (or "plain"): No encryption. Passwords are stored in plaintext. HIGHLY DISCOURAGED.
1 (or "Y"): Use {manpage}crypt(3) function.
2 (or "mysql"): Use the MySQL PASSWORD() function. It is possible that the encryption function used by pam_mysql is different from that of the MySQL server, as pam_mysql uses the function defined in MySQL's C-client API instead of using PASSWORD() SQL function in the query.
3 (or "md5"): Use plain hex MD5.
4 (or "sha1"): Use plain hex SHA1.
5 (or "drupal7"): Use Drupal7 salted passwords.
6 (or "joomla15"): Use Joomla15 salted passwords.
7 (or "ssha"): Use ssha hashed passwords.
8 (or "sha512"): Use sha512 hashed passwords.
9 (or "sha256"): Use sha256 hashed passwords.

documents.title: Option: users.mysql.pam.statusColumn
documents.content:
The name of the column or an SQL expression that indicates the status of the user. The status is expressed by the combination of two bitfields shown below:
bit 0 (0x01): if flagged, pam_mysql deems the account to be expired and returns PAM_ACCT_EXPIRED. That is, the account is supposed to no longer be available. Note this doesn't mean that pam_mysql rejects further authentication operations.
bit 1 (0x02): if flagged, pam_mysql deems the authentication token (password) to be expired and returns PAM_NEW_AUTHTOK_REQD. This ends up requiring that the user enter a new password.

To generate a hashed password run mkpasswd.
If set to an empty string (""), this user will be able to log in without being asked for a password (but not via remote services such as SSH, or indirectly via {command}su or {command}sudo). This should only be used for e.g. bootable live systems. Note: this is different from setting an empty password, which can be achieved using {option}users.users.<name?>.password.
If set to null (default) this user will not be able to log in using a password (i.e. via {command}login command).

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.initialPassword
documents.content:
Specifies the initial password for the user, i.e. the password assigned if the user does not already exist. If {option}users.mutableUsers is true, the password can be changed subsequently using the {command}passwd command. Otherwise, it's equivalent to setting the {option}password option. The same caveat applies: the password specified here is world-readable in the Nix store, so it should only be used for guest accounts or passwords that will be changed promptly.
The {option}initialHashedPassword, {option}hashedPassword, {option}initialPassword, {option}password and {option}hashedPasswordFile options all control what password is set for the user.
In a system where is false, typically only one of {option}hashedPassword, {option}password, or {option}hashedPasswordFile will be set.
In a system where or is true, typically only one of {option}initialPassword, {option}initialHashedPassword, or {option}hashedPasswordFile will be set.
If the option {option}users.mutableUsers is true, the password defined in one of the above password options will only be set when the user is created for the first time. After that, you are free to change the password with the ordinary user management commands. If {option}users.mutableUsers is false, you cannot change user passwords, they will always be set according to the password options.
If none of the password options are set, then no password is assigned to the user, and the user will not be able to do password-based logins.
If multiple of these password options are set at the same time then a specific order of precedence is followed, which can lead to surprising results. The order of precedence differs depending on whether the {option}users.mutableUsers option is set.
If the option {option}users.mutableUsers is false, then the order of precedence is as shown below, where values on the left are overridden by values on the right: {option}initialHashedPassword -> {option}hashedPassword -> {option}initialPassword -> {option}password -> {option}hashedPasswordFile
If the option {option}users.mutableUsers is true, then the order of precedence is as shown below, where values on the left are overridden by values on the right: {option}initialHashedPassword -> {option}initialPassword -> {option}hashedPassword -> {option}password -> {option}hashedPasswordFile

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.isNormalUser
documents.content: Indicates whether this is an account for a “real” user. This automatically sets {option}group to users, {option}createHome to true, {option}home to {file}/home/«username», {option}useDefaultShell to true, and {option}isSystemUser to false. Exactly one of isNormalUser and isSystemUser must be true.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.isSystemUser
documents.content: Indicates if the user is a system user or not. This option only has an effect if {option}uid is {option}null, in which case it determines whether the user's UID is allocated in the range for system users (below 1000) or in the range for normal users (starting at 1000). Exactly one of isNormalUser and isSystemUser must be true.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.linger
documents.content:
Whether to enable or disable lingering for this user. Without lingering, user units will not be started until the user logs in, and may be stopped on logout depending on the settings in {file}logind.conf.
By default, NixOS will not manage lingering, new users will default to not lingering, and lingering can be configured imperatively using loginctl enable-linger or loginctl disable-linger. Setting this option to true or false is the declarative equivalent of running loginctl enable-linger or loginctl disable-linger respectively.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.name
documents.content: The name of the user account. If undefined, the name of the attribute set will be used.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.openssh.authorizedKeys.keyFiles
documents.content: A list of files each containing one OpenSSH public key that should be added to the user's authorized keys. The contents of the files are read at build time and added to a file that the SSH daemon reads in addition to the the user's authorized_keys file. You can combine the keyFiles and keys options.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.openssh.authorizedKeys.keys
documents.content: A list of verbatim OpenSSH public keys that should be added to the user's authorized keys. The keys are added to a file that the SSH daemon reads in addition to the the user's authorized_keys file. You can combine the keys and keyFiles options. Warning: If you are using NixOps then don't use this option since it will replace the key required for deployment via ssh.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.openssh.authorizedPrincipals
documents.content: A list of verbatim principal names that should be added to the user's authorized principals.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.packages
documents.content: The set of packages that should be made available to the user. This is in contrast to {option}environment.systemPackages, which adds packages to all users.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.pamMount
documents.content: Attributes for user's entry in {file}pam_mount.conf.xml. Useful attributes might include path, options, fstype, and server. See https://pam-mount.sourceforge.net/pam_mount.conf.5.html for more information.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.password
documents.content:
Specifies the (clear text) password for the user. Warning: do not set confidential information here because it is world-readable in the Nix store. This option should only be used for public accounts.
The {option}initialHashedPassword, {option}hashedPassword, {option}initialPassword, {option}password and {option}hashedPasswordFile options all control what password is set for the user.
In a system where is false, typically only one of {option}hashedPassword, {option}password, or {option}hashedPasswordFile will be set.
In a system where or is true, typically only one of {option}initialPassword, {option}initialHashedPassword, or {option}hashedPasswordFile will be set.
If the option {option}users.mutableUsers is true, the password defined in one of the above password options will only be set when the user is created for the first time. After that, you are free to change the password with the ordinary user management commands. If {option}users.mutableUsers is false, you cannot change user passwords, they will always be set according to the password options.
If none of the password options are set, then no password is assigned to the user, and the user will not be able to do password-based logins.
If multiple of these password options are set at the same time then a specific order of precedence is followed, which can lead to surprising results. The order of precedence differs depending on whether the {option}users.mutableUsers option is set.
If the option {option}users.mutableUsers is false, then the order of precedence is as shown below, where values on the left are overridden by values on the right: {option}initialHashedPassword -> {option}hashedPassword -> {option}initialPassword -> {option}password -> {option}hashedPasswordFile
If the option {option}users.mutableUsers is true, then the order of precedence is as shown below, where values on the left are overridden by values on the right: {option}initialHashedPassword -> {option}initialPassword -> {option}hashedPassword -> {option}password -> {option}hashedPasswordFile

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.shell
documents.content: The path to the user's shell. Can use shell derivations, like pkgs.bashInteractive. Don’t forget to enable your shell in programs if necessary, like programs.zsh.enable = true;.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.subGidRanges

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.subUidRanges.*.count
documents.content: Count of subordinate user ids

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.subUidRanges.*.startUid
documents.content: Start of the range of subordinate user ids that user is allowed to use.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.uid
documents.content: The account UID. If the UID is null, a free UID is picked on activation.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.useDefaultShell

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.autoPrune.allVolumes.enable
documents.content:
Whether to periodically prune all Docker volumes when auto pruning other docker resources by running {command}docker volume prune --force --all
To prune only anonymous volumes, instead pass --volumes to autoPrune.flags

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.autoPrune.allVolumes.flags
documents.content: Any additional flags passed to {command}docker volume prune --force --all.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.autoPrune.dates
documents.content: Specification (in the format described by {manpage}systemd.time(7)) of the time at which the prune will occur.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.autoPrune.enable
documents.content:
Whether to periodically prune Docker resources. If enabled, a systemd timer will run docker system prune -f as specified by the dates option.
NOTE: by default this does not prune volumes. Anonymous volumes can be pruned by passing "--volumes" to autoPrune.flags.
To prune all volumes (not just anonymous ones) autoPrune.allVolumes.enable must be used.
See upstream documentation for further information.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.autoPrune.flags
documents.content: Any additional flags passed to {command}docker system prune.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.autoPrune.persistent
documents.content: Takes a boolean argument. If true, the time when the service unit was last triggered is stored on disk. When the timer is activated, the service unit is triggered immediately if it would have been triggered at least once during the time when the timer was inactive. Such triggering is nonetheless subject to the delay imposed by RandomizedDelaySec=. This is useful to catch up on missed runs of the service when the system was powered down.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.autoPrune.randomizedDelaySec
documents.content: Add a randomized delay before each auto prune. The delay will be chosen between zero and this value. This value must be a time span in the format specified by {manpage}systemd.time(7)

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.daemon.settings

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.daemon.settings.live-restore
documents.content: Allow dockerd to be restarted without affecting running container. This option is incompatible with docker swarm.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.enable
documents.content: This option enables docker, a daemon that manages linux containers. Users in the "docker" group can interact with the daemon (e.g. to start or stop containers) using the {command}docker command line tool.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.enableNvidia
documents.content:
Deprecated, please use {option}hardware.nvidia-container-toolkit.enable instead.
Enable Nvidia GPU support inside docker containers.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.enableOnBoot
documents.content: When enabled dockerd is started on boot. This is required for containers which are created with the --restart=always flag to work. If this option is disabled, docker might be started on demand by socket activation.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.extraOptions
documents.content: The extra command-line options to pass to {command}docker daemon.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.extraPackages
documents.content: Extra packages to add to PATH for the docker daemon process.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.listenOptions
documents.content: A list of unix and tcp docker should listen to. The format follows ListenStream as described in {manpage}systemd.socket(5).

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.liveRestore
documents.content: Alias of {option}virtualisation.docker.daemon.settings.live-restore.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.logDriver
documents.content: This option determines which Docker log driver to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.package
documents.content: The docker package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.rootless.daemon.settings
documents.content: Configuration for docker daemon. The attributes are serialized to JSON used as daemon.conf. See https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/commandline/dockerd/#daemon-configuration-file

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.rootless.enable
documents.content: This option enables docker in a rootless mode, a daemon that manages linux containers. To interact with the daemon, one needs to set {command}DOCKER_HOST=unix://$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.rootless.extraPackages
documents.content: Extra packages to add to PATH for the docker daemon process.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.rootless.package
documents.content: The docker package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.rootless.setSocketVariable
documents.content: Point {command}DOCKER_HOST to rootless Docker instance for normal users by default.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.docker.storageDriver
documents.content:
This option determines which Docker storage driver to use. By default it lets docker automatically choose the preferred storage driver. However, it is recommended to specify a storage driver explicitly, as docker's default varies over versions.
::: {.warning} Changing the storage driver will cause any existing containers and images to become inaccessible. :::

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.hypervGuest.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Hyper-V Guest Support.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.agent.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Incus agent.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.clientPackage
documents.content: The incus client package to use. This package is added to PATH.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable incusd, a daemon that manages containers and virtual machines.
Users in the "incus-admin" group can interact with the daemon (e.g. to start or stop containers) using the {command}incus command line tool, among others. Users in the "incus" group can also interact with the daemon, but with lower permissions (i.e. administrative operations are forbidden). .

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.lxcPackage
documents.content: The lxc package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.package
documents.content: The incus-lts package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.preseed
documents.content:
Configuration for Incus preseed, see https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/howto/initialize/#non-interactive-configuration for supported values.
Changes to this will be re-applied to Incus which will overwrite existing entities or create missing ones, but entities will not be removed by preseed.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.socketActivation
documents.content: Whether to enable socket-activation for starting incus.service. Enabling this option will stop incus.service from starting automatically on boot. .

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.softDaemonRestart
documents.content: Allow for incus.service to be stopped without affecting running instances.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.startTimeout
documents.content: Time to wait (in seconds) for incusd to become ready to process requests. If incusd does not reply within the configured time, incus.service will be considered failed and systemd will attempt to restart it.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.ui.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Incus Web UI.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.ui.package
documents.content: The incus-ui-canonical package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.incus.useACMEHost
documents.content: Host of an existing Let's Encrypt certificate to use for TLS. Note that this option does not create any certificates and it doesn't add subdomains to existing ones – you will need to create them manually using {option}security.acme.certs.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.kvmgt.device
documents.content: PCI ID of graphics card. You can figure it with {command}ls /sys/class/mdev_bus.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.kvmgt.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable KVMGT (iGVT-g) VGPU support. When enabled on a host, allows Qemu/KVM guests to share host's Intel integrated graphics card. Currently only one graphical device can be shared. To allow host users to access the device without root add them to the kvm group: users.extraUsers.<yourusername>.extraGroups = [ "kvm" ]; .

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.kvmgt.vgpus
documents.content: Virtual GPUs of the host to be used in Qemu. You can find devices via {command}ls /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/mdev_supported_types and find info about device via {command}cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/mdev_supported_types/i915-GVTg_V5_4/description

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.kvmgt.vgpus.<name>.uuid
documents.content: UUID(s) of VGPU device. You can generate one with libossp_uuid.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.libvirtd.extraConfig

documents.content: Hooks that will be placed under /var/lib/libvirt/hooks/daemon.d/ and called for daemon start/shutdown/SIGHUP events. Please see https://libvirt.org/hooks.html for documentation.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.libvirtd.nss
documents.content: libvirt NSS module options.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.libvirtd.nss.enable
documents.content: This option enables the older libvirt NSS module. This method uses DHCP server records, therefore is dependent on the hostname provided by the guest. Please see https://libvirt.org/nss.html for more information.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.libvirtd.nss.enableGuest
documents.content: This option enables the newer libvirt_guest NSS module. This module uses the libvirt guest name instead of the hostname of the guest. Please see https://libvirt.org/nss.html for more information.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.libvirtd.onBoot
documents.content: Specifies the action to be done to / on the guests when the host boots. The "start" option starts all guests that were running prior to shutdown regardless of their autostart settings. The "ignore" option will not start the formerly running guest on boot. However, any guest marked as autostart will still be automatically started by libvirtd.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.libvirtd.onShutdown
documents.content: When shutting down / restarting the host what method should be used to gracefully halt the guests. Setting to "shutdown" will cause an ACPI shutdown of each guest. "suspend" will attempt to save the state of the guests ready to restore on boot.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.libvirtd.package
documents.content: The libvirt package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.libvirtd.parallelShutdown
documents.content: Number of guests that will be shutdown concurrently, taking effect when onShutdown is set to "shutdown". If set to 0, guests will be shutdown one after another. Number of guests on shutdown at any time will not exceed number set in this variable.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.libvirtd.qemu

Changing this option to false may cause file permission issues for existing guests. To fix these, manually change ownership of affected files in /var/lib/libvirt/qemu to qemu-libvirtd.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.entrypoint
documents.content: Override the default entrypoint of the image.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.environment
documents.content: Environment variables to set for this container.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.environmentFiles
documents.content: Environment files for this container.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.extraOptions
documents.content: Extra options for {command}podman run.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.hostname
documents.content: The hostname of the container.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.image
documents.content: OCI image to run.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.imageFile
documents.content:
Path to an image file to load before running the image. This can be used to bypass pulling the image from the registry.
The image attribute must match the name and tag of the image contained in this file, as they will be used to run the container with that image. If they do not match, the image will be pulled from the registry as usual.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.imageStream
documents.content:
Path to a script that streams the desired image on standard output.
This option is mainly intended for use with pkgs.dockerTools.streamLayeredImage so that the intermediate image archive does not need to be stored in the Nix store. For larger images this optimization can significantly reduce Nix store churn compared to using the imageFile option, because you don't have to store a new copy of the image archive in the Nix store every time you change the image. Instead, if you stream the image then you only need to build and store the layers that differ from the previous image.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.labels
documents.content: Labels to attach to the container at runtime.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.log-driver
documents.content:
Logging driver for the container. The default of "journald" means that the container's logs will be handled as part of the systemd unit.
For more details and a full list of logging drivers, refer to respective backends documentation.
For Docker: Docker engine documentation
For Podman: Refer to the {manpage}docker-run(1) man page.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.login.passwordFile
documents.content: Path to file containing password.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.login.registry
documents.content: Registry where to login to.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.login.username
documents.content: Username for login.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.networks
documents.content: Networks to attach the container to

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.podman
documents.content: Podman-specific settings in OCI containers. These must be null when using the docker backend.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.podman.sdnotify
documents.content:
Determines how podman should notify systemd that the unit is ready. There are three options:
conmon: marks the unit as ready when the container has started.
healthy: marks the unit as ready when the container's healthcheck passes.
container: NOTIFY_SOCKET is passed into the container and the process inside the container needs to indicate on its own that it's ready.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.podman.user
documents.content: The user under which the container should run.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.ports
documents.content:
Network ports to publish from the container to the outer host.
Valid formats:
<ip>:<hostPort>:<containerPort>
<ip>::<containerPort>
<hostPort>:<containerPort>
<containerPort>

Both hostPort and containerPort can be specified as a range of ports. When specifying ranges for both, the number of container ports in the range must match the number of host ports in the range. Example: 1234-1236:1234-1236/tcp
When specifying a range for hostPort only, the containerPort must not be a range. In this case, the container port is published somewhere within the specified hostPort range. Example: 1234-1236:1234/tcp
Publishing a port bypasses the NixOS firewall. If the port is not supposed to be shared on the network, make sure to publish the port to localhost. Example: 127.0.0.1:1234:1234
Refer to the Docker engine documentation for full details.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.preRunExtraOptions
documents.content: Extra options for {command}podman that go before the run argument.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.privileged
documents.content: Give extended privileges to the container

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.pull
documents.content: Image pull policy for the container. Must be one of: always, missing, never, newer

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.serviceName
documents.content: Systemd service name that manages the container

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.user
documents.content: Override the username or UID (and optionally groupname or GID) used in the container.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.volumes
documents.content:
List of volumes to attach to this container.
Note that this is a list of "src:dst" strings to allow for src to refer to /nix/store paths, which would be difficult with an attribute set. There are also a variety of mount options available as a third field; please refer to the docker engine documentation for details.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>.workdir
documents.content: Override the default working directory for the container.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.autoPrune.dates
documents.content: Specification (in the format described by {manpage}systemd.time(7)) of the time at which the prune will occur.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.autoPrune.enable
documents.content: Whether to periodically prune Podman resources. If enabled, a systemd timer will run podman system prune -f as specified by the dates option.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.autoPrune.flags
documents.content: Any additional flags passed to {command}podman system prune.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.defaultNetwork.settings
documents.content: Settings for podman's default network.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.dockerCompat
documents.content: Create an alias mapping {command}docker to {command}podman.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.dockerSocket.enable
documents.content:
Make the Podman socket available in place of the Docker socket, so Docker tools can find the Podman socket.
Podman implements the Docker API.
Users must be in the podman group in order to connect. As with Docker, members of this group can gain root access.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.enable
documents.content:
This option enables Podman, a daemonless container engine for developing, managing, and running OCI Containers on your Linux System.
It is a drop-in replacement for the {command}docker command.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.enableNvidia
documents.content:
Deprecated, please use {option}hardware.nvidia-container-toolkit.enable instead.
Enable use of Nvidia GPUs from within podman containers.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.extraPackages
documents.content: Extra dependencies for podman to be placed on $PATH in the wrapper.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.extraRuntimes
documents.content: Extra runtime packages to be installed in the Podman wrapper. Those are then placed in libexec/podman, i.e. are seen as podman internal commands.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.networkSocket.enable
documents.content:
Make the Podman and Docker compatibility API available over the network with TLS client certificate authentication.
This allows Docker clients to connect with the equivalents of the Docker CLI -H and --tls* family of options.
For certificate setup, see https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/protect-access/
This option is independent of .

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.networkSocket.listenAddress
documents.content: Interface address for receiving TLS connections.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.networkSocket.openFirewall
documents.content: Whether to open the port in the firewall.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.networkSocket.port
documents.content: TCP port number for receiving TLS connections.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.networkSocket.server
documents.content: Choice of TLS proxy server.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.networkSocket.tls.cacert
documents.content: Path to CA certificate to use for client authentication.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.networkSocket.tls.cert
documents.content: Path to certificate describing the server.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.networkSocket.tls.key
documents.content:
Path to the private key corresponding to the server certificate.
Use a string for this setting. Otherwise it will be copied to the Nix store first, where it is readable by any system process.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.podman.package
documents.content: The podman package to use. This package will automatically include extra packages and runtimes.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.rosetta.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable Rosetta support.
This feature requires the system to be a virtualised guest on an Apple silicon host.
The default settings are suitable for the UTM virtualisation package. Make sure to select 'Apple Virtualization' as the virtualisation engine and then tick the 'Enable Rosetta' option.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.rosetta.mountTag
documents.content:
The VirtioFS mount tag for the Rosetta runtime, exposed by the host's virtualisation software.
If supported, your virtualisation software should provide instructions on how register the Rosetta runtime inside Linux guests. These instructions should mention the name of the mount tag used for the VirtioFS directory share that contains the Rosetta runtime.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.spiceUSBRedirection.enable
documents.content: Install the SPICE USB redirection helper with setuid privileges. This allows unprivileged users to pass USB devices connected to this machine to libvirt VMs, both local and remote. Note that this allows users arbitrary access to USB devices.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.guest.clipboard
documents.content: Whether to enable clipboard support.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.guest.dragAndDrop
documents.content: Whether to enable drag and drop support.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.guest.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the VirtualBox service and other guest additions.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.guest.seamless
documents.content: Whether to enable seamless mode. When activated windows from the guest appear next to the windows of the host.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.guest.use3rdPartyModules
documents.content: Whether to use the kernel modules provided by VirtualBox instead of the ones from the upstream kernel.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.guest.vboxsf
documents.content: Whether to load vboxsf

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.guest.verbose
documents.content: Whether to verbose logging for guest services.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.host.addNetworkInterface
documents.content: Automatically set up a vboxnet0 host-only network interface.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.host.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable VirtualBox.
::: {.note} In order to pass USB devices from the host to the guests, the user needs to be in the vboxusers group. :::

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.host.enableExtensionPack
documents.content:
Whether to install the Oracle Extension Pack for VirtualBox.
::: {.important} You must set nixpkgs.config.allowUnfree = true in order to use this. This requires you accept the VirtualBox PUEL. :::

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.host.enableHardening
documents.content:
Enable hardened VirtualBox, which ensures that only the binaries in the system path get access to the devices exposed by the kernel modules instead of all users in the vboxusers group.
::: {.important} Disabling this can put your system's security at risk, as local users in the vboxusers group can tamper with the VirtualBox device files. :::

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.host.enableKvm
documents.content:
Enable KVM support for VirtualBox. This increases compatibility with Linux kernel versions, because the VirtualBox kernel modules are not required.
This option is incompatible with addNetworkInterface.
Note: This is experimental. Please check https://github.com/cyberus-technology/virtualbox-kvm/issues.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.host.enableWebService
documents.content: Build VirtualBox web service tool (vboxwebsrv) to allow managing VMs via other webpage frontend tools. Useful for headless servers.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.host.headless
documents.content: Use VirtualBox installation without GUI and Qt dependency. Useful to enable on servers and when virtual machines are controlled only via SSH.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.virtualbox.host.package
documents.content: The virtualbox package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vmVariant
documents.content: Machine configuration to be added for the vm script produced by nixos-rebuild build-vm.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vmVariantWithBootLoader
documents.content: Machine configuration to be added for the vm script produced by nixos-rebuild build-vm-with-bootloader.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vmware.guest.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable VMWare Guest Support.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vmware.guest.headless
documents.content: Whether to disable X11-related features.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vmware.guest.package
documents.content: Package providing open-vm-tools.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vmware.host.enable
documents.content:
This enables VMware host virtualisation for running VMs.
::: {.important} vmware-vmx will cause kcompactd0 due to Transparent Hugepages feature in kernel. Apply [ "transparent_hugepage=never" ] in option {option}boot.kernelParams to disable them. :::
::: {.note} If that didn't work disable TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE, COMPACTION configs and recompile kernel. :::

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vmware.host.extraConfig
documents.content: Add extra config to /etc/vmware/config

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vmware.host.extraPackages
documents.content: Extra packages to be used with VMware host.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vmware.host.package
documents.content: The vmware-workstation package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vswitch.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Open vSwitch. A configuration daemon (ovs-server) will be started.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vswitch.package
documents.content: The openvswitch package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vswitch.resetOnStart
documents.content: Whether to reset the Open vSwitch configuration database to a default configuration on every start of the systemd ovsdb.service.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.waydroid.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Waydroid.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.waydroid.package
documents.content: The waydroid package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.boot.bios.path
documents.content: Path to the Xen multiboot binary used for BIOS booting. Unless you're building your own Xen derivation, you should leave this option as the default value.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.boot.builderVerbosity
documents.content:
The boot entry builder script should be called with exactly one of the following arguments in order to specify its verbosity:
quiet supresses all messages.
default adds a simple "Installing Xen Project Hypervisor boot entries...done." message to the script.
info is the same as default, but it also prints a diff with information on which generations were altered.
This option adds two extra dependencies to the script: diffutils and bat.

debug prints information messages for every single step of the script.

This option does not alter the actual functionality of the script, just the number of messages printed when rebuilding the system.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.boot.efi.path
documents.content: Path to xen.efi. pkgs.xen is patched to install the xen.efi file on $boot/boot/xen.efi, but an unpatched Xen build may install it somewhere else, such as $out/boot/efi/efi/nixos/xen.efi. Unless you're building your own Xen derivation, you should leave this option as the default value.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.boot.params
documents.content:
Xen Command Line parameters passed to Domain 0 at boot time.
::: {.note} Note: these are different from {option}boot.kernelParams. See the Xen documentation for more information. :::

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.debug
documents.content: Whether to enable Xen debug features for Domain 0. This option enables some hidden debugging tests and features, and should not be used in production.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.dom0Resources.maxMemory
documents.content: Maximum amount of memory (in MiB) that Domain 0 can dynamically allocate to itself. Does nothing if set to the same amount as virtualisation.xen.memory, or if that option is set to 0.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.dom0Resources.maxVCPUs
documents.content: Amount of virtual CPU cores allocated to Domain 0 on boot. If set to 0, all cores are assigned to Domain 0, and unprivileged domains will compete with Domain 0 for CPU time.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.dom0Resources.memory
documents.content: Amount of memory (in MiB) allocated to Domain 0 on boot. If set to 0, all memory is assigned to Domain 0, and unprivileged domains will compete with Domain 0 for free RAM.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.domains.extraConfig
documents.content: Options defined here will override the defaults for xendomains. The default options can be seen in the file included from /etc/default/xendomains.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the Xen Project Hypervisor, a virtualisation technology defined as a type-1 hypervisor, which allows multiple virtual machines, known as domains, to run concurrently on the physical machine. NixOS runs as the privileged Domain 0. This option requires a reboot into a Xen kernel to take effect.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.package
documents.content: The Xen Hypervisor package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.qemu.package
documents.content: The QEMU (with Xen Hypervisor support) package to use.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.qemu.pidFile
documents.content: Path to the QEMU PID file.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.path
documents.content: Path to the Xen Store Daemon. This option is useful to switch between the legacy C-based Xen Store Daemon, and the newer OCaml-based Xen Store Daemon, oxenstored.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings
documents.content: The OCaml-based Xen Store Daemon configuration. This option does nothing with the C-based xenstored.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.conflict.burstLimit
documents.content:
Limits applied to domains whose writes cause other domains' transaction commits to fail. Must include decimal point.
The burst limit is the number of conflicts a domain can cause to fail in a short period; this value is used for both the initial and the maximum value of each domain's conflict-credit, which falls by one point for each conflict caused, and when it reaches zero the domain's requests are ignored.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.conflict.maxHistorySeconds
documents.content:
Limits applied to domains whose writes cause other domains' transaction commits to fail. Must include decimal point.
The conflict-credit is replenished over time: one point is issued after each conflict.maxHistorySeconds, so this is the minimum pause-time during which a domain will be ignored.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.conflict.rateLimitIsAggregate
documents.content:
If the conflict.rateLimitIsAggregate option is true, then after each tick one point of conflict-credit is given to just one domain: the one at the front of the queue. If false, then after each tick each domain gets a point of conflict-credit.
In environments where it is known that every transaction will involve a set of nodes that is writable by at most one other domain, then it is safe to set this aggregate limit flag to false for better performance. (This can be determined by considering the layout of the xenstore tree and permissions, together with the content of the transactions that require protection.)
A transaction which involves a set of nodes which can be modified by multiple other domains can suffer conflicts caused by any of those domains, so the flag must be set to true.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.enableMerge
documents.content: Whether to enable transaction merge support.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.perms.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the node permission system.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.perms.enableWatch
documents.content:
Whether to enable the watch permission system.
When this is set to true, unprivileged guests can only get watch events for xenstore entries that they would've been able to read.
When this is set to false, unprivileged guests may get watch events for xenstore entries that they cannot read. The watch event contains only the entry name, not the value. This restores behaviour prior to XSA-115.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.persistent
documents.content: Whether to activate the filed base backend.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.pidFile
documents.content: Path to the Xen Store Daemon PID file.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.quota.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the quota system.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.quota.maxEntity
documents.content: Entity limit for transactions.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.quota.maxOutstanding
documents.content: Maximum outstanding requests, i.e. in-flight requests / domain.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.quota.maxPath
documents.content: Path limit for the quota system.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.quota.maxRequests
documents.content: Maximum number of requests per transaction.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.quota.maxSize
documents.content: Size limit for transactions.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.quota.maxWatch
documents.content: Maximum number of watches by the Xenstore Watchdog.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.quota.maxWatchEvents
documents.content: Maximum number of outstanding watch events per watch.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.quota.transaction
documents.content: Maximum number of transactions.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.ringScanInterval
documents.content: Perodic scanning for all the rings as a safenet for lazy clients. Define the interval in seconds; set to a negative integer to disable.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.xenstored.accessLog.file
documents.content: Path to the Xen Store access log file.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.xenstored.log.file
documents.content: Path to the Xen Store log file.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.store.settings.xenstored.log.level
documents.content: Logging level for the Xen Store.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.xen.trace
documents.content: Whether to enable Xen debug tracing and logging for Domain 0.

documents.title: Option: xdg.autostart.enable
documents.content: Whether to install files to support the XDG Autostart specification.

documents.title: Option: xdg.icons.enable
documents.content: Whether to install files to support the XDG Icon Theme specification.

documents.title: Option: xdg.icons.fallbackCursorThemes
documents.content: Names of the fallback cursor themes, in order of preference, to be used when no other icon source can be found. Set to [] to disable the fallback entirely.

documents.title: Option: xdg.menus.enable
documents.content: Whether to install files to support the XDG Desktop Menu specification.

documents.title: Option: xdg.mime.addedAssociations
documents.content: Adds associations between mimetypes and applications. See the specifications for more information. Globs in all variations are supported.

documents.title: Option: xdg.mime.defaultApplications
documents.content: Sets the default applications for given mimetypes. See the specifications for more information. Globs in all variations are supported.

documents.title: Option: xdg.mime.enable
documents.content: Whether to install files to support the XDG Shared MIME-info specification and the XDG MIME Applications specification.

documents.title: Option: xdg.mime.removedAssociations
documents.content: Removes associations between mimetypes and applications. See the specifications for more information. Globs in all variations are supported.

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.config
documents.content:
Sets which portal backend should be used to provide the implementation for the requested interface. For details check {manpage}portals.conf(5).
Configs will be linked to {file}/etc/xdg/xdg-desktop-portal/ with the name {file}$desktop-portals.conf for {file}xdg.portal.config.$desktop and {file}portals.conf for {file}xdg.portal.config.common as an exception.

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.configPackages
documents.content:
List of packages that provide XDG desktop portal configuration, usually in the form of {file}share/xdg-desktop-portal/$desktop-portals.conf.
Note that configs in xdg.portal.config will be preferred if set.

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable xdg desktop integration.

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.extraPortals
documents.content: List of additional portals to add to path. Portals allow interaction with system, like choosing files or taking screenshots. At minimum, a desktop portal implementation should be listed. GNOME and KDE already adds xdg-desktop-portal-gtk; and xdg-desktop-portal-kde respectively. On other desktop environments you probably want to add them yourself.

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.lxqt.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable the desktop portal for the LXQt desktop environment.
This will add the lxqt.xdg-desktop-portal-lxqt package (with the extra Qt styles) into the {option}xdg.portal.extraPortals option .

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.lxqt.styles
documents.content: Extra Qt styles that will be available to the lxqt.xdg-desktop-portal-lxqt.

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.wlr.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable desktop portal for wlroots-based desktops.
This will add the xdg-desktop-portal-wlr package into the {option}xdg.portal.extraPortals option, and provide the configuration file .

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.wlr.settings
documents.content:
Configuration for xdg-desktop-portal-wlr.
See {manpage}xdg-desktop-portal-wlr(5) for supported values.

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.xdgOpenUsePortal
documents.content: Sets environment variable NIXOS_XDG_OPEN_USE_PORTAL to 1 This will make xdg-open use the portal to open programs, which resolves bugs involving programs opening inside FHS envs or with unexpected env vars set from wrappers. See #160923 for more info.

documents.title: Option: xdg.sounds.enable
documents.content: Whether to install files to support the XDG Sound Theme specification.

documents.title: Option: xdg.terminal-exec.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable xdg-terminal-exec, the proposed Default Terminal Execution Specification.

documents.title: Option: xdg.terminal-exec.package
documents.content: The xdg-terminal-exec package to use.

documents.title: Option: xdg.terminal-exec.settings
documents.content:
Configuration options for the Default Terminal Execution Specification.
The keys are the desktop environments that are matched (case-insensitively) against $XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP, or default which is used when the current desktop environment is not found in the configuration. The values are a list of terminals' desktop file IDs to try in order of decreasing priority.

documents.title: Option: zramSwap.algorithm
documents.content: Compression algorithm. lzo has good compression, but is slow. lz4 has bad compression, but is fast. zstd is both good compression and fast, but requires newer kernel. You can check what other algorithms are supported by your zram device with {command}cat /sys/class/block/zram*/comp_algorithm

documents.title: Option: zramSwap.enable
documents.content: Enable in-memory compressed devices and swap space provided by the zram kernel module. See https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/blockdev/zram.txt .

documents.title: Option: zramSwap.memoryMax
documents.content: Maximum total amount of memory (in bytes) that can be stored in the zram swap devices. If set, the smaller one of this option and memoryPercent would be used. This doesn't define how much memory will be used by the zram swap devices.

documents.title: Option: zramSwap.memoryPercent
documents.content: Maximum total amount of memory that can be stored in the zram swap devices (as a percentage of your total memory). Defaults to 1/2 of your total RAM. Run zramctl to check how good memory is compressed. This doesn't define how much memory will be used by the zram swap devices.

documents.title: Option: zramSwap.priority
documents.content: Priority of the zram swap devices. It should be a number higher than the priority of your disk-based swap devices (so that the system will fill the zram swap devices before falling back to disk swap).

documents.title: Option: zramSwap.swapDevices
documents.content: Number of zram devices to be used as swap, recommended is 1.

documents.title: Option: zramSwap.writebackDevice
documents.content: Write incompressible pages to this device, as there's no gain from keeping them in RAM.
